#413. The Psychology Behind “Overreacting”

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (918 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

The Psychology Behind “Overreacting”

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • According to recent reports, couples don’t break up because they argue.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever thought, “We just can’t communicate,” you might be asking the wrong question.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

According to recent reports, couples don’t break up because they argue. They break up because they feel alone while arguing.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever thought, “We just can’t communicate,” you might be asking the wrong question. The real puzzle isn’t why couples fight. It’s this: Why do people who love each other deeply end up triggering each other so consistently?

It has been revealed that emotionally focused therapy (EFT), an empirically-supported model of couple therapy grounded in attachment science, offers a clear answer: Love is not a negotiation problem; it's a bonding problem (Johnson, 2020). More than three decades of research have established EFT as an effective, evidence-based approach for helping couples move from distress to secure connection (Johnson, 2020). And bonding is biological.

Industry observers note that attachment theory, originally developed by Bowlby (1969, 1982) and extended to adult relationships (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2007), conceptualizes close relationships as emotional bonds that regulate safety, distress, and connection. In this framework, romantic partners become primary attachment figures; people we turn to for reassurance, comfort, and security in moments of stress (Johnson, 2019).

According to recent reports, when your partner turns away mid-argument, your brain doesn’t process it as a small irritation but as a threat. From an attachment perspective, humans are wired to seek emotional closeness in moments of distress. When connection feels unavailable, the nervous system activates what researchers call protest behaviors: anger, criticism, defensiveness, or withdrawal (Johnson, 2008).These responses don't reflect character flaws; they're adaptive survival strategies. Attachment research shows that these emotional reactions are part of an evolved system designed to keep us connected (Bowlby, 1969, 1982; Johnson, 2019). What looks like “drama” is often attachment fear.

In a recent development, we often tell couples to improve their communication by using “I” statements, remaining calm, and compromising. This advice can help but it's not enough. Communication skills do not regulate an activated attachment system. When someone fears abandonment, logic does not soothe them. When someone fears inadequacy, confrontation feels threatening.Lasting change in relationships doesn't occur in arguments. A growing body of EFT outcome research indicates that it occurs through emotional responsiveness—the experience of reaching for a partner and having them respond (Johnson, 2020).Secure love develops when the answer to the question “Are you there for me?” is consistently yes (Johnson, 2008). Without that, technique feels empty.

Attachment unfolds within social systems. Couples live inside structures shaped by race, gender, immigration status, class, sexuality, and power. These contexts shape how safe, or unsafe, connection feels.Recent developments in EFT and related relational frameworks highlight that attachment experiences are deeply influenced by sociocultural realities, including trauma, marginalization, and systemic inequality (Johnson & Campbell, 2022). When one partner has experienced chronic marginalization, their attachment system may be more easily activated. What appears as “oversensitivity” may reflect accumulated threat. Emotional safety is not only created within the relationship; it is also shaped by the world outside it. Dismissing a partner’s lived experience can represent rupture.

The turning point in attachment-based therapy occurs when partners risk vulnerability instead of protection. Instead of saying, “You never care about me," they say things like, “When you walk away, I feel scared that I don’t matter.” Instead of telling a partner they're "too sensitive," they say, “I didn’t realize you felt alone. I don’t want you to feel that way.” These are vital communication—and attachment—shifts.

According to recent reports, process research in EFT reveals that when vulnerability is met with responsiveness, the attachment bond reorganizes, creating a sense of safety and reducing emotional reactivity (Johnson, 2020). The nervous system learns that closeness is safe, and love becomes a regulator rather than a trigger.

Industry observers note that we live in a culture that glorifies independence. We are taught that strong adults should not “need” anyone, that reliance is weakness, and that self-sufficiency is maturity. Attachment science tells a different story: Humans are wired for interdependence. Emotional closeness is not regression but regulation (Johnson, 2019). And secure relationships are built on accessibility, responsiveness, and engagement. Needing a partner is not dysfunction; it's biology.

Love falters when fear replaces responsiveness. The research is clear: Secure love isn’t built on turning toward each other when it would be easier to turn away (Johnson, 2020). In a culture that prizes independence, emotional responsiveness may be one of the most radical acts we can practice.

It has been revealed that carlota Azpiazu Osorio, is a registered marriage and family therapist associate at Pacifica Group in San Francisco, California. Her clinical work is grounded in emotionally focused therapy (EFT), attachment theory, trauma-informed care, and family systems approaches, with a particular focus on helping individuals and couples strengthen relationships and develop more secure emotional connections.

#412. How Music Can Help Us Move Through Climate Anxiety

How Music Can Help Us Move Through Climate Anxiety

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.
  • In November, at the WHO Health Pavilion at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, a packed room of climate scientists and policymakers got to their feet and danced.
  • Many of us know the opposite feeling: another headline about record heat or flooding, a jolt of dread, and we scroll on, more alone with it than before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

In November, at the WHO Health Pavilion at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, a packed room of climate scientists and policymakers got to their feet and danced. On stage, a collective of women musicians played songs built from the sounds of water: melting glaciers, swollen rivers, rising seas. After two weeks of talk about emissions, clean energy, and finance, the climate crisis stopped being something we discussed and became something we felt, together, in our bodies.

Many of us know the opposite feeling: another headline about record heat or flooding, a jolt of dread, and we scroll on, more alone with it than before. Climate anxiety is a reasonable response to a real threat, but carried alone, it paralyzes us. In that room, something moved.

In a recent development, most people do not experience climate change as a graph. It is intense heat, difficult breathing, and worries about water: too little, too much, or whether it’s safe to drink. Women often carry the heaviest load, as do indigenous peoples, long keepers of these waters.

This COP also put health on the agenda by opening with a health day. The numbers explain why: The Lancet Countdown links fossil fuels and climate change to an estimated 3.3 million deaths a year from air pollution and extreme heat alone. The toll on our minds is harder to count, but it is just as real. Heat disrupts sleep and attention, and the slow dread of what is coming shows up as anxiety and paralysis. A WHO Europe report released during the summit, Strengthening Mental Health in a Changing Climate, links floods and wildfires to anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress, and calls for mental health to be part of climate policy.

Recent findings suggest that what helps? The WHO report looked at 20 interventions in 15 countries. Most aimed to build resilience and agency close to where people live. Agency is exactly what the arts can help people find. Art speaks human.

As a drama therapist and scientist, I am interested in how art can help us—projects using music, storytelling, and film to amplify the climate emergency. This isn’t therapy per se, but it draws on the same processes that creative arts therapists use with clients: giving form to hard-to-name feelings, and sharing them so they become bearable. It does two things that research and practice keep pointing to.

In a recent development, it invites people in as authors. Each artist found her own way into water. People engage differently when they are recognized as experts in their own lives.

Sources indicate that it turns feeling into connection. In a survey of 10,000 young people in 10 countries, 59 percent were very or extremely worried about climate change. In my clinical work and in the classroom, I see people shut down when fear and grief have nowhere to go. Music gives those feelings a shared rhythm.

There is good reason to think this helps. Eco-anxiety is closely tied to difficulty regulating emotions, and a meta-analysis of controlled studies found that listening to music reduces anxiety. In a study that followed adults over three years, those who increasingly turned to music to manage their emotions also became more likely to tackle problems head-on. Music doesn’t only soothe. It can help us act.

"When we are emotionally and empathetically tied to the natural world, we are reminded at a more profound, instinctive level of our interdependence with it."—Yo-Yo Ma, in Music and Mind, edited by Renée Fleming.

According to recent reports, this echoes what my colleagues and I found in developing the WHO Europe-Jameel Arts & Health Lab policy brief on the role of the arts and culture in addressing the health impacts of climate change, and it reinforces findings from the first Culture Global Stocktake for Climate Action, also released at COP31. Culture and cultural practices reflect and shape what we value, and it can build the trust and belonging that help people act on what they know.

Industry observers note that listen to these sounds of nature. Then ask yourself: what is your relationship to water where you live? What would it take to protect it, together? Then let the listening lead somewhere. Review these six acts for water that help us move from feeling to understanding to action:.

● Learn how much water your daily life uses.

● Adopt a few water-saving habits.

● Go deeper with films and talks from communities living with water crises.

● Join a group protecting rivers and oceans.

● Find out how you can help restore local wetlands, streams, and soils.

It has been revealed that ● Share your story. Make something with what comes up: a sketch, a few lines, a song. It doesn't have to be good.

If you work with young people or adults, try that last act as a group. Try a simple structure: open in a circle where people name what they feel; write a short song together from a local challenge, a mood, and a beat; perform it; then reflect on creating together rather than alone.

What I saw in Antalya gives me hope: a room full of committed people discovered they could still be moved, and could still move together. In my experience, hope is less a feeling we wait for than something we practice with others. The futures we can feel together are the ones we begin to build.

How Becoming a Parent Can Change Your Memories of Your Own Parents

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it was around Christmas time when Emily* noticed that something was wrong. She had just welcomed her second son in September and still felt emotionally raw from the experience. Part of Emily’s postpartum planning had revolved around having her mum look after her three-year-old while she took care of the fresh baby. But every time she visited her parents, something in her tensed up, her mind went foggy, and instead of feeling the safety and relaxation she had been craving, she felt on edge.

Emily sought help from me in therapy just before Christmas when she realized that the prospect of spending the holidays with her parents was making it difficult for her to sleep and the few precious hours she had between feeds were taken up with anxious rumination. She couldn’t make any sense of it. It was like a switch had flipped and the previously supportive, albeit slightly emotionally disconnected, relationship she had had with her parents was in pieces.

I work a lot with mothers and birthing people in the perinatal phase, and the change they experience in their relationship with their parents is something that comes up very frequently. Sometimes this change is positive, where they become more understanding of parents who were trying their best at the time. Sometimes it’s disorienting, like Emily’s, and the relationship seems to worsen. Either way, it’s important to meet yourself with compassion and curiosity when unexpected feelings or memories resurface during this period of your life and try not to go through this transition on your own.

Sources indicate that emily came to see me for help with anxiety and insomnia, and a few sessions into our therapy she started to talk about memories that had been appearing for her, scenes from her childhood that suddenly had taken on fresh meaning or had popped up out of nowhere. It was as if her memories had changed, which made Emily feel crazy and even more anxious because she felt like she couldn’t trust herself anymore.

In the crudest terms, we tend to think of memory as a filing cabinet—a place where scenes, facts, annoying songs, and embarrassing moments are stored to be recalled, like when we try to remember what we had for dinner last week or where we went on holiday three years ago.

In a recent development, when I talk about memory with my clients, they usually understand that it is not a perfect system, that it can alter over time and be very subjective. What is harder to convey is that decades of research suggest that memory is not in fact a filing cabinet or a library catalogue—it’s a construction. Every time I try to remember where we went on holiday three summers ago, my brain doesn’t retrieve but rather constructs a memory of our trip to Italy. That means that each time we recall something, that memory can change slightly or take on new meaning. Researchers Daniel L. Schacter and Donna Rose Addis found that, in fact, remembering and imagining look very similar in terms of activation in the brain.

According to recent reports, why does that matter? It can help make sense of what happened to Emily and what happens to many of my clients when they become parents and their relationships with their own parents change. Some of this is explained by a shift in roles: When a child becomes a parent, the dynamic of the child-parent relationship naturally has to change, which can be difficult for both parties. Grandparents and upcoming parents might find it challenging to adapt to who is in charge and “who knows best.” But sometimes the difficulty is more subtle, and it’s related to memory.

Recent findings suggest that emily struggled because she had started to have visceral memories of herself at about three to five years old, even though she had never actively thought about her childhood much before. She associated that phase in her life with a feeling of paralysis that she couldn’t explain. She told me how exhausted she felt every time she left her parents’ house now, like she had been holding her breath for hours.

Emily knew from whispered family stories that her mother had dealt with bouts of depression through much of her childhood. She also knew that her parents’ marriage hadn’t always been as placid and quiet as it was now. She had always had memories of them fighting late at night but had never thought much of it. Now she remembered her mother in tears, shouting and doors slamming. She remembered hiding under her bed.

Memory is heavily influenced by our current state of mind. Martin Conway, in his papers on autobiographical memory, explains that when we try to retrieve a memory or remember something spontaneously, we construct that memory in the moment, partly based on our current goals. If we are hungry, we might construct a memory of a cafe we saw on our walk two weeks ago. If we have a fight with our partner, we might suddenly remember all the times they disappointed us, when we usually are able to accept their imperfections.

When Emily became a parent, her goals changed dramatically, and it changed what memories her brain predicted might be useful for her.

Articles that explore holiday stress management, managing conflict, picking gifts, making resolutions, and more.

According to recent reports, emily realized that her experience of being her son’s age was one of bracing and zoning out because she had felt disconnected from her mother and scared of her father at the time. As a parent, Emily was suddenly able to attune to what it felt like for her to be three years old. Her three-year-old self did not feel safe, and she did not believe her child was safe, either.

Conway notes that the memories we are able to construct have to be coherent with how we think of ourselves, our beliefs about ourselves, and the world and people in it. According to Conway’s theory, our brains filter, rationalize, or dismiss memories that are inconsistent with who we believe we are.

It has been revealed that before Emily had children, she believed, largely unconsciously, that her childhood experiences were irrelevant to who she was and that she hadn’t really been affected by them. When she became a mum, her visceral memories of childhood fear did not match up with who she believed she was anymore. Her goals had changed from surviving and rationalizing to tuning in to and protecting her child. Her brain was telling her she had to shield her child from something that she had experienced as frightening as a child.

Other clients of mine have found that becoming a parent had the opposite effect. They were able to look at the younger versions of their parents with more compassion and kindness, reconstructing memories through the eyes of an exhausted parent who was trying and barely coping.

It has been revealed that karen and her parents had had a difficult relationship. Karen’s parents divorced when she was young, and Karen had always felt her mother had been unavailable when she was a child. She experienced a lot of anger when thinking about her childhood. She had memories of having to take on responsibilities too early, looking after her siblings, and cooking and cleaning while her mother was at work. Karen had purposefully moved away from her parents and had spent years asserting her independence. She had never wanted children because she had such strong memories of what it had been like to be a young caretaker and not being able to feel like a child. When she met her husband, she realized that creating her own family was more key to her than she had thought.

In a recent development, karen came to see me for anxiety. She was worried about losing her freedom when she became a mother, and we thought about how her childhood experiences shaped her experience now. I saw Karen for quite some time after she gave birth, and something shifted for her when she became a parent. She remembered instances of seeing her mother frazzled, rushed, and overwhelmed and how hard she had tried to find time to be there for Karen and her siblings. Karen started to realize how impossible it must have been for her mother to raise three children on her own while working.

Karen tried to talk to her mother and learned about how ashamed she was for burdening her daughter and unsure about whether Karen wanted her in her life. To her surprise, Karen experienced her mother’s relationship with her own daughter as reparative. She could make sense of her anger and her need for freedom and see that what happened in her childhood was not something her mother had intended.

Recent findings suggest that for Emily, too, her experiences meant she had to rebuild the relationship with her mother and find a more honest foundation. She was able to have conversations with her about what it would have been like for Emily growing up, and, to Emily’s surprise, her mother also listened and apologized for not having checked in with her sooner. It started a healing process for Emily that involved listening to what her three-year-old self might have felt and acknowledging that she had been trying to rationalize her way out of feeling for most of her life. She had to slowly let herself experience that her parents were safe now; she decided to not rely on them for child care but let the relationship grow more slowly.

Sources indicate that what helped Emily was hearing her mother validate what happened to her as a child. It was something Emily would have needed when she was younger. She was also able to make latest meaning of her relationship with her parents through therapy—an act of shared social construction with another human, the therapist, that fulfills some of our core needs of being heard, seen, and understood.

Industry observers note that karen similarly needed to feel heard by her mother. Her anger dissipated when she was able to put herself into her mother’s shoes and see that her and her mother’s experience could exist side by side.

What can you do if parenthood is shifting your relationship with your own parents? Here are steps that I have found are helpful for my clients.

Sources indicate that find support. The first step in coping with a difficult experience is to not try to go through it alone. We are social beings who need to feel understood by others. Seek out a friend or a sibling if you are struggling with feelings you do not understand.

Meet yourself with self-compassion. When strong emotions come up, we might tell ourselves, “I’m overreacting,” “I’m too sensitive,” “I just need to get on with things and stop complaining.” Self-criticism can perpetuate a cycle in which we invalidate our experiences until they become impossible to ignore. It also won’t help to be overly critical of yourself if you believe you’ve been judging your parents too harshly, now that you have the perspective of being a parent yourself.

Seek out conversations. If thinking back on your childhood memories brings up a perspective change on your childhood, speak to your family, your parents or siblings, and learn about how they experienced that time and you as a child. It might help you feel more compassion with your parents who may have been struggling, and can also help you understand yourself better as a person.

According to recent reports, set boundaries, if needed. If memories from your childhood suddenly take on latest meaning, it might be important to think about boundaries and clear rules to set with your child’s grandparents. If you felt unsafe or uncomfortable as a child, it is OK to make it clear how you expect the adults in your child’s life to behave. This can, of course, be easier noted than done, and it can be useful to seek help to deal with feelings of guilt or anxiety around setting boundaries with your parents.

Sources indicate that seek out professional help. Remember that every experience is subjective—your version of what happened might be different from that of your siblings or your parents. That does not make it any less valid. While Emily was lucky that her mother acknowledged her experience, your family members might not always be so receptive and might be more defensive about any wrongdoing. Seeking professional help can be especially useful when you are dealing with a family system that is less likely to take responsibility or want to change.

Becoming a parent changes your world in a thousand ways and can dramatically alter the way you look at your own childhood. Self-compassion is hugely vital in navigating all the transformations you might go through as a new parent. Finding others that meet you with understanding and care is the first step in making sure you can meet yourself and your child in the same way.

*The stories in this article are a combination of experiences of several clients; any identifying information has been changed.

Sarah Emmerson, PsychD, is a chartered counseling psychologist and cofounder of Talking Women, a private psychology practice in London specializing in women's mental health.

How Thinking Outcomes Can Be More Key Than Being Right

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • A few months back, I wrote a piece here about the viral conspiracy that Earth would lose gravity for 7 seconds on August 12th.
  • Recent findings suggest that the latter cohort, I believe, missed my point, and so I aim to make it clearer in this follow-up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

A few months back, I wrote a piece here about the viral conspiracy that Earth would lose gravity for 7 seconds on August 12th. I discussed how, despite not actually believing that the event would occur—because of a slew of reasons—the open-minded part of me (albeit still skeptical) nevertheless suggested developing a quick “just in case” protocol for the unlikely event. I received some positive feedback on how I exemplified the importance of cautious thinking throughout the piece and how, in context, we can engage two important dispositions towards thinking (Dwyer et al., 2016): open-mindedness and skepticism. On the other hand, though, some implied a level of foolishness in my thinking.

Recent findings suggest that the latter cohort, I believe, missed my point, and so I aim to make it clearer in this follow-up. In that previous piece, I stated on multiple occasions that I didn’t actually believe the event would occur. In fact, I highlighted why it was nearly impossible.

But I used this event prediction as an example to make the point that cautious thinkers are typically happy to make minor mistakes in efforts to avoid risk, even if the risk is extremely low. That is, through cost-benefit analysis (consistent with many existing cost-benefit models we commonly see in psychology; e.g. Lave and March 1975; Thibaut and Kelley 1959; Uehara 1990), good thinkers may often choose a 99 percent likely mistake made out of caution, if the mistake yields minimal negative impact (e.g., looking foolish in front of one’s spouse). This will be selected over doing nothing potentially “foolish” (e.g., in light of being 99 percent “sure”), despite the disastrous impact that 1 percent chance would have because they failed to act (e.g., if the event occurred, death would be a near certainty if we were outdoors).

It has been revealed that simply, good thinkers don’t care about labels of wrong or right; they care about the outcomes of their decisions. It’s cautious thinking… and critical thinkers are cautious thinkers.

It’s much like hope for the best, proposal for the worst. It’s why we develop contingency prepares; it’s why we buy insurance. It’s largely why I don’t go outside in a thunderstorm, despite the odds against getting hit by lightning. It’s why I buy a lotto ticket once every few weeks, when the thought occurs to me on the day of a draw (i.e., I will not notice the loss of a couple of euros [thankfully], whereas winning the lotto would be life-changing). You never know.

According to recent reports, with that, context (as well as moderation) is key. It might be foolish to buy too much insurance, to spend €200 weekly on the lotto, or to waste your time hiding in a cellar for three hours during your run-of-the-mill thunderstorm. Again, caution is considered in terms of cost (be it time, money, or status) relative to benefit or risk avoidance.

According to recent reports, from an epistemological perspective, an established truth is that we cannot see into the future (as of yet, anyway [there’s some doozy of a meta-joke in there]). We do not know what’s going to happen. Objectively, we can place likelihoods on certain events happening, but that’s it. It’s our human interpretation that labels these probabilities as impossible, unlikely, possible, likely, highly probable, definite, etc. We might say definite, but that’s not exactly a guarantee. Consider the late Daniel Kahneman’s work on weather and stock forecasting (see also Kahneman, 2011). If we lived in a world of certainty (which we don’t), you’d never hear the phrase, “Well, that was unexpected.”.

In moments of excitement and uncertainty, good thinkers are able to rapidly evaluate probabilities, not just in terms of odds, but in terms of interpretation of outcomes (e.g., consider naturalistic decision-making [Klein, 2008]). The ability to do this quickly is a result of previous consideration and reflective judgment on priorities and values—things for which good thinkers would be concerned and cautious. They apply these considerations efficiently, if and when they need to. For example, despite less than a half-percent chance of your school burning down during your tenure in that school, how many fire drills were you a part of as a student? A lot, right? But you knew what to do in case it was for real.

In a recent development, bizarrely, what’s your strategy for a zombie apocalypse? Stop for a moment and think about it... Did your answer come to you fairly rapidly? Even in the extreme unlikelihood of such a thing happening, it’s likely you thought about it or something similar before, at least once.

There’s nothing wrong with considering such things. Planning in such a way is a good cognitive exercise. It’s also good for creativity!

It has been revealed that cautious people often think in similar ways. Such cautious thinking might get accused of being “overthinking.” But that’s not necessarily a bad thing, unless it becomes a common or costly focus. Indeed, catastrophizing can be problematic. Moderation is vital. But so too is caution, especially when it comes to ensuring good outcome-focused thinking. So, don’t sweat making small mistakes in life, especially if it’s done out of calculated caution. There’s nothing foolish about it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

Recent findings suggest that each Thanksgiving, nearly 1.3 million Americans participate in a Turkey Trot, typically a morning run with a cute name and sometimes a cute T-shirt. With over 1,500 events organized each year, Thanksgiving is officially the biggest race day of the year. And why do people wake up early on a holiday, when school and work are closed, to run in the cold?

According to recent reports, AI will give you plenty of reasons: family bonding, charity, or just dodging kitchen duty. But the real reason most people lace up in the freezing cold? To “earn the feast.” It sounds like an innocent joke, but clinically, treating movement as currency to pre-pay for calories is known as compensatory exercise. When workouts become a tool to cancel out guilt, research shows, it stops being healthy movement and starts predicting disordered eating.

I want to push back on the idea that we need a psychological pass for a holiday meal.

According to recent reports, food is many things: fuel, culture, comfort, and community. And, holistically, culture, comfort, and community can all be pleasurable. Americans have a complex relationship with pleasure; we’re always vacillating over whether pleasure is a human right or a thing to be earned.

We all know, or maybe have been, the friend who cannot (insert something fun) until they’ve zeroed their inbox, cleaned the house, or crossed off the to-do list, and somehow we never quite balance the books. Whether we forgo the fun or dilute it with guilt, we never think we’ve done enough to earn our relaxation.

This issue of feeling undeserving of pleasure comes up in so many therapy sessions. Trying to leave a bad relationship—do I deserve better? Wanting to pursue your passion—have I done enough to earn the right to follow my dream? Exhausted by a life of obligations—can I do something that is not in service of my job or my kids?

If we distill our culture into two teachers, one teacher tells us we need to earn our pleasure by working hard and being good. And since hard and good are never defined, we always feel like we haven’t yet earned the right to pursue pleasure. The other teacher tells us that life is short and to go find the joy. I’d argue that right now, that teacher is not the one hosting the Turkey Trots.

According to recent reports, thanksgiving. Friendsgiving. A holiday where we share one meal with loved ones we don’t see often enough. A holiday where we feel warm nostalgia as we eat the same pie we’ve had since we were kids. A holiday where we get to see elderly relatives, possibly for the last time. A holiday where we laugh in the kitchen, watch football, spend time with people we love, and yes, eat—because it’s a meal. Why do we think we need to earn any of this? We are allowed to pursue pleasure—in food, in friends—simply because we are human.

In a recent development, and so, the Turkey Trot. My advice:.

When AI Saves a Fast Heartbeat, Who Carries the Conflict?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1244 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • Sources indicate that you just hired an entry-level employee.
  • Your follow-up email carries an edge, and, within seconds, their reply hits your mailbox:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Sources indicate that you just hired an entry-level employee. A week later, they miss an vital deadline, affecting several other projects like dominoes.

Your follow-up email carries an edge, and, within seconds, their reply hits your mailbox:.

“Hello, I sincerely appreciate your feedback and understand the importance of timely delivery. I take full accountability and remain committed to improving our processes moving forward.

It has been revealed that for a moment, it may feel like a perfect reply. Their acknowledgment of your feedback and promise to do better feels almost like a relief, but at the same time raises a red flag: Why haven't they offered any explanation for what happened, and will their mess-up and apology be a repeat?

According to recent reports, conflicts, even minor ones, can raise our heart rate, especially at work, where professional reputation and job security may be at stake. We may act in a way that leads to regret later, and a reality check against AI may not be wrong. I call it "resolution illusion" when a message displays the signs of "this is what the opponent would most like to read in the reply", such as empathy, acknowledgment, and professionalism. At the same time, the underlying problem remains untouched, and that may even build some resentment. This may eventually lead to major conflict.

In a recent development, in an August 2026 Big Think interview, Terence Tao compared scientific research to hiking toward a waterfall. AI, he suggested, can work like a helicopter that takes you straight there. The hike teaches you the terrain, and a wrong turn might lead to a discovery you never set out to make. This, of course, isn't just about hiking.

In any situation, people seem to learn better through understanding and making mistakes. In conflicts, they have to decide what to say after what is already said and/or done. They may question their assumptions and build their own future behavioral "protocol" in similar instances, after considering how their actions may affect themselves and others.

In the workplace, in particular, they may need to revisit where instructions were unclear or ask for help they should have requested sooner; it is all part of getting lost, which leads to latest professional discovery. That learning process may be uncomfortable, but it gives them practice in building their professional role, critical thinking, exercising judgment, speaking up, and establishing personal limits around work. When AI-polished responses are sent within a second, it becomes easier to skip the uncomfortable but necessary path for professional development, from A — the missed deadline — to B — figuring out what went wrong and what needs to change in this case.

In a 2025 survey, knowledge workers reported thinking less critically about tasks they were more confident AI could handle (Lee et al., 2025). In a separate experiment, readers perceived AI-assisted messages as less reflective of the sender’s own values than messages described as entirely human-written.

Sources indicate that philosophers Lai and Archer (2026) stated that relying on AI for emotional communication can deprive people of opportunities to discover what they truly value and who they really are. In the workplace, this is especially key, since it is where most people spend the majority of their time. An apology may sound like the product of reflection even if the sender skipped the necessary steps (remorse, responsibility, impact, and the desire to repair). This is only one part of the problem. The other is: If the reply makes the issue look settled, who absorbs the relational fallout?

According to recent reports, research on unrewarded work suggests an answer. In a study published in the American Economic Review, Babcock and colleagues examined tasks everyone wants done, but no one wants to do, such as writing a report or serving on a committee. Women were more likely than men to volunteer for these tasks, to be asked to do them, and to say yes when asked. The reason was not that women preferred this work. In mixed groups, people expected women to say yes, and in all-female or all-male groups, the difference disappeared (Babcock et al., 2017). Cleaning up — making sure everyone understood what went wrong and what not to do in the future — after a polished AI reply is this same kind of work that may fall to women.

According to recent reports, A woman asked to fix what a polished reply left unresolved can use the following three questions to hand the thinking back to the person who made the mistake: What happened? What will you do differently in the future? How will you know it started working? The questions give the employee a simple checklist and a chance to reflect, explain their side of the story, propose a fix, and take responsibility for following through. For high-achieving women, the relevant boundary may no longer be knowing when to say no; it may be knowing when not to perform another person's unfinished thinking.

Imagine the employee had noted what they were actually thinking:.

"Hello, I thought someone said it's due Friday.

Now the manager has something to work with – the scheduling issue, miscommunication, role clarification, and how the process works.

Recent findings suggest that the manager learns how the employee understood the process, who they depend on, who depends on their work and responsibilities, and who to speak with. Exchanges like this can serve as a reference point in case of similar problems.

A polished message that solves conflict skips all that, allowing the same or more errors in the future, which may eventually lead to job loss.

Sources indicate that it's not to say we shouldn't use AI for conflicts. Some workplace conflicts can be hostile, and for an entry-level employee, it can take time to spot; AI can help organize a timeline, clarify thoughts, brainstorm ideas, or find words for a boundary they already understand. This allows them to express themselves to the best of their knowledge and genuinely mean every word of an AI-assisted reply. The end product is what matters — the next deadlines should be handled based on the lessons learned from the first mistakes.

Conflicts may raise your heart rate, and AI can save a heartbeat, but it should not become another person’s unresolved conflict tomorrow.

#407. Latest Update: Gen Z, Careers, and Money: Navigating an Uncertain Future

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1008 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Latest Update: Gen Z, Careers, and Money: Navigating an Uncertain Future

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • You've probably heard the advice: Work hard, build a career, and save for the future.
  • The employment landscape keeps changing, with AI introducing new uncertainty about which jobs will exist, which skills will matter, and what building a career will require.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Co-written by Huong Diep and Jason Wang.

You've probably heard the advice: Work hard, build a career, and save for the future. But how much does that reflect the working world you're navigating?

The employment landscape keeps changing, with AI introducing new uncertainty about which jobs will exist, which skills will matter, and what building a career will require. Meanwhile, the income you are working toward may not seem sufficient to afford the life that work is supposed to make possible, making your future feel uncertain too.

It has been revealed that you may have watched others devote years to an employer and still lose their jobs. Perhaps you have pursued an education, developed skills, and taken your career seriously, only to encounter limited opportunities or disappointing pay.

Dedication and hard work do not ensure an employer’s loyalty, and careful career decisions cannot always protect you from economic shifts.

Sources indicate that it makes sense to reconsider how much of your identity and self-worth you want to tie to productivity, professional status, or earnings. Losing a job or struggling to earn enough can have significant practical and emotional consequences, but these experiences do not mean that you lack ability, have not tried hard enough, or are worth less as a person.

If homeownership, a wedding, having kids, or other traditional milestones feel financially out of reach, making sacrifices for them can feel less worthwhile. How much enjoyment are you giving up for something you may never be able to afford? Some milestones may not appeal to you anyway.

A concert with friends or a long-anticipated trip offers something you can experience now, without sacrificing for a future that may not be attainable.

However, this reasoning can shift into financial fatalism: If the future is so uncertain, what is the point of saving or planning at all?

It has been revealed that notice the all-or-nothing thinking. Not being able to guarantee a particular future does not mean you have no influence over what happens next.

Meet John*, whose story reflects experiences we encounter among young adults in our practices.

John followed the conventional roadmap to success: solid grades, a four-year degree in a field that promised job security, extracurriculars, internships, and networking. Yet, he finds himself struggling to enter the workforce.

Sources indicate that after submitting hundreds of applications, John is exhausted and increasingly discouraged. When he does land an interview, it may be with an AI interviewer, followed by being “ghosted” afterward. Still living at home with his parents, he feels stuck in a cycle with no clear way forward. He begins to wonder, “Why did I even go to college?”.

For John, buying a concert ticket or treating himself to an iced coffee offers more than momentary pleasure. Choosing to spend money, and deciding what to spend it on, provides a sense of autonomy and control amid so much uncertainty. Enjoying his coffee is an escape before the slog of yet another job application. Having fun at a concert with friends lets him live in the present, instead of always feeling weighed down by the pressures of building a life and career.

According to recent reports, let’s be clear: An occasional iced coffee now is not why homeownership might be out of reach later. At the same time, relatively small amounts saved and invested when you are young can grow by compounding over decades in ways that are difficult to fully appreciate today. Similarly, what will be within financial reach (and what you will want to purchase) in the future is hard to predict today. Debt can also build over time, as balances accumulate and interest or fees add to what you owe, creating significant financial strain.

As financial psychologists, we empathize with John's frustration while also recognizing an important tension: The very spending behaviors that help young adults cope with feelings of powerlessness in the short term may begin to create a pattern of spending (and even a sense of financial identity) that will not be helpful in the long term.

It has been revealed that money set aside might help you move, change careers, or leave an unhealthy workplace. Planning can help you prepare for needs and choices that differ from the milestones you originally imagined.

According to recent reports, of course, if your income barely covers necessities, saving may not be possible. That financial constraint should not be treated as a failure of discipline or willingness to plan.

In a recent development, spending on a nice dinner or vacation with friends can be enjoyable. But how much of its meaning comes from the setting, and how much comes from having time to connect?

If connection is important to you, there may be other less costly ways to experience it: cooking together, taking a regular walk, or simply making time to talk.

Investing time in friendships, family, and community can support both your present and your future. You can enjoy those relationships now while building connections that deepen and provide support through life’s changes.

There is no easy answer to how much you should invest in your career, save for later, or spend today. Your circumstances matter, and the balance may change over time.

In a recent development, what matters is continuing to grapple with notable questions over time, and letting the answers evolve as your life evolves. Ask yourself:.

Taking these questions seriously acknowledges what is outside of your control, while still helping you think about what you can shape, and leads to decisions that reflect your circumstances and values.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Jason Wang is a licensed psychologist based in Washington, DC, specializing in the psychological dimensions of work, career, and money. His practice focuses on helping adults navigate life transitions and build more meaningful, sustainable, and values-aligned lives. Learn more at Inflection Points Therapy.

#406. Brain Computes Motion Direction Independently From the Eye

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1125 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Neurosciencenews

Brain Computes Motion Direction Independently From the Eye

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, researchers have developed a high-throughput brain-mapping tool that reveals the brain does not simply rely on pre-calculated motion signals from the eye, but also computes the direction of movement independently.
  • Whether ducking a fast-moving ball, stepping back from an oncoming vehicle, or evading an approaching predator, survival depends on the brain’s ability to determine not just that an object is moving, but its exact trajectory in real time.
  • For decades, visual neuroscientists knew that specialized neurons in the mammalian retina fire selectively when stimuli move in specific directions, left, right, up, down, or diagonally.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, researchers have developed a high-throughput brain-mapping tool that reveals the brain does not simply rely on pre-calculated motion signals from the eye, but also computes the direction of movement independently. The study mapped nearly 46,000 mouse brain cells to uncover a dual visual system in the superior colliculus, separating localized object tracking from global self-motion sensing.

Source: UC San Francisco / Nature.

Whether ducking a fast-moving ball, stepping back from an oncoming vehicle, or evading an approaching predator, survival depends on the brain’s ability to determine not just that an object is moving, but its exact trajectory in real time.

For decades, visual neuroscientists knew that specialized neurons in the mammalian retina fire selectively when stimuli move in specific directions, left, right, up, down, or diagonally.

According to recent reports, because these retinal ganglion cells already encode directional vectors, researchers widely assumed the brain simply inherited that pre-calculated motion data passively from the eye. However, no mapping technology existed that could simultaneously trace exact synaptic connections from the retina while identifying the molecular identity of every receiving brain cell.

Now, in a study published in Nature, researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) have bridged that technological gap.

According to recent reports, led by co-senior authors Dr. Xin Duan, professor of ophthalmology, and Dr. Evan Feinberg, professor of anatomy, alongside postdoctoral fellow Dr. Fei Wang, the team built a scalable eye-to-brain wiring atlas revealing that specialized circuits in the midbrain compute motion direction completely on their own.

Over the past decade, Duan’s laboratory pioneered anterograde trans-neuronal tracing, a technique in which a fluorescent molecular tracer delivered to the eye crosses synaptic junctions to illuminate only those downstream brain neurons directly receiving retinal input.

To scale this tool from single-circuit tracing into a comprehensive atlas, Wang paired the trans-neuronal tracer with MERFISH (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization), a spatial transcriptomic method that reads gene activity across thousands of individual cells in a tissue slice simultaneously to pinpoint each neuron’s exact genetic identity.

Applying this combined platform across nearly 46,000 cells in the mouse visual system, the investigators uncovered hundreds of distinct retinal-to-brain connection pairs.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s like an entire atlas we’ve built,” Wang said. “We’ve uncovered hundreds of pairs of connections between the eye and the brain. We ended up focusing on only one page of this atlas, but there are many left to study in the future.”.

Focusing on the superior colliculus, an evolutionarily conserved midbrain hub essential for visual orientation and rapid motor reflexes, Wang, Feinberg, and Duan recorded real-time neural firing while showing mice high-contrast black bars scrolling across a screen in eight distinct directions.

Combining functional recordings with their molecular wiring map exposed two separate motion-processing architectures operating side by side:.

“We think these sets of cells are doing slightly different things from each other,” Wang explained. “The eye cells detecting direction may specialize in small, local motions like prey or food. The brain cells computing direction sense a larger background movement.”.

The investigators hypothesize that this global background motion signal informs an organism of its own self-motion and spatial trajectory as it navigates through the environment.

Industry observers note that beyond resolving a foundational question in visual neuroscience, the high-resolution wiring atlas carries direct translational implications for regenerative medicine and neuroengineering. As researchers advance toward optic nerve regeneration, whole-eye transplantation, and high-resolution visual brain-machine interfaces for patients with glaucoma, trauma, or multiple sclerosis, restoring functional sight requires reconnecting damaged axons to their exact functional targets.

Industry observers note that “This is a fundamental mechanism that has been understudied from a basic science perspective, but it also has applied value,” remarked Duan. “If we ever want to repair or restore vision in people, we need to know which neural connections need to be rewired for functional vision.”.

“In addition to providing a blueprint for revealing structural maps of the brain, our study illustrates how the resulting maps can be used to answer longstanding questions regarding brain function,” added Feinberg.

The team notes that their scalable tracer-plus-MERFISH platform can be adapted to map how the eye regulates circadian rhythms, and generalized to chart cell-to-cell connectivity across any organ system in the body.

Does the eye do all the work of detecting which way things move?

No. While specialized cells in the retina detect motion direction and send that data to the brain, UCSF researchers discovered a second group of neurons in the brain’s superior colliculus that independently calculates motion direction using basic visual inputs, even when the eye’s own direction-sensing cells are turned off.

Why does the brain have two different systems for sensing motion?

Researchers believe the two pathways handle different visual jobs: the eye’s direction-sensing cells appear specialized for tracking small, local moving targets (like food, prey, or a flying ball), while the brain’s independent motion-computing cells detect large-scale background movement to help track how your own body is moving through space.

How could this brain-mapping tool help restore vision in the future?

Sources indicate that to successfully develop eye transplants, optic nerve repairs, or visual brain-machine interfaces for conditions like glaucoma or multiple sclerosis, scientists need an exact wiring diagram showing which eye cells connect to which functional brain circuits. This latest atlas provides that precise rewiring blueprint.

TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits.

Sources indicate that A major goal in neuroscience is to map the transformation of information as it flows through the brain. For example, neurons at many levels of the visual hierarchy are attuned to motion direction. However, links between motion-selective computations and cell types at various stages of the visual hierarchy remain unidentified. A key first step in delineating these relationships is to map the wiring diagrams that connect different motion-selective cell types.

In a recent development, here we establish a systematic, cell-type-specific circuit-mapping method, combining an anterograde trans-neuronal fluorescent tracer (mWGA–mCherry) with spatial transcriptomics (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)) to establish TransA-MERFISH. We used TransA-MERFISH to comprehensively map the synaptic target cell types of four retinal ganglion cell subclasses in superior colliculus (SC) at cell-type resolution.

These experiments unexpectedly revealed that retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cells (ooDSGCs) innervate several direction-selective SC cell types, but do not innervate a SC cell type that was previously reported to display strong direction-selective responses.

We validated these results using orthogonal approaches and demonstrated the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH. Functional studies of SC activity before and after ablation of retinal direction-selective circuits confirmed that these computationally distinct, ooDSGC-dependent and -independent direction-selective cell types are commingled in SC.

Together, our study establishes TransA-MERFISH as a robust framework for mapping wiring diagrams at the cell-type level and uncovers divergent computational mechanisms of motion detection in early visual processing.

#405. Breaking: Reciprocal Mentorship: Why Intergenerational Arts Matter

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1745 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Breaking: Reciprocal Mentorship: Why Intergenerational Arts Matter

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • In a recent development, when I was in high school, I spent my afternoons in a retirement home across the street from campus visiting with a resident.
  • The cost of this segregation runs in both directions and is measurable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

In a recent development, when I was in high school, I spent my afternoons in a retirement home across the street from campus visiting with a resident. What started as a weekly visit became two to three visits a week. We would watch old black-and-white films she loved when she was young, make art together, and she’d tell me about her life. High school is tumultuous and isolating. Being 80 in a retirement home, I learned, can be, too. Through spending time together, we each stepped outside the isolation of our separate worlds; as a result, we both felt less lonely. I didn’t understand the mechanics then, but what we both experienced—the quiet power of being needed, of having someone show up week after week, of creating something together—is exactly what community-based knowledge and a growing body of research now show: intergenerational connection works.This scene repeats itself across the United States, though mostly unseen. In Montgomery County, Maryland, high school students and adult artists co-design creative workshops in affordable housing communities through Arts for the Aging’s Empower Project. In the American South, Alternate Roots—a 50-year coalition of artists and community organizers—brings together emerging and veteran creatives in social justice work (Merin, 1977). In Los Angeles, parents and children sit together making altars for Día de los Muertos, co-creating around cultural traditions through programs like Multigenerational Afterschool Arts (Kane & Kunisaki, 2025). These programs reflect the understanding that different ages need each other.Our contemporary world segregates by age in ways that would astound people living just 150 years ago. Schools for the young. Workplaces for the “productive years.” Retirement facilities for the old. This age segregation is remarkably recent; a product of early-20th-century industrialization and its drive for efficiency (Freedman & Stamp, 2021). Graded education, child labor laws, Social Security, and mandatory retirement all contributed to the reshuffling. Sun City, which opened in Phoenix in 1960, pioneered the modern age-segregated retirement community. In contrast, 19th-century America was thoroughly age-integrated: multigenerational households, mixed workplaces, even almshouses that housed the old, young, orphaned, and poor together.

The cost of this segregation runs in both directions and is measurable. Young people may lose consistent relationships with adults who’ve navigated complexity and failure, and a sense of historical continuity that can anchor identity (Freedman & Stamp, 2021). Older adults lose something equally vital: the felt sense of being needed. Research demonstrates that people over 60 who live in age-segregated communities experience higher levels of loneliness (Kim and Choi, 2025). A 2018 survey found that the two loneliest groups in America are younger people and older people—the very populations most separated by design (Freedman & Stamp, 2021). Social isolation and loneliness are linked to higher risks for depression, cognitive decline, heart disease, and early mortality (Hodgson et al., 2020; National Institute on Aging, 2019). Purpose, or the concrete experience of being relied upon, is an exceptionally strong predictor of mental health and longevity (Boyle et al., 2009; O’Súilleabháin et al., 2026). When that sense of purpose is ripped away, the same neurobiological threat response triggered by chronic loneliness is activated (Eisenberger and Cole, 2012). For communities of color, age segregation compounds existing healthcare barriers. Traditional mental health services are often inaccessible due to systemic racism, historical harm, and documented mistrust in the medical system (Alang, 2019). Community-based arts spaces, rooted in cultural knowledge and embedded in neighborhoods, reach people that formal systems do not. Research shows that culturally tailored, community-led arts programs improve mental health outcomes in underserved communities and create what researchers call “essential social infrastructure” for mental wellness (Aguirre et al., 2025; Hand & Golden, 2019; GBHI, 2024).The programs that work best operate on a principle increasingly recognized in intergenerational research: mutual benefit rather than hierarchical mentorship. Traditional models, such as younger people “helping” elders or elders “sharing wisdom,” recreate the hierarchies we’re trying to dismantle. Instead, effective programs support what researchers call “equal group status,” where both ages are genuinely needed to complete the work and knowledge flows bidirectionally (Cheng et al., 2026; Jarrott, 2023).Arts for the Aging’s Empower Project pairs high school artist assistant fellows with adult artists in residence. Both are paid and are equal decision-makers. Young people and professionals learn from each other, and both contribute to designing and leading workshops for their community (Arts for the Aging, 2026). Alternate Roots works similarly. A younger artist reflected: “Older, more experienced people shared resources that helped my personal development. Later, I generated opportunities for others.” (Clark et al., n.d.). This is reciprocal mentorship. The evidence for what this creates is substantial. The Wallace Foundation’s study of 35 community-based arts organizations across eight U.S. cities, which followed youth of color over 18 months, documented measurable outcomes: increased sense of belonging, skill mastery, sense of purpose, leadership development, and community connection (Osai et al., 2025). Such intergenerational programming can have positive rippling effects on mental health and well-being for both generations, and across the lifespan (Arring et al., 2026; Jenkins et al., 2021; Park, 2015).

Furthermore, studies show that arts-based programs reduce mental health stigma (Beato et al., 2024; Gaiha et al., 2021). More recent research examining intersectionality-informed art interventions with Black, Indigenous, and People of Color girls ages 14-16 found that art-based work supported narrative agency, processing of intergenerational trauma, and community connection (Birnkammer et al., 2026). Why does this work? In part, it is due to biological factors. Chronic loneliness activates threat-response systems throughout the nervous system (Eisenberger and Cole, 2012). Being part of a genuine collaboration and feeling needed activates the reward system. Creative work engages the brain differently compared with talk therapy; it is embodied, non-verbal, and grounded in making something material. There’s also something that neuroscience alone may not be able to measure: these programs offer the felt experience of belonging across differences, of mattering to someone. They offer reciprocal vulnerability.These programs also provide something foundational: spaces where genuine connection across ages is built, and where respect is reciprocal. Where in your community could genuinely reciprocal creative work happen, and what would it take to build such a space?

Maya Lakshman, MPH, is a doctoral candidate at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, where she uses neuroimaging, geospatial, and qualitative methods to understand the impacts of structural and interpersonal violence on development and mental health across the lifespan. She is a writer, educator, and researcher with an interest in translating evidence into equitable, justice-centered public health policy.

Ultraprocessed Foods Alter Food-Reward Brain Activity

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A controlled feeding trial reveals that just two weeks on a diet high in ultraprocessed foods alters brain reward responses in emerging adults ages 18 to 21, while leaving adults ages 22 to 25 unaffected.
  • Recent findings suggest that ultraprocessed foods, products formulated with industrial processing methods and ingredients rarely found in a home kitchen, account for more than half of the calories consumed by young adults in the United States.
  • In a controlled feeding study published this month in the journal Obesity, researchers at Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at VTC and Department of Human Nutrition, Foods, and Exercise found that emerging adults ages 18 to 21 exhibit distinct neural changes in food-reward circuitry after consuming an ultraprocessed diet for just two weeks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A controlled feeding trial reveals that just two weeks on a diet high in ultraprocessed foods alters brain reward responses in emerging adults ages 18 to 21, while leaving adults ages 22 to 25 unaffected. The fMRI study indicates blunted activation in the developing orbitofrontal cortex, a key region for food valuation and self-control, even when diets are strictly matched for calories, sugar, fat, and nutrients.

Source: Virginia Tech / Obesity.

Recent findings suggest that ultraprocessed foods, products formulated with industrial processing methods and ingredients rarely found in a home kitchen, account for more than half of the calories consumed by young adults in the United States. While extensive research links these foods to obesity, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease, neuroscientists are increasingly uncovering how industrial processing directly interacts with the developing human brain.

In a controlled feeding study published this month in the journal Obesity, researchers at Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at VTC and Department of Human Nutrition, Foods, and Exercise found that emerging adults ages 18 to 21 exhibit distinct neural changes in food-reward circuitry after consuming an ultraprocessed diet for just two weeks.

Industry observers note that led by first author Dr. Emma Leslie alongside neuroscientist Dr. Alex DiFeliceantonio and registered dietitian Dr. Brenda Davy, the findings complement earlier results from the same trial showing that 18- to 21-year-olds consumed excess calories at a buffet meal after eating ultraprocessed foods, even when they were no longer hungry.

It has been revealed that to separate the effects of industrial food processing from basic nutritional content, the researchers recruited 22 healthy adults ages 18 to 25 (including seven participants ages 21 or younger) for a randomized crossover feeding trial. Each participant followed two strictly controlled diets for two weeks apiece, separated by a four-week washout period:.

Critically, both diets were engineered to have identical macronutrient profiles (50% carbohydrates, 35% fat, 15% protein), matching levels of fiber, added sugars, saturated fat, sodium, energy density, and overall nutritional quality, calibrated to keep each participant’s body weight stable.

Before and after each two-week dietary phase, participants underwent functional MRI (fMRI) brain scans while receiving small sips of an ultraprocessed milkshake or a tasteless control solution through a specialized delivery tube.

When the researchers analyzed the neuroimaging data, they discovered a striking developmental divide:.

“Among the younger participants, consuming a diet high in ultraprocessed foods for just two weeks was associated with decreased brain response to a rewarding food — a milkshake — in the orbitofrontal cortex,” explained Leslie, who conducted the work as a doctoral student at Virginia Tech and is now a postdoctoral associate at the University of Michigan.

Located just behind the eyes, the orbitofrontal cortex is one of the final regions of the human brain to finish maturing, continuing to remodel into the mid- to late 20s. It plays a central role in evaluating food rewards, regulating cravings, and exerting executive self-control to stop eating.

Because the two diets were matched across nutritional metrics, the findings point toward non-nutritive properties of ultraprocessed foods, such as chemical additives, emulsifiers, texture alterations, or compounds generated during industrial processing, as potential drivers of altered brain signaling.

In a recent development, “This study is important because you have this change in an area of the brain known to govern self-control and potentially put a stop to eating,” stated DiFeliceantonio, associate professor at the Fralin Biomedical Research Institute and interim co-director of its Center for Health Behaviors Research. “This is giving us insight into how ultraprocessed foods are affecting the bodies and brains of younger people, who might be especially vulnerable to their effects. And that’s important to know for things like dietary guidelines, doctor recommendations, and policy decisions.”.

While the researchers note that the sample size was small and the age-based findings were exploratory, and did not directly correlate individual fMRI shifts with buffet calorie intake, the results highlight adolescence and early adulthood as critical windows of neurodevelopmental sensitivity.

Next, DiFeliceantonio and Davy initiative to investigate whether adolescents under 18, who consume the highest proportion of ultraprocessed foods of any U.S. demographic, show even stronger neural sensitivity, and whether brain responses recover once individuals return to whole-food diets.

How do ultraprocessed foods affect the brains of young adults?

In a recent development, A Virginia Tech study found that after eating a diet high in ultraprocessed foods for just two weeks, young adults ages 18 to 21 showed decreased brain activity in the orbitofrontal cortex, a region involved in food reward, valuation, and self-control, when tasting a milkshake. Adults ages 22 to 25 did not show these brain changes.

Was the brain effect simply caused by extra sugar, fat, or calories?

No. Both the ultraprocessed diet and the unprocessed comparison diet contained the exact same amounts of calories, carbohydrates, fat, protein, added sugars, saturated fat, fiber, and sodium. This suggests that industrial food processing or additives themselves, rather than basic nutrients, drove the brain changes.

Why are 18- to 21-year-olds more sensitive to ultraprocessed foods than slightly older adults?

Industry observers note that the orbitofrontal cortex is one of the last brain regions to finish developing, continuing to mature into the mid- to late 20s. Because this self-control and reward-evaluation circuit is still actively wiring in 18- to 21-year-olds, it appears more sensitive to dietary shifts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A large-scale meta-analysi reveals that intolerance of uncertainty, a core cognitive driver of clinical anxiety, has climbed steadily among North American college students since 1992, accelerating threefold faster after 2012. The analysis of over 35,000 participants indicates that rising youth anxiety reflects genuine shifts in psychological distress rather than mere mental health awareness.

Source: Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

Over the past decade, rates of anxiety and mood disorders among adolescents and college-aged adults have climbed sharply across North America. Yet clinicians and epidemiologists have hotly debated a central question: does this statistical surge reflect a true rise in underlying psychological distress, or are young people simply more familiar with clinical terminology and more willing to report symptoms?

Upcoming research led by Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and Boston University School of Public Health provides compelling evidence that underlying cognitive vulnerability is genuinely intensifying.

Published in JAMA Psychiatry, the study tracks three decades of data on intolerance of uncertainty (IU)—a foundational psychological mechanism characterized by acute distress when facing ambiguous situations, missing information, or unpredictable outcomes.

Analyzing data from more than 35,000 college students in the United States and Canada between 1992 and 2023, the researchers found that intolerance of uncertainty increased steadily over 30 years—and accelerated dramatically around 2012, growing roughly three times faster over the past decade than during the 1990s and 2000s.

Recent findings suggest that to track population-level shifts in how young adults tolerate ambiguity, first author Dr. Jeroen M. Van Baar, postdoctoral associate in epidemiology at Boston University School of Public Health, and senior author Dr. Katherine M. Keyes, professor of epidemiology at Columbia Mailman School of Public Health, conducted a systematic temporal meta-analysis using the Web of Science database.

Sources indicate that after screening nearly 300 full-text peer-reviewed studies published between 2007 and 2025, the team synthesized data from 138 studies encompassing 35,296 college-aged participants across the U.S. and Canada who completed standardized 27-item or 12-item versions of the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale.

Across the entire 31-year window from 1992 through 2023, average IU scores increased by approximately 0.65 points annually. Crucially, the trajectory bent sharply upward around 2012: between 2012 and 2023, intolerance of uncertainty rose at roughly triple the annual pace recorded between 1992 and 2011.

In a recent development, “Our results provide updated insights into one of the core building blocks of anxiety: intolerance of uncertainty,” explained Keyes. “IU is not itself a health outcome or a root cause of disease, but an intermediary cognitive process that contributes to the development of anxiety.”.

In a recent development, for an individual with high intolerance of uncertainty, everyday unpredictability, such as attending a upcoming class without knowing every expectation or navigating an unstructured social event, can trigger disproportionate cognitive threat and emotional distress. Elevated IU is a well-established transdiagnostic risk factor linked to generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and depression.

Crucially, because “intolerance of uncertainty” remains a specialized clinical metric largely unfamiliar outside psychology, it provides a vital safeguard against reporting bias.

“Some researchers have argued that increases in anxiety and mood disorder symptoms among young people may partly reflect greater mental health awareness,” noted Van Baar. “Because young people are now more familiar with terms like ‘anxiety’, they may be more likely to report symptoms in surveys even if their underlying feelings have not changed. On the other hand, intolerance of uncertainty remains a relatively unfamiliar concept outside psychology, making this study less vulnerable to that criticism.”.

“The fact that we observed a consistent increase in intolerance of uncertainty that mirrored trends in anxiety and mood disorder symptoms suggests these patterns are unlikely to be explained solely by greater mental health awareness and may instead reflect genuine changes in underlying mental health,” Keyes added.

While the study did not isolate a single environmental trigger, the authors point to a convergence of mutually reinforcing societal shifts—including the rapid adoption of smartphones and social media around 2012, escalating academic competition, rising loneliness, economic instability, childhood adversity, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

According to recent reports, “It is likely that these factors are intertwined and mutually reinforcing, jointly contributing to population-level increases in intolerance of uncertainty and anxiety among young adults,” Van Baar noted. “Any explanation will be strongest if it accounts for both the long-term upward trend since the 1990s and the inflection point observed around 2012.”.

It has been revealed that despite the sobering trajectory, the researchers emphasize a clear path forward: unlike broad macroeconomic forces, intolerance of uncertainty is a modifiable cognitive habit. Targeted cognitive-behavioral therapies specifically designed to build tolerance for ambiguity already exist, and scaling these interventions for young adults could help curb the youth anxiety crisis at its cognitive roots.

What is “intolerance of uncertainty,” and how does it relate to anxiety?

Intolerance of uncertainty is a psychological tendency to feel distressed, overwhelmed, or threatened when facing unpredictable outcomes or missing information. It acts as a core cognitive building block that significantly increases a person’s vulnerability to developing anxiety and mood disorders.

How much has intolerance of uncertainty increased among college students?

Industry observers note that analyzing data from 35,296 U.S. and Canadian college students between 1992 and 2023, researchers found that scores rose steadily by about 0.65 points per year, and accelerated three times faster between 2012 and 2023 compared to the previous two decades.

Does this prove rising youth anxiety isn’t just due to greater mental health awareness?

Yes, it provides strong evidence against the “awareness-only” theory. Because “intolerance of uncertainty” is a specialized psychological concept rather than an everyday term young people use to self-label, its steep rise mirrors anxiety trends without being skewed by changing vocabulary or awareness.
