📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • In a recent development, pope Leo’s Magnifica Humanitas (2026), subtitled “On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence,” has been heralded as one of the most significant and morally serious visions for how humanity ought to think about and navigate the advent of the AI era.
  • According to recent reports, for Leo, protecting and fostering the dignity of the human person must be the goal of everything we do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

In a recent development, pope Leo’s Magnifica Humanitas (2026), subtitled “On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence,” has been heralded as one of the most significant and morally serious visions for how humanity ought to think about and navigate the advent of the AI era. Acknowledging “the ambiguity of tools,” which are neither morally good nor bad in and of themselves but “can cause harm when not oriented toward the good,” the Pope insists that the end toward which our aspirations aim is as important as the aspirations themselves.

According to recent reports, for Leo, protecting and fostering the dignity of the human person must be the goal of everything we do. Contrasting two images taken from Scripture, the Pope calls us to consider how the desire that orients our ambitions changes the things we create.

In Leo’s first example, the construction of the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9) is motivated by fear and vainglory:.

Fearing being scattered across the earth, they [the builders] sought to guarantee stability and power for themselves, and above all to ‘make a name’ for themselves.” Such motives cannot but end in ruin. Leo continues, “When a city is built on pride and the claim to self-sufficiency, communication breaks down, languages are confused and people no longer understand each other. The result is not unity, but dispersion. Babel thus reveals the limits of any effort that, however grandiose, arises from self-affirmation, sacrifices human dignity for efficiency and aspires to reach heaven without God’s blessing.

In his second, which comes from the Book of Nehemiah, Nehemiah returns to the city of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile only to find it in ruins. Heartbroken, he takes in the destruction in silence. Then, before setting to work, he “convened the families, assigned each of them a section of the wall to rebuild, listened to their concerns, coordinated their efforts and addressed any opposition.”.

Industry observers note that nehemiah, that is, kept the dignity of those around him at the center of his project rather than running headlong toward apparent solutions. In so doing, he was able to resurrect what had been lost while simultaneously creating something new. The Pope writes:.

Recent findings suggest that the narrative reveals how the city is reborn, not through the initiative of one man, but through the shared responsibility of all: men, women, priests, artisans, heads of households and young people all play a part. It is an undertaking with God at the center, which rebuilds relationships before rebuilding with stones. Thus, ancient Jerusalem rediscovers a common language—not one of uniformity, but one of communion, namely the harmony that arises when all persons assume their own role and recognize that their strength comes from the Lord.

According to recent reports, what makes these images apt for our current moment—and what many commentators have overlooked—is the role language plays in each. For, if the desire of those constructing the Tower of Babel was to create a single, unified language with which all could understand and be understood, so too is the aim of Artificial Intelligence to provide a kind of totalizing language capable of flattening ambiguity and rendering difference obsolete. And if Nehemiah’s success was rooted in the fact that he sought out the input of those he hoped to serve, and even (perhaps especially) those with whom he disagreed, so too must dialogue be at the foundation of technological advance.

Consider another example, this one taken from contemporary fiction, that draws out this tension inherent in language—the tension between the desire to communicate directly, if only superficially, and the desire to express how fraught and complex human experience actually is, even if that expression can only be accomplished indirectly and ambiguously.

Industry observers note that it comes from Paul Auster’s great work of metareal fiction City of Glass (1987), in which the story’s chief antagonist Peter Stillman—is he still a man, still human, or has he been deformed by his mad pursuit of “perfectibility”?—obsesses over the duplicity of language, the way one word can mean two equal and opposite things. For instance, the word cleave “means both ‘to join together’ and ‘to break apart.’”.

For Stillman, the Genesis narrative to which the Pope alluded “records not only the fall of man, but the fall of language” from clarity to opacity. Once, he conjectures, language was simple, direct, and stated exactly what it meant to say without confusion or ambiguity. There was a time when “words had not been merely appended to things . . . they revealed their essences . . . A thing and its name were interchangeable.” But after the destruction of the Tower of Babel, this was no longer true. Now words conceal as much as they reveal, and deception is built into the very nature of how we communicate.

Sources indicate that driven mad by the desire to use language to reunify what appears to him to be a fractured and fragmentary existence, Stillman sets out to realize a utopian future in which his model of a single, unified language makes absolute knowledge and mastery possible. (Sound familiar?).

If the fall of man also entailed a fall of language, was it not logical to assume that it would be possible to undo the fall, to reverse its effects by undoing the fall of language? . . . If man could learn to speak this original language of innocence, did it not follow that he would thereby recover a state of innocence within himself?

The trouble is that Stillman is not able to conjure up this mythical language model, and his attempts to do so inflict immense suffering on those around him.

In an ironic twist, Stillman ultimately resorts to deception himself in a vain attempt to accomplish his goal. Creating a character named Henry Dark, a fictional disciple of John Milton, he attributes his most controversial ideas to Dark and even falsifies the historical record to make it appear as though Dark had heralded his, Stillman’s, project over 300 years in advance.

Sources indicate that what could offer a better image of the LLMs that seem so powerful and omniscient today—with their false citations and hallucinated facts—than a fictional character invented by a mad genius to dupe others into believing that his language model could solve the mysteries and riddles of the human condition? And yet, what could offer a better reason to hope? For, although Dark was invented by Stillman to serve darker ends, still his creation was—as Pope Leo recently called the craft of writing fiction—a profound “act of humanity,” one which points to the supreme dignity of its author even if he, like many of us today, is too consumed with his utopian ideas to appreciate it.

Industry observers note that auster, P. (1987). City of Glass. Upcoming York, NY: Penguin Books.

Leo XIV. (2026). Magnifica Humanitas: On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence. Encyclical letter. The Holy See.

#385. 5 best essential oils for anxiety (and how to use them)

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1772 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Calm

5 best essential oils for anxiety (and how to use them)

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • In a recent development, it’s mid-afternoon, and your to-do list keeps growing.
  • Essential oils are everywhere these days, from store shelves to social media feeds, and you’ve probably heard the promise that lavender can ease stress and anxious feelings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

In a recent development, it’s mid-afternoon, and your to-do list keeps growing. You reach for the small bottle of lavender essential oil on your desk, hold it a few inches from your nose, and breathe in slowly. Your shoulders drop, and the list feels a little more manageable.

Essential oils are everywhere these days, from store shelves to social media feeds, and you’ve probably heard the promise that lavender can ease stress and anxious feelings. When worries pile up, a quick ritual like that can sound appealing. Still, it’s worth asking how much these oils can really do for anxiety.

Ahead, we’ll cover what the research says about essential oils for anxiety, and how to try them at home.

Essential oils are concentrated plant extracts. Makers draw the aromatic compounds out of flowers, leaves, bark, peel, or resin, usually by steaming or pressing the plant. What’s left is a potent oil that carries the plant’s scent.

In a recent development, aromatherapy is the practice of using these scents to ease stress and lift your mood. When you inhale a scent, the molecules reach receptors high in your nose that connect to the limbic system, a part of the brain involved in emotion and memory. That link is one reason a smell can bring back a memory or shift your mood before you've had time to think.

Essential oils may take the edge off anxiety, but think of them as a comfort alongside established treatments, not a substitute for them.

A 2023 systematic review pooled dozens of randomized trials and found that essential oils lowered both in-the-moment and overall anxiety levels compared with unscented oil or usual care.

Early results look promising, though they come with a few caveats. Most of those trials were small, and many measured anxiety in medical settings, such as the nervous stretch before surgery, rather than the everyday worry most people deal with. Results also varied widely from study to study.

If your anxiety is intense and disruptive to your daily life, talk with a doctor or therapist.

Recent findings suggest that 💙 Not sure if it’s stress or anxiety? Here’s how to tell the difference.

According to recent reports, some essential oils have far more anxiety research behind them than others. These five come up most often in studies and in aromatherapy practice. Your scent preference matters here, so you might respond to one oil and not another. Start with the one that appeals to you most.

In a recent development, lavender smells floral and herbal, with a clean, slightly woody edge. It’s the most studied oil for anxiety by a wide margin, and its main compound, linalool, may help calm the nervous system.

Recent findings suggest that A lavender oil capsule called Silexan was tested in a 10-week trial of adults with generalized anxiety disorder, where it reduced anxiety more than a placebo capsule. Since Silexan is swallowed rather than inhaled, the results say little about lavender aromatherapy.

If you’re new to essential oils, lavender is a gentle place to start: its scent is familiar to most people, and it’s widely available.

In a recent development, neroli comes from the blossom of the bitter orange tree, Citrus aurantium. Its scent is sweet and floral, with only a hint of citrus.

In the 2023 meta-analysis, bitter orange oil ranked at or near the top of the oils tested for both in-the-moment and overall anxiety. It didn’t clearly outperform lavender, though, and far fewer trials back it up.

Sources indicate that unlike bergamot and other citrus peel oils, neroli hasn’t shown sun-sensitivity problems. Even so, as with any oil, dilute it and patch-test first (see the safety notes below).

Rose, often sold as Damask rose oil, smells sweet and floral. In the same 2023 review, it was the second most studied oil after lavender. Rose oil was linked to lower in-the-moment anxiety, mostly in trials of people facing medical procedures.

Pure rose oil is one of the pricier options, since it takes a mountain of petals to make a small bottle. Fortunately, a little goes a long way, and a few drops in a diffuser can scent a room.

Chamomile oil smells soft, warm, and a little like apple, which suits an evening wind-down.

In a randomized trial, older adults who inhaled chamomile oil for a month had lower anxiety scores than those who received a placebo.

In a separate hospital trial, people with heart conditions who breathed in chamomile oil for two nights had lower anxiety than those given an unscented oil.

Bergamot is the citrus that gives Earl Grey tea its signature scent: fresh and zesty, with a softer, sweeter edge.

In a recent development, in one randomized controlled trial, people in treatment for substance use were given bergamot aromatherapy. They reported lower anxiety than those who received standard care alone.

Industry observers note that bergamot and other citrus peel oils can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. If you apply them to your skin, keep that area out of direct sun for a day or so.

There are several ways to use essential oils, so try a few and see what works for you. Here are the four main methods:.

Sources indicate that diffuse: Add a few drops of oil and water to an electric diffuser to scent a room. This gentle method suits a bedroom or home office.

Sources indicate that inhale: Hold the bottle a few inches from your nose and take a slow breath. You can also put a drop on a tissue and smell that instead.

Industry observers note that apply to skin: Always dilute essential oil before it touches your skin. Mix a few drops into a carrier oil, such as jojoba or coconut, then rub a little on your wrists, temples, or the back of your neck. If you’d rather skip the mixing, pre-diluted rollers are a convenient option.

Add to a bath or shower: For a bath, mix a few drops into a carrier oil or unscented bath base, then pour it into warm water. For a shower, put a few drops on the shower floor, away from the running water, and let the steam carry the scent. Oil can make the floors slippery, so step in carefully.

💙 At bedtime, turn on your diffuser and listen to The Lavender Valley, a Sleep Story on Calm that follows a stroll toward a heavenly scent.

Buy from a reputable brand, since the U.S. Food and Drug Administration doesn’t check essential oils for purity or strength.

Patch-test first: dab diluted oil on a small area of skin and wait 24 hours to check for redness or itching.

Avoid direct sun on skin where you’ve applied citrus peel oils, like bergamot, because they can make skin more sensitive to sunlight.

Don’t swallow essential oils without guidance from a qualified healthcare professional.

Keep essential oils away from children and pets, since some oils are toxic to animals.

Check with your doctor if you're pregnant, breastfeeding, or managing a health condition, as some oils aren't recommended.

Aromatherapy can be one part of a wider wellness routine. Use oils alongside other habits that may help with anxiety, like gentle movement, breathing exercises, time outside, and meditation. For instance, smelling lavender before a guided meditation can help you settle in.

💙 To round out your routine, explore these six natural ways to ease anxiety.

💙 Pair your aromatherapy with Calming Anxiety, a five-minute breathing meditation on Calm.

Lavender is the most studied oil for anxiety, which makes it a popular first pick. That said, scent preference matters, so the oil you enjoy most may suit you best. Neroli, rose, chamomile, and bergamot are also common choices, with some research to support them.

Sources indicate that essential oils may help you feel less anxious, and studies have found a modest calming effect, especially in stressful moments. However, the research is limited, especially for everyday anxiety.

In a recent development, if your anxiety feels frequent or intense, or if you’re having panic attacks, reach out to a doctor or therapist for support. Oils can be one small part of your routine, but they can’t replace medication or therapy.

It has been revealed that you can put diluted essential oil on pulse points, like your wrists, temples, the back of your neck, or behind your ears, where body warmth helps release the scent. Mix the oil into a carrier oil first, and avoid putting citrus oils on skin that will be in direct sun.

Industry observers note that at home, you can diffuse a few drops of essential oil, inhale from the bottle, apply diluted oil to your skin, or add an oil blend to a bath. Pick the method that fits your space and routine.

Frankincense is a popular choice for relaxation, but research on its effects on people is still limited. Most of the evidence comes from animal studies on one of its compounds, incensole acetate, which reduced anxious behavior in mice. If you enjoy its warm, woody scent, it may still be worth trying.

Aromatherapy uses essential oils on purpose, while smelling something nice can mean anything pleasant, from fresh-baked bread to your favorite candle. With aromatherapy, you can pick a scent and diffuse it or breathe it in from the bottle. Both can lift your mood, but aromatherapy makes smelling the scent a habit.

Essential oils can irritate sensitive skin, so it helps to dilute them in a carrier oil and patch test first. If you have a skin condition like eczema, ask your doctor before trying aromatherapy, or skip skin contact and use a diffuser instead.

International Essential Oils Day is on July 11 every year. It’s a day to celebrate essential oils and the ways people use them for well-being. If you’ve been curious about aromatherapy, it’s a good time to try it.

It has been revealed that you don’t need much to take part. Choose an essential oil that appeals to you, such as lavender or rose, and add a few drops to a diffuser. Then take in the scent with a few slow breaths or a short meditation. If you already use oils, you could try a newly introduced scent or build a wind-down habit around a favorite.

Sources indicate that mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Chris Moody was a senior political correspondent with CNN for many years and is now a journalism professor at Appalachian State University in Boone, NC. He lives in a log cabin in a mountain hollow with his wife and their three-year-old son. The cabin has no cell signal. Over three years ago, they cancelled their home internet and went with a landline (intended to be a temporary measure for one summer). They write about it all in their Substack, The Opt Outers. I interviewed him about why willpower can’t compete with our devices, and what people who can’t move to the mountains can do instead.

Recent findings suggest that yael Hallak: I deleted my social media accounts six months ago. Then I came across the password to an old Instagram account, and I'm back to scrolling. I can't move to the mountains. What can we do as a species?

Chris Moody: The tech companies know what grabs our attention, and they feed it to us (that's how they make their money). Billions of dollars are being thrown at us, and no human will ever be able to win that battle every time, whether you're trying to find an old password or simply want to switch your mind off.

Recent findings suggest that so create what I call a Sabbath space — a room, a floor, a corner of the house, where these technologies simply can't go in. Some people go down the route of "landlining," where the phone is left plugged in on the kitchen counter, and you're only allowed to use it there, standing. What would have been three hours on the couch comes down to three minutes. Think about whether you actually need Wi-Fi at all or whether a wired connection in one room would be sufficient. And make the rules when you're sober; you don't want to be relying on yourself when you're drunk.

YK: Why not just go with discipline?

According to recent reports, CM: Even if you're not using it, the phone is still calling; it's like the sirens calling out to Odysseus. Every moment is a decision, and decision fatigue wins. That's why we have a scoop of ice cream at 9 p.m. and not at 9 a.m.

According to recent reports, I drove fifteen minutes to a studio for this interview. My couch would have been far easier, but it's worth it. When I'm finished in town, the laptop goes down, and at home I couldn't have checked email if I'd wanted to. The people who need me have my landline. I'm not living in the 1890s, more in the 1990s.

YK: During the recent bank and flight outages, I was constantly refreshing X. Information is what makes me feel in control. My husband is always telling me to put the phone down and look out of the window.

CM: Today's channels don't give you any data that's going to help. They just feed an appetite that can't be quenched; they're just empty calories. You can learn what you need from the Sunday New York Times once a week. A reporter on a presidential campaign needs real time. Most people don't.

According to recent reports, look at the boomers, the richest generation in history, spending their days being angry online. Do they have more information? Possibly. Are they any happier? No.

YK: You teach undergrads; how are they getting on?

It has been revealed that CM: They know the monster is coming for them and they think they've been had. Some of them, the ones brought up by phone-obsessed parents, are completely radicalised: "I'll never ignore my child the way my own did." When they see my Nokia flip phone, they go absolutely mental, and a few of them come back with "I've got one!" They're just as hooked as everyone else, just as keen to get their hands on one, but they're thinking about it very carefully. I'm hopeful.

Recent findings suggest that YK: So many people want this life. What enabled you to get it?

CM: My first real job post-college was in social media (at the very beginning of it), and I saw what the algorithms did to my friends. I'm an extrovert, a golden retriever when the doorbell rings, and suddenly everyone just went off and into their screens. Mostly it's my wife, really. She's the one who drives it. Left to my own devices, I go with the flow.

YK: What do you do at dinners where everyone's on their phone?

Recent findings suggest that CM: At our place, it just works itself out as we don't have phones. People come and ask for the Wi-Fi password, and I say we don't have one; there's a landline if you want it. They never do. We don't have to take the rubbish we've been given; we can just eat the better stuff.

According to recent reports, YK: Is there anything you're missing? Podcasts, audiobooks?

Industry observers note that CM: Not at all. I download the episodes in town and listen to them at home whilst doing the dishes. On Friday nights we watch a library DVD on a projector and a pull-down screen. It takes ten minutes to set it up, and that friction is important. Everything has a beginning and an end. It's not "let's just scroll to the next forever." It's: that's all we've got.

YK: So you just have more willpower than the rest of us?

CM: No! I have absolutely no willpower. I'm a disaster. When I'm on the road, and there's Wi-Fi all over the place, I just go absolutely mad and end up with no idea how the time has gotten away from me. The solution is systems, really. Less friction for the good things, more for the bad. In New York, we put our phones in baskets by the door, and we had the router on a timer, which would turn it off from 8 p.m. to 8 a.m. If we're going to rely on willpower, we're all going to fail. We all are.

#383. Tech Report: Study: Menstrual Cycle Irregularities Linked to ADHD, Depression, Anxiety in Girls

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1023 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Additudemag

Tech Report: Study: Menstrual Cycle Irregularities Linked to ADHD, Depression, Anxiety in Girls

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a new study.
  • Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1.
  • The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a new study.

Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1.

The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.

Industry observers note that study participants self-reported the severity of premenstrual symptoms, such as irritability and fatigue, and the intensity of period pain (categorized as mild, moderate, or severe). Findings demonstrated that severe menstrual pain was associated with higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptoms.

Premenstrual symptoms demonstrated a graded pattern in their association with mental health outcomes. Mild premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety symptom scores. Moderate premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety and depression symptom scores. Severe premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores.

The researchers offered several social and biological factors as potential explanations for these results.

“Psychosocially, menstrual pain and [premenstrual symptoms] may result in functional impairment – including missed school, disrupted sleep, reduced social participation – which may contribute to emotional distress,” they wrote.

The study explained that intense period pain and premenstrual distress may activate inflammatory and pain-sensitivity pathways, increasing vulnerability to anxiety and depression. Researchers also noted that the neurobiological mechanisms for processing pain may overlap with those involved in attention and focus, which could help explain the connection between menstrual pain and ADHD symptoms.

Researchers also suggested that fluctuating estrogen and progesterone may help to explain the connection between severe premenstrual symptoms and higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores. These hormones heavily affect serotonin, dopamine, and GABA in the brain. Serotonin is linked to mood; dopamine controls motivation and reward processing; and GABA is crucial for emotional processing and regulation. When hormones fluctuate before a menstrual cycle, these neurotransmitters are impacted too, which, in turn, may influence symptoms of anxiety, depression, and ADHD.

The relationship between ADHD and hormonal fluctuations is a pressing subject for many ADDitude readers with lived experience. In an ADDitude survey of nearly 2,000 women with ADHD, almost one in two respondents said that hormonal fluctuations had a “life-altering” or “severe” impact on their ADHD.

“I know that the week before my period I am a complete mess,” Addison, an ADDitude reader, mentioned. “I have to prepare for the fact that my world feels like it’s falling apart emotionally, and I hate the way that I look the most that week. These are weeks I often avoid being with people, as I know I am not the most positive and am the most sensitive.”.

“I used to have lots of irritability, food cravings, tiredness, and was fuzzy-headed three to four days before my period started,” said Connie, another reader.

“I suffer from symptoms like uncontrolled fits of anger and crying spells and feeling extremely overwhelmed the days before my period. I’m even more moody, irritable and have more trouble concentrating,” noted ADDitude reader Elena.

Moreover, women with ADHD are disproportionately affected by premenstrual disorders with more than 40% of women with ADHD experiencing premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) compared to 3% to 9% of women overall.2, 3 PMDD is also heavily tied to hormonal shifts and mental health.

“PMDD is caused by a high sensitivity to fluctuations in estrogen and progesterone, as well as decreases in serotonin – hormonal changes that happen during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle,” wrote Dara Abraham, D.O. in an ADDitude article. “During the luteal phase that follows ovulation, estrogen decreases, as do dopamine, serotonin, and eventually progesterone. These changes cause painful and distressing symptoms until the menstruation begins and hormone levels rise again.”.

The study also found that irregular menstrual cycles were linked to higher depression and anxiety symptom scores. The longer a girl had been having her menstrual cycles, the stronger the link between irregular periods and depression and anxiety symptoms became. Likewise, earlier age at menarche was associated with higher depression symptom scores.

While the study focused specifically on early age at menarche, previous research suggests that early puberty more broadly may have an association to ADHD.

Sources indicate that “Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children,” wrote Molly Nikolas, Ph.D. in an ADDitude article. “In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.”.

According to recent reports, the researchers listed several limitations to the study. Menstrual cycle characteristics were gathered through an annual self-report, and parents reported mental health symptoms. In addition, the relationship between menstrual characteristics and mental health symptoms may be bidirectional. The researchers also reported the associations were modest and that future studies are needed to further explore the potential social and biological mechanisms involved.

The study’s authors said they hope their findings will help healthcare professionals consider menstrual cycle characteristics as potentially meaningful insight when evaluating the mental health of adolescent girls.

Industry News: When Life Becomes Frantic, We Slip into Autopilot

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that when demands become constant, unrelenting, and urgent, your brain likely shifts from deliberate decision-making mode to automatic routines to save mental energy (Wirz, Bogdanov, and Schwabe, 2018).
  • According to recent reports, learning to live with more intention starts by cultivating an awareness that your days have become blurred and indistinct, filled with routines and unexamined habits, and dominated by pressured reactions rather than intentional responses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Sources indicate that the world moves faster now than ever before. Rapidly accelerating technology and AI development build on each other exponentially, compressing the time it takes for major shifts to occur. Digital tools and instant communication are efficient but can also foment a work culture that embraces around-the-clock demands. Nonstop access to news, social media, and other content floods our brains with more input than we can process. This is all compounded by the overwhelming experience of poly-crisis, that is, multiple global challenges that are continuous, interconnected, and amplify one another as they collide. The bombardment of these factors can keep our brains in a low-grade fight-or-flight state.

Sources indicate that when demands become constant, unrelenting, and urgent, your brain likely shifts from deliberate decision-making mode to automatic routines to save mental energy (Wirz, Bogdanov, and Schwabe, 2018). Research shows that approximately two-thirds of our daily actions are driven by habit rather than conscious decision-making (Rebar and colleagues, 2026). When your days fly by on autopilot, they become indistinguishable and leave you feeling spent, overwhelmed, and exhausted. Living a more intentional life and staying grounded in your body and the present moment means stepping away from autopilot and bringing conscious choice back to your days.

According to recent reports, learning to live with more intention starts by cultivating an awareness that your days have become blurred and indistinct, filled with routines and unexamined habits, and dominated by pressured reactions rather than intentional responses. Stop for a moment and ask: Where is all my urgent energy taking me? Is there a clear finish line? Do I just push through, day after day?

From Autopilot to Mindful Presence.

Becoming more intentional means knowing the direction you are aiming for, with the sense that your goals are worth pursuing. A strong sense of purpose has been linked to better physical health and emotional well-being, including better sleep, lower cortisol/stress, greater mental clarity, a stronger immune system, and enhanced resilience (Kim and colleagues, 2022).

Recent findings suggest that intention means taking the time to notice a moment with your full attention. When your mind is busy replaying events from the past or is perseverating on what might happen in the future, you are no longer present. You become disconnected and are likely stuck on high alert. When this happens, your brain’s ability to encode latest information becomes impaired, making it harder to take in what is happening around you. Living with intention means paying attention and staying present in the moment, with mindfulness and without judgment. You can practice this with simple behaviors aimed at increasing brief moments of noticing. For example, pause for a few deep breaths before entering a meeting and ask yourself what matters most as you arrive. You can simplify this further. Whenever you switch tasks or enter a new setting, take a deep, mindful breath and say to yourself, “Arriving.”.

Another way to enhance your awareness is to turn routine tasks, such as washing the dishes or taking a shower, into anchors for staying present. We tend to rush through these without really taking notice. These tasks offer perfect opportunities to slow down and notice what the water feels like and listen to the sounds around you. Adding a moment of gratitude, where you acknowledge small joys or blessings, helps shift your perspective from what is missing to what you have in the moment.

Small Changes Interrupt Automatic Habits.

Recent findings suggest that you do not need to retool your entire schedule to feel present. Small, low-effort shifts can interrupt automatic habits. Any little thing that introduces novelty can move your brain from automatic processing into active awareness—use your non-dominant hand while brushing your teeth or take an unfamiliar route home. When your brain encounters something unexpected, your internal predictions fail, and you are rewarded with a dopamine surge as your focus sharpens and awareness is enhanced as your brain moves out of autopilot.

Recent findings suggest that setting clear boundaries with yourself is something else to consider. Rather than a cluttered mind and desk, intention means actively choosing where your energy goes. Multi-tasking can take you away from intentionality. Instead, train yourself to be present with each activity. When you are eating, just eat. If you are driving, just focus on the drive. Your decisions, massive and small, can be honed to better reflect your genuine priorities, such as health or creativity.

In a recent development, finally, think about how you respond to messages and questions throughout your day. Rather than urgently reacting to each communication, you might pause for a reflective breath before responding. Slow down so that your nervous system remains balanced and calm. If you notice tension building or you rush through messages, step away for a brief time-out to bring yourself back into the present. Ask yourself whether the speed is actually necessary or just an ingrained habit.

Recent findings suggest that living with intention is not a single decision. It is an ongoing practice. At the end of the day, take a moment to look back and ask, “Where did my time go? What reflected my values? What did not?” These small practices add up so that the gap between the life you are living and the life you intend to live begins to narrow.

Recent findings suggest that the unemployment rate for workers with autism is staggering. One Australian tech giant is aiming to change that.

In Australia, the unemployment rate for neurodivergent adults hovers around 34%, nearly eight times the national average. Clearly, there is a stigma around hiring neurodivergent people and it stems from a fear of the unknown. One not-for-profit organization, Australian Spatial Analytics (ASA), is working to fix that.

ASA was established in 2020 to increase workforce participation among young neurodivergent adults by training them in significant data for the geospatial and digital engineering fields, then placing them in corporate and government sectors. At ASA, we leverage these employees’ cognitive strengths — attention to detail, pattern recognition, laser-sharp focus, and innovative problem-solving skills, all of which are invaluable in these fields.

Recent findings suggest that about 80% of ASA’s staff identify as neurodivergent, which includes ADHD, autism, dyslexia, dyscalculia, and dyspraxia. ASA’s recruitment process goes beyond conventional practices; it assesses potential candidates based on transferable skills, hobbies, and interests, rather than relying on formal qualifications or previous experience. Many of the upcoming data analysts we have successfully placed in jobs are in paid positions for the first time.

[Read: We’re Hiring – ADHD-Friendly Careers].

Yet the analysts’ value to their employers is without questions. Executives have praised the ASA-trained analysts who have joined their companies, citing their work ethic, dedication, and problem-solving skills.

During the job-seeking process, ASA provides candidates with sample interview questions 48 hours in advance to help minimize anxiety. Once hired, employees receive comprehensive and paid on-the-job training that includes soft skills like communication and self-advocacy coaching.

[Read: Nail Your Job Interview – 3 Strategies for Neurodivergent Applicants].

According to recent reports, based on our experience, creating a supportive and productive environment requires only minor accommodations. Flexible start and finish times, predictable routines, the option for hybrid work to reduce commuting stress, adjustable lighting, noise-canceling headphones, and direct communication make a profound difference, not only for neurodivergent people, but for everyone in the workplace.

It has been revealed that to help change paradigms, ASA offers a Neurodiversity in the Workplace Training Program for other organizations. It covers neurodiversity awareness, plus effective strategies for communication, managing anxiety in the work environment, leading neurodiverse teams, and promoting neurodivergent inclusion.

Ultimately, our goal is to put ourselves out of business.

Karly Ischenko is a Human Resources Business Partner at Australian Spatial Analytics.

#380. "You'll Change Your Mind": The Messages Asexual Women Remember

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1190 w)

"You'll Change Your Mind": The Messages Asexual Women Remember

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • Recent findings suggest that co-written by Abigail Heuton, M.A., a current Ph.D.
  • Have you ever been told something that stuck with you long after the conversation ended?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

Recent findings suggest that co-written by Abigail Heuton, M.A., a current Ph.D. student.

Have you ever been told something that stuck with you long after the conversation ended?

Maybe it was a piece of advice from a parent, like "money doesn't grow on trees," or encouragement from a teacher who believed in you when you didn't believe in yourself.

In a recent development, as communication researchers, we call these memorable messages—statements that stay with us over time, shaping how we understand ourselves, our relationships, and the world around us. Some offer reassurance or guidance. Others communicate expectations about who we should be or how our lives should unfold.

Industry observers note that asexuality is commonly defined as experiencing little to no sexual attraction, although it exists on a spectrum. Asexual individuals may experience romantic attraction, pursue relationships, marry, or have children. Their sexual orientation does not necessarily determine their interest in relationships, sexual activity, or parenthood.

Despite this diversity, asexuality remains widely misunderstood and is often characterized as an invisible sexuality. Asexual individuals frequently encounter assumptions that their identity is temporary, invalid, or something that needs to be fixed.

For asexual women, these misconceptions intersect with societal expectations surrounding relationships, marriage, and motherhood. When these milestones are treated as universal expectations, women whose identities or choices differ may find themselves having to explain or defend them.

To better understand these experiences, we asked asexual women across the United States to recall memorable messages they had received about childbearing. Of the 126 individuals who participated in our study, 107 recalled a memorable message—and 94% were negative.

Five themes emerged from their responses:.

1. Motherhood as an obligation. Some women recalled messages framing motherhood as a biological, religious, or social responsibility rather than a personal choice.

Industry observers note that one woman recalled being told by a male friend that she was "selfish by 'choosing' to be asexual and not having children and... wasn't really a woman.".

In a recent development, 2. Family expectations and interpersonal pressure. Other messages emphasized the desires of parents and grandparents, particularly their expectations of having grandchildren.

Another woman recalled, "My mother insisted that she was suffering because I was depriving her of grandchildren.".

According to recent reports, 3. Fear of a life without children. Participants also received warnings suggesting that choosing not to have children would inevitably lead to loneliness or regret.

One woman remembered being told, "[I]f you don't have children you'll end up forgotten as an elderly person and die alone.".

According to recent reports, 4. Identity invalidation through future predictions. Some of the most familiar messages suggested that participants' identities or reproductive preferences were temporary. As one participant explained, "I remember hearing what most people used to say: 'It's a phase', 'You'll change your mind one day', 'I used to think I didn't want kids either until I met your father/mother.' Because what if I don't? What if I really don't want children?".

Rather than accepting women's understanding of their own identities and aspirations, these messages assumed their futures would eventually align with conventional expectations.

5. Social scrutiny and judgment. Participants described having their sexuality and reproductive choices questioned or dismissed. One participant recalled being told, "[A] woman can't be asexual and want kids. That is senseless...just say you're a lesbian.".

These messages share common assumption: There is a particular way women are supposed to experience sexuality, relationships, and motherhood.

One of the most striking findings from our study was what participants were told, but by whom. Nearly 70% of the memorable messages were communicated by other women (e.g., mothers, other family members, and friends). This raises an interesting question: Why do women sometimes reinforce the same expectations that have historically limited their own choices?

Gender norms are learned, communicated, and reproduced through everyday interactions, including conversations between mothers and daughters, among friends, and across generations.

Women who have been taught that motherhood is central to a fulfilling life may communicate that belief to others, sometimes without recognizing the pressure it creates.

For instance, one participant recalled, "My mom and grandma talk about it every time I see them because I'm getting older. They make fun of me for not having kids yet and me ending our bloodline.".

Industry observers note that in this example, motherhood becomes more than an individual decision. It becomes a family expectation, one tied to ideas about lineage, responsibility, and what women owe to previous generations. Of course, we cannot know whether the women sending these messages intend to cause harm. A mother expressing concern about her daughter's future may genuinely believe she is offering helpful advice. But intentions and impacts are not always the same. These interactions illustrate how cultural expectations can be passed down through relationships, even by people who have experienced those same pressures themselves.

The consequences of these memorable messages extended beyond the original conversations. Some participants described feeling ashamed, misunderstood, or uncertain about their identities. Others reported becoming more confident in their decisions, even when the messages themselves were hurtful.

In a recent development, one participant described how her mother's repeated comments about motherhood affected their relationship: "It has negatively affected my relationship with my mother even though she does not realize it. I am content with being asexual and my stance on being childfree.".

Some participants became more outspoken about their boundaries. One woman recalled being told that her asexuality must have resulted from trauma and that therapy could "fix" her. Rather than reconsidering her identity, she explained, "It's made me more proactive about telling people children are entirely off the table for me. I don't allow others to even entertain the thought that they can convince me or somehow change my mind.".

Although our research focused on asexual women, the findings invite us to reconsider how we talk about other people's futures. How often do we ask about marriage, relationships, or children without considering whether those are milestones someone actually wants? And how frequently do we respond to someone's choices by insisting they'll eventually change their mind?

Industry observers note that of course, asking about someone's future is not inherently harmful. These conversations can be meaningful ways of connecting with people we care about. But there is a difference between expressing curiosity about someone's life and communicating that their life should follow a particular path.

Sources indicate that the messages we communicate can stay with people for years. Perhaps the most meaningful ones are those that make people feel understood rather than expected to become someone else.

Heuton, A. E., & Edwards, A. L. (2026). “You’ll change your mind”: A mixed-methods study of asexual women’s memorable messages about childbearing. LGBTQ+ Family: An Interdisciplinary Journal. doi.org/10.1080/27703371.2026.2748623.

Cooke-Jackson, A., Gunning, J. N., & Rubinsky, V. (2025). Theory of memorable messages. Journal of Communication, 75(4), 259–272. doi.org/10.1093/joc/jqaf016.

#379. MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1663 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily

MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that while we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults.
  • According to recent reports, the findings raise key questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that while we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste. But new research from MIT suggests that this natural cleaning system becomes less effective as we grow older, revealing another way aging can change the brain beyond simply disrupting sleep.

Recent findings suggest that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults. The decline appears to be connected to changes in the slow electrical waves that occur during deep sleep, as well as changes in how blood moves through the brain. Importantly, the reduced fluid movement cannot be explained simply by older people spending less time asleep.

According to recent reports, the findings raise key questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. The team now hopes to determine whether changes in these fluid waves could eventually help identify people at greater risk of cognitive decline.

According to recent reports, "We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis and her colleagues also want to investigate whether treatments or other interventions could strengthen this waste-clearing process in older adults.

The study was published in Nature Aging, with Lewis serving as senior author. Its lead authors are Sydney Bailes, a postdoctoral researcher in MIT's Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former MIT visiting student who received her PhD from Boston University in 2026.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Clear Waste.

Sources indicate that deep sleep does much more than leave us feeling refreshed. During its deepest stages, known as non-REM sleep, the brain produces powerful, slow electrical waves that support physical recovery, strengthen memories, and help regulate other essential functions.

In 2019, Lewis and her colleagues discovered that these slow brain waves also help generate rhythmic movements of cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid moves through spaces around the brain and plays an key role in carrying away waste products.

That earlier discovery led to a new question. Because slow brain waves typically weaken with age, could the fluid movements responsible for clearing waste also become less effective?

Previous research had produced conflicting results. Some studies suggested that cerebrospinal fluid movement declined with age, while others reported increases. However, those investigations had not directly monitored the fluid during sleep, when the brain's natural cleaning activity is especially crucial.

To investigate, the MIT team recruited two groups of volunteers. Younger participants were between 18 and 39 years old, while the older group ranged from 60 to 84.

Industry observers note that each volunteer completed a testing session lasting approximately two hours. The sessions began late at night, increasing the likelihood that participants would become sleepy during the measurements.

According to recent reports, the researchers combined several techniques to observe what was happening inside the brain. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, allowed them to track changes in cerebral blood flow. A specialized MRI method developed by Lewis measured cerebrospinal fluid movement, while electroencephalography, or EEG, recorded the brain's electrical activity.

Many participants fell asleep inside the scanner, providing an opportunity to compare their brain activity and fluid movements during wakefulness and sleep.

According to recent reports, the results revealed a striking age difference. As younger adults entered non-REM sleep, their slow brain waves grew stronger and were accompanied by larger waves of cerebrospinal fluid. In older adults, however, the average fluid waves were substantially smaller.

The findings highlighted that aging was associated with a weakening of the fluid movements that normally accompany deep sleep.

Why the Aging Brain's Cleaning Waves Weaken.

According to recent reports, the researchers next investigated what might be causing this decline. In a separate set of experiments conducted while participants were fully awake, they examined how the brain's blood vessels responded to different demands.

One possible explanation involved neurovascular coupling, the process that connects brain activity with blood flow.

Sources indicate that when a particular region of the brain becomes more active, its cells require additional oxygen and nutrients. Nearby blood vessels normally widen to deliver more blood, ensuring that the active cells receive the resources they need.

Industry observers note that to measure this response, the researchers revealed volunteers a flickering checkerboard pattern while monitoring blood flow with fMRI. The rapidly changing visual pattern stimulates activity in regions involved in processing vision, which should trigger an increase in local blood supply.

It has been revealed that in many older participants, the brain's electrical activity increased as expected, but the corresponding rise in blood flow was much smaller. This suggested that aging had weakened the ability of blood vessels to respond to the brain's changing oxygen requirements.

The team then performed a second experiment to examine the brain's broader vascular responsiveness.

Participants were instructed to hold their breath while researchers monitored changes in cerebral blood flow. Holding one's breath causes carbon dioxide to accumulate in the bloodstream, which normally prompts blood vessels in the brain to widen and increase blood flow.

Once again, the older group showed a weaker response. On average, their cerebral blood flow increased less than it did in younger volunteers.

Together, these experiments indicated that changes in the brain's vascular system could help explain why its waste-clearing fluid waves diminish with age.

Using a statistical model, the scientists found that weakened neurovascular coupling and reduced blood flow responses accounted for much of the decline in cerebrospinal fluid movement. However, the two mechanisms did not explain the entire difference, suggesting that additional biological changes associated with aging are also involved.

"Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it's really hard to disentangle the individual factors," Bailes notes. "We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual's CSF flow might be more or less impaired.".

Could Weaker Brain Cleansing Increase Dementia Risk?

The discovery may have key implications for understanding neurological diseases associated with aging.

Earlier studies have linked disrupted sleep to a greater risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Because cerebrospinal fluid helps remove waste from the brain, researchers are particularly interested in whether age-related changes in its movement might contribute to neurodegeneration.

None of the volunteers in the MIT study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder. However, brain scans revealed that some older participants revealed signs of gray matter atrophy, meaning a loss of brain tissue in regions containing large numbers of nerve cells.

Those changes were associated with greater reductions in cerebrospinal fluid movement.

Sources indicate that the relationship does not establish that weakened fluid flow causes brain tissue loss or dementia. Nevertheless, it provides a reason to investigate whether these changes might serve as early warning signs of neurological decline.

The researchers hope to follow some of the participants over time to determine whether reduced cerebrospinal fluid movement is associated with a greater likelihood of developing a neurodegenerative condition.

Can the Brain's Nighttime Cleaning System Be Restored?

Beyond understanding why brain cleansing declines, the MIT team is exploring whether it might be possible to improve the process.

One promising possibility involves sound stimulation during sleep.

In a separate recent study, Lewis' laboratory found that brief bursts of "pink noise" could increase cerebrospinal fluid movement in younger adults. Pink noise is a type of sound that contains a broad range of frequencies, with greater emphasis on lower frequencies than white noise.

Although the approach has shown potential in younger people, researchers have not yet tested whether it can produce similar effects in older adults.

Another intriguing finding could provide clues about how to preserve the brain's natural cleaning abilities.

While older participants generally had weaker cerebrospinal fluid waves than younger adults, the decline was not universal. Some older volunteers retained fluid movements that were comparable to those measured in healthy younger people.

This raises the possibility that certain biological or lifestyle factors may help protect the brain's waste-removal system against aging.

Recent findings suggest that "It's really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults," Lewis states. "We are really interested in what's different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes.".

Understanding why some older brains maintain these youthful fluid movements could ultimately help researchers identify ways to support healthier brain aging and investigate whether preserving the brain's nighttime cleaning system can reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program.

#378. Industry News: When Psychiatry Becomes Mind-Blind

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1056 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Industry News: When Psychiatry Becomes Mind-Blind

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1056 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.
  • Industry observers note that I once sat in a room while a psychiatrist discussed with my parents his belief that I would face a lifetime of institutionalization.
  • I borrow this term from biologist and natural philosopher Michael Levin: Mind-blindness is the inability to recognize the minds of others.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Industry observers note that I once sat in a room while a psychiatrist discussed with my parents his belief that I would face a lifetime of institutionalization. At 15, I was perfectly capable of understanding him. The conversation excluded me not because I couldn’t grasp it but because that doctor had uttered the word “schizophrenia.” Once he did, the sense that anything real might exist in my head, even the most basic sense, evaporated.

The people around me became mind-blind.

I borrow this term from biologist and natural philosopher Michael Levin: Mind-blindness is the inability to recognize the minds of others. Michael was gracious enough to chat with me about it. He believes humans exist in a world full of minds, with cognition a potential not just for other creatures, but for cells, large language models, even algorithms.

“We tend to think of things as either dumb like rocks or smart like humans and angels,” Levin remarked. Instead, Levin believes that the sciences of cybernetics and the tools of behavior science now show mind exists on a continuum, involving testable traits like whether a being can learn and what its competencies are.

Mind-Blindness Begins With Other Humans.

As Levin puts it, it’s more a question of what kind of intelligence exists, and how much, than a yes-or-no distinction.

Industry observers note that when I told Michael Levin I believed humans’ mind-blindness begins with other humans, he said, “You’re absolutely right.” And he added, “I think the problem is a scarcity mentality with respect to compassion. It’s as if people thought, if we allow too many into the club of cognition, there will not be enough care or love for me.”.

I once spoke in sign language with an orangutan named Chantek, who indicated he found his cage mate Sibu a bit messy. Remembering the thoughtfulness of his eyes still makes seeing a caged animal unbearable to me. I live with two cats who often let me know, with headbutts and meows, that I’m about to get sick before I know it; I know we overlook the capacities of the beings around us.

And humans can be highly mind-blind to each other.

White Europeans have historically demonstrated mind-blindness to other racial groups, to the point of enslaving them. Jeffrey Epstein was mind-blind to women, which no doubt made him feel better about his abuse. And based on their testimony, Lindsay Clancy’s caregivers remained mind-blind to the actual thoughts she was having. They slotted her pain into symptom categories, missing the awful acts her mind pushed her toward.

According to recent reports, psychiatry, and the culture that accepts its premises, has been mind-blind. This isn’t only true of my early doctor. Autistic people have suffered with the stigma that they lack “theory of mind,” or an understanding that the people around them have minds and feelings.

When I taught, fellow professors often shared their conviction that students who bothered them must be “on the spectrum.” Though “spectrum” has gotten to be a shorthand for a jumble of traits that don’t even fit together: insensitivity, oversensitivity, bluntness, shyness. These biases still lead to real discrimination, though they’re based largely on misunderstandings of subtle differences.

Then there is the child I was, turned to vapor by the word “schizophrenia.” My diagnosis changed ultimately. But I would be who I am with or without a word from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual next to my name.

Sources indicate that mental states, which DSM terms try and fail to pin down, are less hardwired, binary differences between people than they are part of the human condition, one piece of all our potential. They reflect inborn flaws less than they show the tumult of living a life in this human body.

Recent findings suggest that A good share of the population—as many as 15 percent or more of adults—will at some point in their lives hear voices. Up to 38 percent will experience visual hallucinations, a high enough number to suggest this alone shouldn’t be enough to diagnose psychosis, though it very well could be. And one-quarter to one-third of people who have what is diagnosed as a full-blown schizophrenic episode will never have another one. Those whose conditions become chronic may be impaired as much or more by the treatment as the underlying mental state.

Trauma makes the experience of psychosis far more likely, certainly a factor for me as a girl. Difficult life experiences can also plant the seeds of creativity and novel thought. This was true of mind pioneer Carl Jung. An early exposure to death, and later sexual abuse, traumatized Jung, and as an adult he had an extended period of hallucinations.

It has been revealed that jung described “incessant visions” in his Red Book and compared their impact to thunderstorms and floods. Though this period wasn’t a pointless bout of “illness” in Jung’s life—he called that time the root of his most notable ideas, such as the existence of archetypes and the collective unconscious.

Michael Levin has more to offer the field of psychiatry than the helpful idea of mind-blindness. He believes that in the future we might practice a somatic psychiatry that exploits bioelectricity, the “cognitive glue” aligning cells toward organ-scale anatomical goals, using bioelectrical signaling as an interface through which to communicate desired healthy form and function.

Levin also told me, “Our cells provide another level of intelligence in the body,” and communicating at these other levels might offer pathways to mind care.

Before we fully understand the many ways we can help ourselves, we need to drop narrow beliefs about minds.

Carl Jung wrote that our inner worlds are “truly infinite, in no way poorer than the outer one,” so powerful and individual that “humans live in two worlds.” We share the former world with a dizzying array of other beings. Perhaps, in ways that are not always easy to understand, we share the inner world as well.

“What I hope is that when we can acknowledge that the mind can belong to things that don’t look anything like us,” Michael Levin told me, “our differences become laughably small.”.

#377. Tech Report: The Family Table: Finding Your Place as an Elder

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (878 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Tech Report: The Family Table: Finding Your Place as an Elder

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Note: This post may stir feelings of grief, estrangement, and old wounds.
  • With the holidays approaching, many of us think about our actual family tables and where everyone will sit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Note: This post may stir feelings of grief, estrangement, and old wounds. Not every family table was safe, and that distance or estrangement can be a valid, even necessary, choice.

With the holidays approaching, many of us think about our actual family tables and where everyone will sit. The idea of a family table is also a metaphor for our relationships. For example: Who sets it? Who is served first? Who sits at the head? Who was not invited? Over the course of our lifetimes, our place at the table shifts and rearranges itself, often because of losses, marriages and divorces, grandchildren, aging siblings, distance, and the chosen family members who have pulled up a chair.

We begin our lives at the children’s table; then we are perhaps the chef and server; and as elders, we might be lucky enough to become guests at our children’s or chosen family’s tables.

In a recent development, lately, many people in middle age and beyond have spoken about the changing dynamics of their relationships with their adult children. These feelings can be magnified during the holidays. Things are simply not what they used to be. When our children were young, their world revolved around us and our world revolved around them. Many of us have read books on parenting children and teenagers, but few of us were offered books or conversations about navigating life with our adult children. For many parents of adult children, there’s a deep ache in realizing that their role isn't what it used to be.

In a recent development, we move from managing our children’s lives to being something of an outsider. We are no longer involved in their everyday activities, and sometimes we don’t even know what they’re up to. We might have taught our children the power of independence, and now there is a lot of holding on and letting go.

According to recent reports, becoming a mother-in-law is another challenging role shift. Sharing our children with spouses and in-law families is not always an easy transition, especially if the partner is different from what we imagined for our child and/or if the couple lives far away.

Another shift is that children might begin worrying about their parents rather than the other way around. Perhaps the parents have physical or psychological health problems that call for their children’s intervention and care. It’s vital for elders to accept help while maintaining their dignity. At the same time, many elders are still caring for aging parents or grieving them.

Sadly, estrangement has become increasingly common. Perhaps more common than people care to admit. Very often, because of shame, it’s carried in silence, which can be very painful.

It has been revealed that one woman shared the story of organizing a holiday with her three adult children and four small grandchildren at a beautiful resort. One minute they were a happy family, and the next minute they were estranged. She still isn’t sure what happened, but on the last day of the trip, one of her adult children picked a fight about something that had happened years earlier, leaving the grandparents speechless. Everyone went home, and the adult child who picked a fight simply cut off contact and never really understood why.

Recent findings suggest that those who were close with their grandparents understand how vitally vital this relationship can be. I am the daughter of immigrants, and my parents worked very long hours to make ends meet, so my grandmother was my primary caretaker. Because I remember the closeness of that relationship, I was eager and excited to become a grandmother. I thought long and hard about what kind of grandmother I wanted to be and how I would handle certain situations.

Recent findings suggest that one thing grandparents learn swiftly is the importance of keeping their opinions to themselves. They realize this is vital, especially if they want to keep the lines of communication open with their adult children. This can be difficult, especially when they reach a stage of life when they might have—at a stage of life when they may hold strong opinions that their children don’t want to hear. Many elders say that their children really don’t want their advice. The truth is, younger generations can find most of what they want online, especially now that AI has become an integral part of our lives. The challenge is knowing when to speak and when to stay quiet.

It has been revealed that for those without children, with distant children, or whose friends have become their truest family, the holiday table might look different from what they imagined. Holidays remind us that change is always happening. Sometimes there are empty chairs at the table, sometimes upcoming faces, and sometimes more than one table. Some people might choose new or different traditions, and change requires acceptance. Change calls for acceptance, which leaves room for something new. Remember, nobody ever promised that things would stay the same. Enjoy whatever gathering you're part of. There will always be new stories to tell.
