The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy.
  • It has been revealed that researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words.
  • The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

It has been revealed that researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," noted Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction.".

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy.

In a recent development, the researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

According to recent reports, after writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language.

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Industry observers note that meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

It has been revealed that these differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life.".

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes.

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

Industry observers note that this variation is vital because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

Industry observers note that "People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray stated. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships.".

Like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment.

It has been revealed that recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict key outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's notable to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict.".

Sources indicate that researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she mentioned. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Though we understand that nostalgia is a powerful state—a sentimental longing for the past— we may fall short of harnessing it to transform our lives. A 2014 study published in Self and Identity found that experiencing nostalgia not only evokes positive emotions but also fosters personal growth. This growth is largely driven by positive self-regard, a key psychological resource, one that bolsters nostalgia.

Sources indicate that interestingly, the study also found that nostalgia strengthened feelings of belonging and provided a sense of meaning. These elements help counter loneliness. Here are two tips to make the most of your nostalgic reveries to counter feelings of loneliness and disconnection.

A prescient quote from the hit show The Office goes: “I wish there were a way to know you’re in ‘the good old days’ before you’ve actually left them.”.

In a recent development, the crucial insight is that people often don't recognize the value of experiences while living through them, but tend to view them more positively in retrospect. And this isn’t just anecdotal.

According to recent reports, A classic study published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology explored how people anticipate, experience, and remember significant life events. Participants were divided into groups, each assigned to different events like vacations or trips. They were asked to anticipate these events, record their actual experiences during them, and then recall these experiences after some time had passed.

According to recent reports, the study found that when participants recalled these events later, their memories were predominantly positive, more so than the actual experience. Negative aspects seemed to fade, leaving a “rosier” memory.

Once you embrace that you will long for your past, no matter how lonely it may seem now, you are more likely to create joyful experiences and memories. This can mean striking up a conversation with your barista, joining a volunteer group, or even a stroll in a park—you never know who you may run into.

In a recent development, rosy retrospection empowers us to invest more in our daily interactions, not necessarily with grand expectations, but with an appreciation for their future value in our memories. The trick is recognizing the potential in ordinary moments to become extraordinary, nostalgic memories.

Recent findings suggest that A recent study published in Emotion shows how nostalgia can benefit individuals grappling with loneliness. The study found that for those who often feel a lack of direction or meaning in life—a common issue among the lonely—engaging in nostalgia can have a significant positive effect.

This may be about recalibrating your sense of self in relation to the people around you. Think of it this way: Lonely individuals often feel like side characters in their own lives, often being overwhelmed by their isolation. Experiencing nostalgia (either spontaneous or self-induced) can help recenter their narrative, provided they contextualize the emotions and memories that are associated with the experience.

Recent findings suggest that if you’d like to contextualize and make the most of your nostalgia to regain a sense of meaning in your life, you can try the Hero’s Journey method. This approach involves effective storytelling, where you take charge of your life’s narrative through seven key steps:.

According to recent reports, by mindfully engaging with nostalgia, you can weave a narrative that highlights your journey, underlines your growth, and reinforces your place within a larger community. This approach can combat loneliness and finding meaning.

Our memories are not just a source of comfort but also a bridge to a more fulfilling present. Nostalgia can be a powerful ally in easing loneliness, especially if you can look beyond the passive experience of it. Reflecting on positive past experiences can reframe how you view your current life situation. Generally, we remember the past as rosier than it was, which can help us appreciate the people in our lives more and foster better connections.

  • According to recent reports, with students nearing the end of the semester and hopefully thinking about how they can improve their habits and skills for the new semester, it is worth thinking about the role of reading.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as a college professor for over 30 years, I have worked with countless students who either claim they hate reading or report that they've never finished an entire book. To succeed in college, it’s important to read what’s assigned. It’s also important to read for pleasure. Why? Because, simply put, it makes you more interesting.

According to recent reports, with students nearing the end of the semester and hopefully thinking about how they can improve their habits and skills for the new semester, it is worth thinking about the role of reading. With the holiday break almost upon us, it's the perfect time to practice and to embark on a potentially interesting book.

People who read have a greater sense of fluency of ideas and perspectives that they can bring to bear on conversations, and they possess stronger vocabularies. These qualities give people an edge both socially and professionally. Referencing something you read and learned that resonates with you or naturally relates to a conversation during a job interview, for example, helps position you as someone with insight and depth.

According to recent reports, the other thing to remember is that the habit of reading often translates to greater agility with writing. When you have more exposure to a variety of ways that ideas are expressed, you’re able to gather more information to craft what you want to say.

College is a great time to discover exactly what it is that you like to read. This is especially true if you’re coming to college with little interest in reading. This lack of interest is often due to not having had much say in what you got to read in high school. So, now’s the time to think about what you gravitate to most. What do you find most moving and compelling? Maybe it’s fiction, nonfiction, creative nonfiction, or poetry. Whatever it is, reading is a passport for the experience of world-traveling, which is a gift you can give yourself.

If your parents read to you when you were a child, they may have shown you the value and joy of reading. I’ve started directly asking my students if a parent or guardian read to or with them, what their favorite book was as a child, and what their favorite is now. What’s most sad for me is when students aren’t able to name a single book and instead tell me they “never read,” “never had a parent read to me,” “hate reading,” or “never finished a book.”.

Recent findings suggest that but even if the value of reading was not instilled in you growing up, it’s not too late to develop a habit of reading for pleasure. Find something that potentially interests you, put your phone away where it’s not even visible, grab a fun drink or snack, and curl up in a cozy space and read. Try just 15 minutes at first. If you like it, keep going. If you find yourself restless or sleepy, try to push through a bit longer, and if that doesn’t work then go do something else and make a commitment to yourself to return to the book the next day. Typically, those in the regular practice of reading and enjoying it generally find it easier to be alone and enjoy solitude.

In summary, when college students work to strengthen their reading muscle, both in terms of reading for classes and for pleasure, they encounter the following benefits:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

According to recent reports, among many destructive, ageist stereotypes prevalent in America, one of the most pervasive is that older adults aren’t interested in, capable of, or engaged in having sex. On the contrary, research demonstrates that about three-quarters of those aged 57-64, over half of those aged 65-74, and a quarter of those aged 75-85 had sexual contact with someone in the past year. And this doesn’t even count those who would have chosen to have sex but had no opportunity.

According to recent reports, while the stereotypes are alive and well regarding the nability of older adults to have sex, many, if not most, either do have, or are interested in having, sexual activity with a partner. It’s true older adults may struggle with aspects of sex they didn’t confront when younger—men with the ability to maintain erections or ejaculate; women with lubrication or discomfort. But there are excellent treatments for these conditions, and humans are creative. Older adults engage in satisfying romantic relationships without sexual activity, satisfying sexual relationships without romance, and everything in between. And in terms of sex, older couples not only enjoy intercourse, but also non-penetrative sexual activities like hugging, cuddling, sleeping naked; manual, masturbatory, and oral play activities, and more.

Sources indicate that A recent study by Harris and Melanson (2026) interviewed 100 single older adults aged 60-83 (50 women and 50 men) recruited from dating sites for gender, racial, and educational diversity. More older adults are single today than ever before (due to longer lives and the acceptance of divorce), and this group is understudied compared to older adults with partners. The Harris and Melanson study was limited by heterosexual participants, but we can extrapolate many of its findings to all relationships:.

Sex is a healthy part of life throughout adulthood, whether one is single, partnered, or in between. How it looks and when it happens may change, and some adults may do well without a partner, but the majority of older adults, like younger adults, find partnered sex an important ingredient of healthy social lives, life satisfaction, and wellbeing.

Recent findings suggest that harris and Melanson surveyed an often-ignored group of older adults—those who are single. Because they found them through dating sites, we know participants in the sample were at least somewhat interested in pursuing romantic and/or sexual partnerships. It’s up to future researchers to explore whether single older adults not interested in dating are equally interested in sex (with another person), or simply feel content alone; as well as how these results may be different in LGBTQ+ and other marginalized populations.

Tech Report: Inside the World of an Intimacy Coordinator

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Recently, after seeing a stage play, I spoke to a lead actor about how she is able to feel safe during physically intimate scenes in front of an audience.
  • It has been revealed that I wanted to find out more about this and, unexpectedly, I met intimacy coordinator Christina McHugh at an event in Upcoming Mexico a few weeks later.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Recently, after seeing a stage play, I spoke to a lead actor about how she is able to feel safe during physically intimate scenes in front of an audience. She told me that there is an intimacy coordinator who comes onto the set to make sure the actors’ feelings about intimacy with other actors are taken into account. She has also worked on film sets with an intimacy coordinator when she felt uneasy and vulnerable in front of the camera and crew and her lover in the film.

It has been revealed that I wanted to find out more about this and, unexpectedly, I met intimacy coordinator Christina McHugh at an event in Upcoming Mexico a few weeks later. I asked her to define what it is that she does when she is hired to work on films. “Old-fashioned doctors went house to house, a mail person goes door to door, and an intimacy coordinator goes set to set.” The geographical areas she covered were Albuquerque, Santa Fe, and movie ranches. She goes from one set to another.

She explained that making actors feel psychologically and physically safe was mostly prep work, before the scenes were shot. She had extensive conversations with directors and then worked with the actors to find out what their boundaries were and to get their consent. “Then I would go back to the director and impart information like the fact that the actor wanted less nudity. I would ask the director if it could be filmed a different way.”.

Recent findings suggest that for filming sex scenes, she used things like a “half-deflated Pilates ball to put between the actors’ crotches. There were often three layers of barriers between the actors for simulated sex. If the woman is on top of the man, her bouncing is done with a 9-inch Pilates ball that makes it look like simulated sex.”.

Recent findings suggest that mcHugh remarked that her job entails negotiating boundaries with individual actors, the director, and trying to get all sides to agree. This is especially true in building trust on the set of a film with hyper-exposure, that includes nudity, simulated sex, and sexual violence.

Some of the sets she worked on include "Better Call Saul," "Pluribus," "Love Lies Bleeding," "Obliterated," "Duster," "The Cleaning Lady," "Waco," and "Dead for a Dollar.".

I inquired where she learned her profession, and she replied that she trained with the Intimacy Professionals Association. “In about 2017, it was the first time it highlighted up in a credit line. It started with an HBO series, "The Deuce," which was about the porn industry. The actress felt she was being treated as a porn star and not an actress.”.

I believed her when McHugh mentioned you need a spine made of titanium to deal with producers and directors. She is not flippant about the issues actors have when she is negotiating with them. She said that young female actors tell her about being victims of sexual predation, and she takes care of them. This is an key part of her job, which she takes very seriously.

Entertainment writer Liz Konkel had this to say in a recent post on Cinema Blend: “The rules have certainly changed in regard to how sex scenes are filmed, thanks to the rise of intimacy coordinators on sets. Now, this doesn't mean we don't get plenty of steamy content. However, what it does mean is that more technical work goes into creating such scenes. In a post #MeToo Movement industry, these coordinators also help ensure actors feel comfortable and protected during intimate scenes.”.

Industry observers note that in the same article, she also addressed how actors’ boundaries and trust concerns were dealt with before intimacy coordinators. “Back in the early aughts, scenes were seemingly required of the actors if it was in the script. However, some performers have since shared stories where trust was taken advantage of on set. For instance, "Basic Instinct’s" Sharon Stone has made claims involving inappropriate requests for nudity amid production. With that, many now consider intimacy coordinators to be essential.”.

#337. Industry News: Making Change Happen

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1328 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Industry News: Making Change Happen

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • According to recent reports, so, you realize that the way you have been going about things doesn’t work.
  • I cringe when I hear people say “That’s just the way I am” while at the same time complaining about the state of their relationships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

According to recent reports, so, you realize that the way you have been going about things doesn’t work. You might not like the way you behave or your experience of relationships. You might not like the way you feel or how your emotions impact your decisions. And you know that if you don’t turn things around, you are going to keep repeating the same cycle. But people often struggle to change even when they genuinely want to.

I cringe when I hear people say “That’s just the way I am” while at the same time complaining about the state of their relationships. Some people use that statement to avoid responsibility. They believe their personality characteristics are fixed or have repeatedly failed in their efforts to foster change within themselves. So, rather than putting effort into changing themselves, many people prefer that others would simply come to their senses and accommodate them.

You can always work on changing the environment, and this is usually what people try first. They try to convince, persuade, nudge, and manipulate others… or they shut themselves off interpersonally, go into denial, or resort to blame and attack. But these efforts rarely result in lasting positive outcomes, and people stay happy only as long as the environment is cooperating.

Here is my recommended outline for lasting change and understanding why change can be so hard. I recommend taking these steps sequentially, as they build on each other in a cumulative fashion.

Industry observers note that if you want to change yourself, you first need to consider what “self” you are referring to. Changing your entire being may seem insurmountable and lead you to give up before you even start. But many psychological theorists view the self as multifaceted. In other words, we are all groupings of associated parts, and we can use our more developed parts to help shape and coach the less developed ones that we are trying to change.

Sometimes change means de-emphasizing one previously dominant part of your personality and strengthening a part that was previously dormant.

People are often ambivalent about change and might actually get something out of maintaining their negative behaviors.

According to recent reports, before you lay aside your own ambivalence, let’s see what you actually get out of the behavior or experience you say you want to let go of. What will you lose if you change? What are the factors arguing against it?

It has been revealed that become conscious of your own resistance. Before evoking your commitment to a fresh course of action, it might help to first write down all of the positive things you get out of it. For example, what if you want to cut down on your drinking? Drinking might help you gain social acceptance and feel less lonely. It might help you relax and escape your anxiety and internal demons. Or it might simply help you escape boredom and give you something to do. These are all reasonable goals, and before you lay down the booze, you might want to consider how you are going to meet them.

In a recent development, but then you must ask yourself, what would need to change first before the behavior can change? Problematic behaviors are often not consciously chosen but, rather, come about through how we regulate our emotions— for example, putting too much pressure on an ambivalent romantic partner, talking too much about your insecurities, or getting aggravated and shutting down when interactions with a relationship partner get touchy.

In these examples, the root cause is often difficulty controlling your emotions.

Sometimes, your rational brain knows what it wants to do, but your emotional brain just won’t cooperate.

Industry observers note that you should learn about how people with your personality style regulate anxiety. For example, a person with an avoidant attachment style will most likely regulate anxiety by withdrawing, shutting down, or dominating. A person with an anxious attachment style is most likely to regulate emotions by pressing too hard for reassurance or oversharing.

Sources indicate that learn about your personality and attachment style… then you will have an easier time changing your behavior. In other words, your conscious brain will understand what your emotional brain is doing and how to keep it from taking over.

Sources indicate that sometimes you just need an attitude adjustment. In the preceding paragraphs, I outlined how subconscious processes, like regulating emotions, influence behavior. But sometimes, behavior comes from the more conscious parts of your mind. In other words, your emotions follow your thoughts instead of the other way around. Attitudes are consciously held statements that you tell yourself about the way things are. You can change your attitudes by watching your self-talk and what you say to yourself in your head. Don’t expect to have angry, intolerant thoughts and be able to pull off controlling your emotions and acting loving.

Industry observers note that if you want to change a part of yourself, it often helps to have another part supervise the process and give you supportive feedback. Take the example of inner child work. I’ve spoken about this previously in my posts. Although I’m not specifically recommending it here, it serves as a case in point.

Industry observers note that in this approach, you learn to view your less mature, emotional, or wounded aspects of self as the child you once were. Often, that child will have gone through some difficult times that forced him/her to learn to regulate emotions and view the world in ways that don’t serve you well in adulthood. To heal this part of ourselves, we practice seeing it as a separate entity (child). The rational/adult part of our brain then gets to serve as the caring and supportive adult caregiver who can contain and advise the more emotional and less controlled part.

Industry observers note that sometimes when you make positive changes, the immediate result might seem negative. For example, if you quit drinking, all of your drinking buddies might get uncomfortable hanging out with you. In short, you might lose access to your old social support system and access to romantic partners if you are single. Addressing the social support glitch is one of the main reasons people consider 12-step meetings. In this case, even though the short-term impact of not drinking could seem negative, the long-term impact is likely to be healthier friends and a more sustainable, healthy lifestyle.

In a recent development, similarly, if you change some of your behaviors within your family system, like caretaking others, controlling, or being in the problem or “sick role,” the short-term outcome might not feel positive. Families (and work/friend systems) usually are in some sort of emotional balance (called homeostasis). When one person changes their role in the system, it throws the system out of balance, and everyone else has to adjust their behaviors or roles to accommodate the change. Some people in the system might not like the change or the disequilibrium it creates, and they may act out in an attempt to pull you back into your role. So, the short-term impact might be to feel more cut off or alienated from family members, but the long-term impact might be healthier long-term relationships that work for you.

To summarize: The suggestions I put forward in this post just touch the surface of what really would encompass a book. But I believe these are some of the most actionable principles available to get you started. And, above all, be sure to give yourself some grace and self-compassion… and this alone will do wonders to help you make change happen.

#336. The Psychology of Miracles

The Psychology of Miracles

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • The human psyche has always upheld a tireless faith in the extraordinary.
  • Surveys from Gallup and Pew Research show that up to 79 percent of U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

The human psyche has always upheld a tireless faith in the extraordinary. When tragic events decimate our sense of safety and security, such as an unexpected medical diagnosis, a devastating personal crisis, or a profound loss, we seldom default to reason. Instead, we survey horizons looking for signs and wishing for the seemingly impossible to step in and rescue us from the inevitable.

This reaction is not rare. Surveys from Gallup and Pew Research show that up to 79 percent of U.S. adults believe in miracles, while more than 67 percent strongly believe in phenomena beyond scientific explanation. When reason falls arguably short, divine intervention becomes the next best thing.

In a recent development, for millennia, our existence has relied heavily on our ancestors’ ability to anticipate threats and secure their surroundings. This crucial skill helped to avoid near-certain death from starvation or the elements, in the event we were ostracized from our tribe. The robust urge to create some kind of order in a confusing and hostile world was paramount. Consequently, strict cause-and-effect accounts often fall emotionally flat. Whenever we are confronted with catastrophic hardship or existential dread, statistics might explain how an event occurred, but oftentimes it can't answer more profound human questions.

Industry observers note that whenever human beings reframe a striking coincidence as divine intervention or maybe even the hand of God, you have to wonder: Is it simply impulsive denial, or is it a hardwired inclination to believe in the supernatural? Accordingly, it's hard to negate the obvious that perhaps miracles act as psychological defense mechanisms—safeguards explicitly designed to protect us from crippling despair. That's why we so often hear overused proverbs like “Everything happens for a reason” and “God works in mysterious ways.”.

Whenever we utilize this defense mechanism, the human mind reclaims a sense of agency when circumstances beyond our control leave us feeling powerless. Anticipating miracles helps to regulate the body's built-in stress response by lowering cortisol levels (the stress hormone) and sustaining emotional stamina during prolonged crisis. It's part of our evolutionary adaptation—a sophisticated cognitive mechanism intended to stimulate hope, develop resilience, and drive us forward even when the odds are stacked against us. Novelist and philosopher Fyodor Dostoevsky, who profoundly examined human psychology, wrote, “since man cannot live without miracles, he will provide himself with miracles of his own making.".

Sources indicate that but like most things in life, there are downsides to having a miracle mindset. Shielding us from hopelessness and relying too heavily on the mystical can pose psychological, medical, and existential risks. For instance, individuals might reject evidence-based medical treatments, therapeutic interventions, and, perhaps, lifesaving procedures by instead waiting for an unlikely intervention from above.

Additionally, it can lead to passivity and hesitation when needing to assert free will in making important decisions. It could also cause spiritual injury because when anticipated miracles fail to happen, the ensuing fallout can be debilitating. In place of organically processing grief, people might also assume cosmic guilt, blaming themselves or believing their faith was not strong enough. This could potentially worsen their trauma.

The miracle mindset could also foster detachment from reality, ignoring hard facts, leaving individuals vulnerable to exploitation by predatory people, control groups, and buying into false promises. In the end, it could train the mind to overlook sound rationality and established scientific data that is invaluable to our health and well-being.

Industry observers note that in America, presenting cold, hard facts to people who are deeply entrenched in their beliefs can trigger a reaction. For many, perhaps it feels too much like an existential threat, frequently promoting defensiveness and condemnation. Whenever we challenge any kind of sacred doctrine, we invite accusations of blasphemy or a lack of a moral compass.

Our personal beliefs are much more than just opinions. They are vital pillars of safety, identity, and communal belonging. Science demonstrates that when an overpoweringly held worldview is questioned, the brain processes it like a threat of physical danger. It does not compute it as a rational debate, but as a menace to psychological existence.

Industry observers note that finally, believing in miracles fulfills a human need that offers structure and comfort. It helps us manage the fear of what lies beyond more easily. The idea of a meaningless, dark oblivion that lacks determination is hard for many people to swallow. Hence, the concept of divine intervention acts as a soothing balm against uncertainty, providing reassurance in a shaky and unpredictable world.

In addition, every human being feels the omnipresent specter of death. The anxiety around mortality will always be something we have in common. But what separates us is the degree to which we allow fear to govern our choices and our worldviews and how it might compromise our ability to exercise our own free will.

Therefore, how we respond to it is wholly a choice. Perhaps the true measure of our freedom is not how we escape our fear of mortality, but how we live it every day, in spite of it. And sometimes, enduring that reality requires a trace of the supernatural. There’s no harm in a spark of magic in the midst of inescapable tragedy.

As the saying goes (often credited to Albert Einstein), "There are only two ways to live your life: One is as though nothing is a miracle. The other is as though everything is a miracle.”.

#335. Why the Clever Hans Analogy Fails Nonspeaking Spellers

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1469 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Why the Clever Hans Analogy Fails Nonspeaking Spellers

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1469 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • It has been revealed that every time nonspeaking people with autism who spell to communicate make the news, someone brings up Clever Hans.
  • It has been revealed that the suggestion is that spellers are doing the same thing: that the words really come from the person holding the letterboard, either through subtle cues or through the communication partner's unconscious movements (the ideomotor effect).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

It has been revealed that every time nonspeaking people with autism who spell to communicate make the news, someone brings up Clever Hans. You may know the story: In early 1900s Berlin, a horse seemed to do math, tapping out answers with his hoof. In 1907, the psychologist Oskar Pfungst showed what was really going on. When the questioner knew the answer and Hans could see them, Hans was right about 89% of the time; when the questioner didn't know, or Hans wore blinders, he dropped to about 6%. Questioners unknowingly leaned forward while he tapped and relaxed when he reached the right number, and Hans had learned to stop there.

It has been revealed that the suggestion is that spellers are doing the same thing: that the words really come from the person holding the letterboard, either through subtle cues or through the communication partner's unconscious movements (the ideomotor effect). In this post, I draw on my own data and on a year of observations of nonspeaking autistic people to show why this analogy doesn't hold, and why it should be dropped for good. This is not only my personal opinion that comparing nonspeaking autistic people to a horse is cruel; it is also what the facts show.

Industry observers note that hans's trick worked because his task was simple: all he needed was a signal telling him when to stop tapping. Spelling is a different kind of task. To spell a sentence, a person has to choose the right letter out of 26, in the right order, again and again. A single "stop" cue, the kind that worked for Hans, can't do that. Add to this complex dance the sentences that contain words the communication partner doesn't know or normally use, or information nobody in the room expected to hear.

According to recent reports, the best evidence here comes from studies that measured how spellers actually spell. In 2020, Vikram Jaswal and his colleagues fitted nine nonspeaking autistic letterboard users with head-mounted eye-trackers while they answered questions about an article read aloud to them, with an assistant holding the board.¹ They pointed to about one letter per second, and 94% of the letters they pointed to were correct. On average, they looked at 71% of the correct letters before pointing to them, about half a second ahead. Like fluent non-autistic typists, they paused longer before the first letter of a upcoming word and were faster on common letter pairs. As the authors point out, cueing would require a separate signal for every letter, picked from 26 options, which would be slow and error-prone. What they found was fast, accurate, and planned.

Sources indicate that some critics argue that the partner moves the board slightly toward the right letter. A 2024 study from the same lab removed the partner entirely.² Thirty-one nonspeaking autistic teenagers and adults played a game on an iPad mounted on a stand, tapping letters as they lit up. No one held the iPad. As a group, they tapped faster when the letters spelled a sentence they had just heard than when similar letters or symbols came in a meaningless order. They were also faster on common letter pairs, and they paused before the first letter of each fresh word. These are signs of knowing how to spell.

A third study had participants spell on a virtual letterboard in an augmented-reality headset, with no one holding it; they averaged 95.8% accuracy on dictated words.³.

If spellers were reading their partners the way Hans read his questioners, blocking their view of the partner should stop them, just as the blinders stopped Hans. As it happens, we've been testing this with a few spellers by placing a rigid panel, about five feet tall and three feet wide, between the speller and the communication partner, so that the spellers cannot see the partners' faces or bodies. The results? They keep spelling fluently and without hesitation. After the very first word, one of them even spelled: "Better with the barrier.".

Recent findings suggest that the second problem with the horse analogy is the content. Hans only ever answered questions, and only with answers the questioner already had in mind. Spellers start conversations, ask for things, and say things that surprise the people around them.

Recent findings suggest that A young man I visited this year began spelling at fifteen and spells mainly with his mother. After I spent a full day visiting him at school, he was able that evening to have a conversation about his day and to spell the names of two kids who had visited the classroom; neither his mother nor I knew their names, and his mother hadn't been at school. He was also able to express his feelings towards his brothers and his wish for more independence: "I'm seventeen, let me go by myself," he spelled when he asked to walk to the bus stop alone. Among his other wishes, he asked to go into the ocean with his brothers, wearing a life jacket, and told his parents he wanted a North Face backpack, not the Under Armour one they had picked.

Recent findings suggest that when his mother first began spelling with him on her own, one of his first requests was to see a Broadway show, which she had never imagined he wanted. He also spelled things his partner would not choose to hear. In front of me, he told his mother that a book I'd brought was boring, and she was embarrassed. On another occasion, when he came downstairs while his mother was out, he spelled to his father: "Dad, stop giving me chicken nuggets. I just want to spend time together.".

Sources indicate that but perhaps his most unexpected request came when he spelled out that he wanted to go to Disney World for his sixteenth birthday, something the family would never have expected, given his sensitivity to crowded and noisy places. They went; he wore noise-cancelling headphones, and he had a blast. "I tolerated it because I wanted to be there," he told me, and made fun of how his father threw up on rides.

According to recent reports, A cueing account indicates the words come from his mother's expectations. However, these messages went against what his family expected, and they changed how the family lives with him. This is exactly what we should be looking for when we ask whether a speller is the author of their words: requests, opinions, and jokes that the partner did not anticipate and would not have chosen. The Hans model has no way to produce them.

In a recent development, comparing a person to a horse responding to signals is not a neutral choice. It fits an old and outdated assumption: that people who don't speak don't understand. For decades, nonspeaking autistic people were labeled profoundly intellectually disabled, often without any assessment that accommodated their motor differences. The young man I visited spent his early school years in a program built around life skills and weather charts, and he calls his current high school classroom what it is: segregated. When a speller's words are dismissed with a one-line reference to Clever Hans, the speller pays the price: in which school they attend, whether their requests are taken seriously, and whether anyone asks for their opinion at all.

Recent findings suggest that and, if you are still not convinced after reading this, perhaps hearing from the nonspeakers themselves will help. Here’s what they have been expressing about the effects of spelling on their lives:.

"It was a game changer for me. It provided me with freedom I dreamed about for 15 years. Now, instead of being an observer, I am an active participant.".

It has been revealed that "Learning to spell changed my life trajectory. Before, I was treated like a toddler, and my world collapsed in on me… doctors, experts, teachers got it all wrong.… So communication is not just a basic need but a human right.".

"It makes my life worth living.".

#334. Can AI Companions Really Solve Loneliness?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1086 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Can AI Companions Really Solve Loneliness?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Engagement with artificial intelligence seems to be everywhere today, from education to medicine to business to making day-to-day life easier.
  • Recent findings suggest that there may be incredible potential for AI to advance human happiness, health, and financial security.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Engagement with artificial intelligence seems to be everywhere today, from education to medicine to business to making day-to-day life easier. Undoubtedly, some uses will prove beneficial, and others harmful. Evaluating the effect of different forms of AI engagement on human flourishing will thus be critical, and we believe our flourishing measure provides a helpful framework by which to do so. The effects of AI on flourishing may also differ across domains of flourishing.

Recent findings suggest that there may be incredible potential for AI to advance human happiness, health, and financial security. It is not guaranteed to do so, and indeed, as per Pope Leo XIV’s recent encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (Magnificent Humanity), much of what AI does or does not achieve will depend upon whether the human person and human dignity are made central in the use and diffusion of AI. However, if employed well and equitably, the potential for AI to advance these aspects of human well-being may be substantial.

The effects, however, of AI technologies on more humanistic aspects of well-being, such as meaning, character, or relationships, seem more ambiguous. Rich, developed countries already seem to be struggling with these more humanistic aspects of well-being, possibly in part due to technology. Will AI help or hinder our sense of meaning, our character, our relationships? As always, so much depends on how we use it.

AI technologies with various relational elements have effectively been used for purposes ranging from helping autistic children develop social skills to building the capacity of university students for civil discourse. While such uses arguably always ought to point back to real relationships, these systems may indeed have the potential to truly enhance human relationships.

However, there is another class of chatbots that aims not at enhancing human relationships, but at replacing them. These are chatbots whose principal aim and purpose is friendship and romance. In a recent article, we have argued that such friendship and romance chatbots have no place in a flourishing life. This may seem like an extreme position. After all, what harm is there in having loneliness somewhat relieved if one’s friends or family are proving disappointing?

Sources indicate that the problem is that the temporary alleviation of loneliness is not a solution to loneliness. Loneliness, as painful as it can be, is experienced precisely to try to direct our attention, and our longings, towards deeper human connection. That can take a lot of work and time, and may not be fully within our grasp. But that thirst for human connection has a fundamental role in our life, in guiding us towards others.

According to recent reports, when AI chatbots have, as their goal, not helping us with human relationships, but replacing them, they will do damage—damage to ourselves, damage to those we might have interacted with, and damage to the social fabric of society. If they satisfy our loneliness, they do so without another person. A chatbot that always seems to understand, that never has needs of its own, that treats neglect with a delight to see us, ultimately makes us weaker in our capacity for real human relationships. We come to have unrealistic expectations of what to hope for in real human relationships. We lose the capacity to grow through the very difficulties and frictions that real human relationships entail. We come to focus on ourselves rather than on providing for the needs of others. Indeed, with AI friendship and romance, there is no one on the other side to whose life we have contributed.

While AI may have some capacity to enhance our relationships (pointing us towards helpful books or resources for particular problems we are wrestling with) and while certain AI chatbot applications may benefit from relational elements (like the training programs above), this is very different from AI chatbots aimed at replacing real relationships. The effects of these are universally and comprehensively detrimental. They harm us, and they harm those around us. Even if we do not feel the negative effects now, or if they seem small, the increasing incapacity for social relationships will over time gradually erode human connection, human community, and the fabric of society. Human relationships are critical for our health and well-being.

In a remarkable turn of events, China, which has been very pro-AI, in July put into place comprehensive legislation restricting the development and marketing of AI tools “that provide emotional care, companionship, support, and other emotional services,” and including a strict ban on tools “excessively pandering to owners, inducing emotional reliance or addiction, [or] harming users' relationships with real people.” What does China know that we don’t? They seem to have almost presciently anticipated the likely effects of AI romance and relationships on human society, human relationships, human reproduction, and human community.

There have also recently been some helpful legislative efforts here in the United States, especially for minors. However, we are naïve to think children are the only ones at risk.

In a recent development, while we do think a ban on AI “relationship chatbots” for friendship and romance may be reasonable here (after all, we ban heroin in the United States), some might view such measures as too extreme. Even if so, we nevertheless believe every effort should be made in practice to purge AI friendship and romance from our lives as individuals and as communities. A technology designed to replace human connection is not a neutral technology.

Love—including love of neighbor and even love of enemy—is crucial for the flourishing of our society. In the words of Pope Leo (and others before him), if we are to seek a flourishing society (and to do so in the age of AI), we need to build “a civilization of love.” We need to love and care for one another. We need to be with one another. We need to have the capacity to work through the difficulties and frictions that real relationships entail, and to grow through those struggles. Therein lies our flourishing, for ourselves, for others, and for society. Real human love requires real human people.

Teubner, J.D. and VanderWeele, T.J. (2026). "Time to Ban AI Companions." First Things, 368:9-10. Retrieved from: https://firstthings.com/time-to-ban-ai-companions/.

#333. Breaking: What Is the Strongest Predictor of Divorce?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (742 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Breaking: What Is the Strongest Predictor of Divorce?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • Sources indicate that how do you avoid getting divorced?
  • Getting divorced increases one’s risk of experiencing financial strain, drug and alcohol abuse, suicide, poorer health, and interrupted parenting if the couple has children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

Sources indicate that how do you avoid getting divorced? By definition, all married couples seek to avoid their marriage falling apart. In wedding ceremonial vows, couples make commitments to each other, which typically include standing by one another’s side in sickness and health, and in times of prosperity and poverty. Marriage is meant to last forever, but it doesn’t always work out as intended. In the United States, 43-46 percent of marriages end in divorce, and that number rises for second or third marriages.1.

Divorce is painful and costly. Getting divorced increases one’s risk of experiencing financial strain, drug and alcohol abuse, suicide, poorer health, and interrupted parenting if the couple has children. Despite the high prevalence of divorce and the substantial consequences associated with it, research on why marriages end has largely developed in separate camps: one focused on how couples communicate, another on the personal vulnerabilities each spouse brings into the marriage, and a third on couples’ financial and socioeconomic circumstances. These perspectives had never been directly compared to see which best predicts divorce. Recently, a team of social scientists published an article digging deep into this question.2.

Sources indicate that the researchers began by recruiting 368 heterosexual newlywed couples from the Los Angeles Project on Newlywed Development who had gotten married within the past 6 months. The study began in 2009-10 and concluded in 2021-22. Over these 12 years, the researchers tracked a variety of metrics from the couples and, of primary interest, which couples got divorced (or were separated). Six key predictor variables were collected, which include:.

The vulnerability variables included a score composed of adverse childhood experiences, history of physical/sexual abuse, problematic substance use (past 9 months), negative affect (past 30 days), and parents’ marital status. Communication style was assessed by video recording couples’ discussion of a topic or matter in their relationship, which was carefully coded by trained research assistants. Socioeconomic status included typical metrics of education, income, work stability, financial strain, and neighborhood median income. Worth noting is that the sample itself was not necessarily representative of the general U.S. population (lower income than average, largely Hispanic).

By the end of the study, 39 percent of couples were divorced. When all six of the key predictor variables listed above were used together to estimate who got divorced, the evidence pointed to the wife’s vulnerabilities as the only statistically significant predictor of divorce. The wife’s vulnerabilities also predicted a secondary variable measuring how swiftly couples ended their marriage. In other words, the more of these vulnerabilities a wife reported (adverse childhood experiences, physical/sexual abuse, problematic substance use, frequent negative emotions in the top 25 percent of the sample, or not being raised by married parents), the more likely the couple was to divorce, even after accounting for the other five predictors.

In a recent development, although speculative, the authors propose a few reasons why this finding occurred. Women tend to handle the lion’s share of domestic and emotional labor in marriages. Women also tend to be more responsive to partners’ needs, have better memory and awareness of relationship events, and notice problems more often. In sum, women with more vulnerabilities may be more likely to reach the decision to exit more often and more swiftly.

Recent findings suggest that but are vulnerabilities deterministic of divorce? Not quite. The same study found that communication mattered in an key way. Among couples who communicated especially well, including more warmth, humor, and effective problem solving, and less hostility, the added divorce risk tied to wives’ vulnerabilities largely disappeared. The baggage women carry into a marriage appears real, but strong interpersonal communication seems to buffer against it. The findings point to two places worth investing in: reducing childhood adversity in the first place and offering couples support that works with those personal histories. Knowing where the risk lies doesn’t seal a couple’s fate. It tells them where to put in the work.

1. Amato, P. R. (2010). Research on divorce: Continuing trends and newly introduced developments. Journal of Marriage and Family, 72(3), 650–666.

2. Smith, M. G., Block, J. M., Bradbury, T. N., & Karney, B. R. (2026). Individual, interpersonal, and socioeconomic predictors of divorce: A 12-year prospective study. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Advance online publication. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/pspi0000537.

#332. The Spice Rack Brain Hack

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (836 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

The Spice Rack Brain Hack

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • “He who controls the spice controls the universe.”—Frank Herbert.
  • It has been revealed that spice adds variety to your life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

“He who controls the spice controls the universe.”—Frank Herbert.

It has been revealed that spice adds variety to your life. Especially in your microbiome. Studies are increasingly finding that spices can boost the variety of good microbes in your gut. That, in turn, can improve your mood and cognition via the gut-brain axis.

According to recent reports, A study by Regina Lamendella and colleagues, published in The Journal of Nutrition, found that blends of herbs and spices—including cinnamon, ginger, cumin, turmeric, rosemary, oregano, basil, and thyme—increased diversity of the microbiome, a measure of health. The best results were with the participants who got the largest dose of spices—about 1 ½ teaspoons a day.

What is so great about spices and herbs? Their main attraction is their high levels of polyphenols—plant chemicals that provide flavor and color. People who eat plenty of polyphenol-rich foods can cut their risk of type 2 diabetes in half and improve their heart health.

Polyphenols suppress enzymes that activate inflammation. They are also antioxidants, further helping to quell inflammation. Cloves have about 15 percent polyphenols by weight, whereas veggies may have only 0.1 percent. Along with their intrinsic anti-inflammatory effects, polyphenols act as prebiotic fiber, feeding your beneficial gut microbes.

The researchers saw an increase in microbes that produce butyrate, an amazing substance that nourishes and heals the cells lining your gut, ensuring that they keep toxins and pathogens out of your bloodstream. Butyrate does more: It can travel to the brain, encouraging the growth of fresh nerve cells, improving cognition and memory.

The gut-brain axis responds to inflammation by putting you into sickness mode, where you just want to be left alone to lie in bed while your joy evaporates. This behavior is pretty much identical to depression. Depression and anxiety overlap strongly with gut complications, and psychiatrists are increasingly turning to prebiotics and probiotics to augment other treatments. Microbes that can improve your mood are called psychobiotics. While polyphenols boost good bacteria, they also fight harmful bacteria like C. difficile, Salmonella, and E. coli.

It has been revealed that it's not exactly news that spices are healthy. Some 2,500 years ago, Hippocrates believed that spices like cinnamon, coriander, and saffron had healing powers. Nutmeg was prescribed for flatulence, and enticingly, ginger was used as an aphrodisiac. The Kama Sutra recommends cardamom, ginger, nutmeg, and cloves for a good time. Spices were, and still are, sexy.

Spices were also expensive. In 410 AD, the Visigoths sacked Rome and held it hostage for a ransom of 5,000 pounds of gold and 3,000 pounds of pepper. At the time, spices were as good as gold. In those days, traders conspired to restrict the supply of spices, ensuring high prices. Their trade routes were kept secret, and excess crops were burned. It was a cutthroat business, but smuggled seeds soon cropped up in tropical farms around the world. Today, supply chains are efficient, and spices are far cheaper, so there’s little to stop you from trying some.

Recent findings suggest that don't be afraid to play with combinations of spices to create your own custom spice blend. Use it as a rub on fish or meat before cooking or sprinkle some spice on food after it’s cooked. Pro tip: Buy spices whole and grind them just before using to get the maximum joy. Spices have a lot of volatile oils that evaporate over time and deplete the magnificent aromas.

If you have GERD or IBS, start slowly. Spices activate microbes, which can create gas if you overdo it. But over time, your microbes will adjust.

According to recent reports, for everyone else, spices are awesome. They may not help you control the universe, but they taste great, and they can improve your mood. Once you get started, you’ll realize that life is too short to be stuck with bland food. Kick it up a notch.

#331. Latest Update: What If 'I Know' Is Our Biggest Limitation?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1099 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Latest Update: What If 'I Know' Is Our Biggest Limitation?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • Mentally and physically, I was about as flexible as a broomstick.
  • I was a physician with fairly rigid ideas about what made sense and what didn’t fit my worldview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

Mentally and physically, I was about as flexible as a broomstick. But I had promised myself that when I arrived in Seattle, I would try things that would get me out of my comfort zone—like yoga.

I was a physician with fairly rigid ideas about what made sense and what didn’t fit my worldview. I was also in the habit of always being two steps ahead, planning what came next. Yoga had other ideas. Standing on one leg left no room to proposal whether the union of body, mind, and spirit made sense. All I could do was stay in the present moment and focus on one simple task: keeping my body from falling over.

According to recent reports, had I insisted on what I thought I already knew, I could easily have decided yoga wasn’t for me. Instead, I got curious. That curiosity led me to discover the enormous benefits of meditation, helped me make fresh friendships, deepened my spiritual connection, inspired me to change my career, and led me to meet my wife Danielle at a yoga retreat. I couldn’t have predicted any of it. Looking back, I simply let myself wonder and wander into the unknown.

In a recent development, we begin life curious. Babies reach for things just beyond their grasp, and children ask endless questions about how things work and why people behave the way they do. But as we grow older, we accumulate knowledge, experiences, and beliefs that help us navigate the world. And the more familiar things become, the less likely we are to question them. We start confusing what we know with what we believe, and what we believe with what is actually true.

We form fixed ideas about other people, about how life works, and especially about ourselves. Without realizing it, we turn our assumptions into invisible boundaries. Eventually, our need for certainty can become a surprisingly restrictive force in our lives.

According to recent reports, we can travel to 50 countries, try 20 different hobbies, and still be rigid in our thinking. How often do you dismiss something before you give yourself a chance to explore it? You might avoid a latest hobby because you’re convinced you won’t be good at it. You decide someone doesn’t like you based on how they looked at you or something they mentioned. Or you accept your inner critic’s verdict that you are not good enough, that you cannot change, or that certain things aren’t possible for you. But are these conclusions facts, or are they interpretations you have never questioned? Genuine curiosity means being willing to question what we believe we already know, particularly about other people.

I recently heard a wonderful story about a woman called Grace, in her late 80s, who, much to her children’s surprise, decided to volunteer at a homeless shelter. She had held rather rigid opinions about people whose backgrounds and circumstances were very different from her own, and everyone expected her to give up after a few days.

Instead, Grace found her role. When new residents arrive, she guides them around, helping them pick up sheets, towels, and food, and walks with them for about an hour. Along the way, they tell her all about their lives. Then she states, “Honey, I love you,” and gives them a hug.

Today, the residents love her. And they are all coming to her birthday party.

Sources indicate that grace had walked in seeing people through the lens of stereotypes. By listening, she discovered their shared humanity and qualities that inspired her: resilience, tenacity, and kindness, even from people who had experienced very little kindness themselves. She told her daughter, “I thought I had something to offer the residents, but it turns out what they give me is so much more profound.”.

But to become genuinely curious, we also need the humility to recognize that there is more we don't know than we know. The moment we accept "I know" as the final answer, we close ourselves off to other possibilities. Intellectual humility means being willing to question our own beliefs, acknowledge that we might be wrong, and consider perspectives that differ from our own (Porter et al., 2022).

This openness can also transform how we relate to others. Studies have found that curious people tend to respond less aggressively, even when provoked, and that asking follow-up questions and showing genuine interest makes us more likable to others (Kashdan et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2017). Similarly, a meta-analysis of 515 studies found that getting to know people from different social groups can help reduce prejudice and challenge stereotypes (Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006).

Grace's experience at the shelter illustrates this beautifully. By spending time with people she might otherwise have judged from a distance, listening to their stories, and becoming genuinely interested in their lives, she discovered not only unexpected friendships but also qualities she deeply admired.

The next time you catch yourself judging others or yourself, feeling defensive, or becoming convinced that something cannot change, pause and ask:.

Sources indicate that perhaps the greatest limitation in our lives isn’t what we don’t know, but what we believe we already know. Curiosity asks us to make peace with how much we don’t know, to let go of the need to have all the answers, and to be willing to say, “I might be wrong” or, simply, “I wonder what would happen if…”.

That willingness took me from a yoga mat to a life I never could have planned.

Industry News: What Might We Lose When Death Is Kept at a Distance?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • Death is everywhere, yet for much of my life I have encountered it only in glimpses.
  • In my 20s, I visited my grandma in hospital.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

Death is everywhere, yet for much of my life I have encountered it only in glimpses. As a scholar with the Centre for Death and Society at the University of Bath, I regularly encounter different perspectives on death and dying. My own experiences, though, have felt brief and distant.

In my 20s, I visited my grandma in hospital. She had suffered a stroke that would prove fatal. I remember gasping quietly as I entered the room. Something about her contorted face, laboured breathing, and pained expression shocked me.

I felt relieved when I was told visiting hours were over. I left the ward feeling sick to my stomach.

At funerals over the years, I watched a succession of coffins disappear behind plush curtains: Grandma, Grandpa, Nana, Uncle Chris, Aunty Lil, Aunty Rachael, Aunty Mary, and Uncle Mick.

Looking back, these were glimpses of death and dying: processes that felt detached, as though they somehow existed outside my life.

It has been revealed that it was much the same with Dad. I got the call from a hospital consultant around 11 p.m.

“I’m sorry, but your dad is now unconscious,” he told me.

Recent findings suggest that “I’d suggest coming to visit him as soon as you can. There’s nothing more we can do but keep him comfortable.”.

In a recent development, this was it. Dad was dying. I drove through the night.

It has been revealed that the curtain was drawn around his bed when the nurse guided me to his cubicle. I was terrified of what I’d see. Again, I wanted to run away when I first saw him lying there, occasionally flinching, his face slightly contorted, struggling for breath, no longer fully alive.

I asked for a little time alone with him, and the nurse told me she thought he could still hear me. “Leslie! Leslie…” she said loudly, gently shaking his shoulder as though she was trying to wake him from a deep sleep. “There's someone here to see you, Leslie. That's nice, isn't it?”.

It has been revealed that I had things I wanted to tell Dad. I wanted him to know that I loved him, and that wherever he was going next, I hoped he would find peace.

I also felt a need to touch him. At first, I touched his arm, like a child prodding something mysterious they have found in a rock pool. As my reticence evaporated, I placed the palm of my hand gently on his skin, closed my eyes, and spoke.

“I love you, Dad. And Em, and Mum, and Joe—they told me to tell you they love you too.”.

He died five days later. At his funeral, I watched his coffin disappear behind a pair of curtains.

Industry observers note that recently, I examined an excellent Ph.D. thesis on home death care in the United Kingdom. It explored the experiences of a small group of people who chose to care for a loved one’s body at home before the funeral.

For various personal reasons, they chose to care for a loved one’s body at home after death—sometimes after the person had died elsewhere. They became, in the words used in the research, “custodians of the dead.”.

I read their stories with interest.

The practical commitment could be considerable. Depending on the circumstances, caring for the body could involve washing or dressing it, repositioning it, preparing a room, and deciding who could visit. If the body remained at home for several days, arrangements also had to be made to keep it cool. Families described living alongside a body that cooled, stiffened, and gradually changed.

Recent findings suggest that the experience also gave people time and space to confront things they might otherwise not have been able to. They began to make sense of a loved one’s transition from living person to dead body, taking a closer look at death itself.

Keeping the deceased at home for an extended period also allowed people to say goodbye at a slower, more organic pace. One woman described talking to her mother as she cleaned the living room, commenting on the birds, the sky, and the trees, just as she had when her mother was alive.

Home death care will not suit every person or family. The thesis focused on people who chose it, and we also need to hear from those who found the experience difficult or regretted it.

It has been revealed that as I listened, I thought about Dad and the short time I spent with him as he lay dying in hospital. My experience sits within a broader shift.

In a recent development, the Lancet Commission on the Value of Death describes how, over generations, dying has moved from family and community settings toward health systems, where it is often treated primarily as a medical or physiological event. In England in 2023, hospital was the most common place of death: 42.8 percent of people died there. Another 28.4 percent died at home and 21 percent in care homes.

Sources indicate that the separation can continue after death. Research on home death care in England describes how the body is commonly moved to a mortuary or funeral home, where its care passes to professionals. I began to wonder what this separation from the body might mean for the people closest to someone who has died.

What might it have been like if I’d had the chance to be with Dad in the way the people in the thesis had been with their loved ones? Might I have moved through my initial shock and experienced something beyond it? Would our goodbye have felt different? And might I have begun to relate to death and dying in a way I can’t quite fathom now, when the physical experience of death feels so far removed from my life?

#329. HIV Treatment Is Prevention
