4 Types of Dead-End Relationships

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Sara and Keith have been married for nine years and have three children.
  • I’ve met hundreds of couples like Sara and Keith whose relationship has been pushed to the back burner, and intimacy has essentially reached a dead end.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Sara and Keith have been married for nine years and have three children. Both work full-time, do their share of chores and parenting, and fill weekends and many evenings with soccer games, ballet lessons, or overflow work. Is it an okay life? Yes, they would agree it is okay, but in the next breath, they'll admit there’s little affection or intimacy between them.

I’ve met hundreds of couples like Sara and Keith whose relationship has been pushed to the back burner, and intimacy has essentially reached a dead end.

Here are four of the most common relationship patterns:.

Child- or work-centered. This is Sara and Keith. Essentially, they stopped being a couple and instead became mom and pop or worker bees. Such couples often complain that they wish they had more time for couple time, but they're so busy with work and kids.

Roommates. If they don’t have the demands or distractions of work or children, many couples downshift to roommate status. They do spend time together, which they usually enjoy; they may even describe the other as their best friend, but the affection has long since dried up. And like roommates, there’s plenty of talk about schedules and chores.

Sources indicate that parallel lives. This takes the roommate scenario to another level. No best-friend status; no doing things together; each does their own thing; they essentially just share the same space.

Recent findings suggest that habit/routine-driven lifestyle. This can bleed into all the above variations, where, like Sara and Keith, they do what they do because they do it. They run on autopilot most of the time, and habits and routines kill any hope of spontaneity or anything different.

Industry observers note that what holds all these types of couples together is that they're defined by bad solutions to other problems lying beneath. Here are some of the common sources:.

Recent findings suggest that problems that are swept under the rug. If problems go unresolved, they stack up and act like a wedge pushing you apart. You create a long list of "things we don't talk about" and fill in the space with the demands and distractions of work and kids—or you devolve into parallel lives.

It has been revealed that A power struggle. Here, problems are never solved because the individuals are unwilling to reach win-win compromises. Sometimes this attitude is fueled by anger and resentment from old wounds; sometimes it is simply a matter of personality—perhaps high anxiety they try to manage through control, self-centeredness, or a need for power. Neither is willing to bend because it feels like letting the other guy win, and coming out on top is always the priority.

Conflict avoidance. Some individuals have learned to fear conflict and others' strong emotions, often because of a childhood environment in which parents were frightening or modeled passivity and avoidance. As a result, anger is internalized or turned into self-blame, and problems are never discussed or resolved. Periodically, one person may act out or explode in anger, which only further fuels their fear and internalization.

In a recent development, unhealed wounds. Past affairs and sudden, traumatic decisions, such as abruptly quitting jobs or being forced to move—painful incidents that shattered safety and trust and linger, coloring the relationship—have become a grudge that is always there; an open wound that never heals.

An expired relationship contract. Whatever Sara and Keith needed from each other nine years ago, they likely no longer need it now. Each has grown into different needs and desires, but like many couples, they’ve built a life in a box of rules and routines that no longer fit them. Some couples divorce; others, like them, downshift their relationship.

If you’re ready for a change—to get your relationship back on the front burner and bring back intimacy and affection—here are some tips to get you started:.

Acknowledge the state of the relationship. In some ways, this can be the hardest step. Like "The Emperor's New Clothes," it requires breaking the code of silence, refusing to ignore reality, and having the courage to be honest. Once you say how you’ve been feeling and start that conversation, you can’t unsay it or the other can’t unhear it. You’ve opened the door to change, and that’s a good place to start.

According to recent reports, change the emotional climate through action. Resist the urge to think change is about getting the other person to change: this leads to nagging, manipulation, or a blink contest where each waits for the other. Instead, think about changing the overall emotional climate of the relationship, breaking ingrained habits and patterns, and stopping autopilot behaviors. The key is action: Proposal a date night; snuggle together on the couch while you watch a movie; move the kid’s bedtime earlier so you have time as a couple to simply chat at the end of the day. Something, anything that is different and positive.

Sources indicate that repair old wounds. I’ve heard partners say they just need answers to questions that have been lingering for years—about the affair, the job, or the move. Or sometimes it is just the opportunity to get things off their chests and finally feel heard and understood, without avoidance or defensiveness. Sometimes you can do this on your own; sometimes it helps to start by writing a letter or email; sometimes you need to bring in a professional to help mediate and moderate the conversation.

Industry observers note that tackle unresolved problems. The best way to do this is to chip away at them in baby steps. I suggest that couples set aside a good time to talk when they’re not tired or distracted. Treat it like a staff meeting at work: Set an agenda with one or two items, focus on you, and work toward a win-win compromise while controlling your emotions. Meet for 30-45 minutes. And if it is hard to do, bring in a professional.

In a recent development, resist the urge to think your feelings need to change before you can act; if you keep doing what you’re doing, you’ll keep feeling the same way. Instead, challenge yourself to break out and take action.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

Recent findings suggest that new research demonstrates that attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a systemic condition influencing respiratory patterns, subjective time pressure, brain iron levels, and alcohol use risk across the lifespan. Source: Society for Neuroscience.

According to recent reports, affecting approximately one in nine children in the United States, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is among the most prevalent neurodevelopmental conditions of childhood. While clinical assessments have historically focused on hallmark behavioral traits, inattention, impulsivity, and motor hyperactivity, mounting evidence indicates that ADHD exerts far-reaching effects on physical and mental health well into adulthood.

Presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience, four latest studies illuminate how ADHD shapes fundamental physiological and cognitive processes, ranging from involuntary breathing rhythms and subjective time perception to regional brain iron regulation and substance use vulnerability.

Taken together, the emerging findings map distinct physiological and behavioral signatures across development:.

By connecting autonomic physiology, neurochemistry, and lived cognitive stress, these studies challenge narrow definitions of ADHD as purely an attentional or behavioral disorder.

According to recent reports, “It is becoming clear that ADHD is a broader systemic condition affecting a host of brain and body variables beyond just motor hyperactivity,” stated press conference moderator Dr. Chandan Vaidya, a cognitive neuroscientist at Georgetown University who studies how regulatory behavior goes awry in neurodevelopmental conditions. “Together, these new findings tackle timely topics and showcase the diversity of areas where work is needed to better understand ADHD and ultimately improve diagnosis and treatment.”.

How does ADHD affect physical functions outside of attention and hyperactivity?

Upcoming research presented at Neuroscience 2026 shows that ADHD is linked to distinct breathing patterns in young adults, lower iron levels in specific regions of the developing brain, and chronic psychological time pressure, demonstrating that the condition involves both brain-wide neurochemistry and bodily physiology.

What did researchers discover about brain iron in children with ADHD?

Brain scans conducted by researchers at UC San Diego revealed that children and adolescents with ADHD have lower levels of iron in specific brain regions compared to peers without ADHD. Because iron is crucial for producing neurotransmitters like dopamine, tracking these regional changes may offer latest insights into ADHD neurobiology.

Can treating ADHD help reduce alcohol misuse in young adults?

Yes. Emerging clinical data from the University of Florida indicates that ADHD medication may help decrease problem drinking behaviors among young adults who experience both ADHD and alcohol use disorder.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The sense of smell maintains an unusually direct anatomical highway to the brain’s emotional and memory hubs, bypassing the thalamic relay used by other senses to project straight into the amygdala and hippocampus.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A memory and olfaction study reveals that diffused lavender scent alone does not automatically boost memory performance in young or older adults. unless it is experienced as a novel cue at the very start of learning. The findings show that older adults who encountered the scent during the initial learning block recalled objects significantly better, highlighting how sensory novelty and intact smell function support cognitive aging.

The sense of smell maintains an unusually direct anatomical highway to the brain’s emotional and memory hubs, bypassing the thalamic relay used by other senses to project straight into the amygdala and hippocampus. Because a single familiar whiff can trigger vivid autobiographical flashbacks, aromatherapy, particularly using lavender essential oil, has frequently been touted as a simple tool to sharpen memory and stave off age-related cognitive decline.

However, rigorous empirical evidence supporting aromatherapy as a universal memory enhancer has remained mixed.

Now, a study published in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience by neuroscientists at UCLA and Rice University reveals that the relationship between scent and memory depends heavily on timing, sensory novelty, and baseline olfactory health.

Led by UCLA neuroscientist and corresponding author Dr. Stephanie Leal, the investigation demonstrates that while lavender scent alone did not act as a blanket memory booster, encountering the scent as a fresh, novel stimulus at the beginning of a learning session significantly enhanced recall in older adults.

Because age-related olfactory dysfunction is increasingly recognized as an early warning sign of Alzheimer’s disease, Leal and colleagues set out to examine how olfactory cues interact with memory encoding in cognitively healthy younger and older adults.

Participants first completed standardized olfactory assessments to measure baseline smell sensitivity before entering either a room diffused with lavender essential oil or an unscented room. Volunteers viewed two sequential blocks of everyday household objects, such as a tomato or a blow dryer, on a computer screen. Crucially, the design was counterbalanced: participants who experienced the lavender scent during the first image block completed the second block in an unscented room, and vice versa.

Industry observers note that following a delay, participants underwent a nuanced memory test featuring images that were either identical to, slightly altered from (e.g., changing a red blow dryer to blue), or completely different from the original items. This paradigm allowed researchers to separate general recall (recognizing the object category) from high-resolution detail memory (remembering exact visual features).

In a recent development, “When we looked at general and detail memory measures, older adults struggled to remember the details, which we expected,” explained Leal. “Interestingly, the presence or absence of odor made no difference for older or younger adults. We were kind of scratching our heads because that was surprising based on prior work that highlighted olfaction might enhance memory.”.

A deeper look at the experimental order, however, uncovered a striking pattern among older adults:.

These results suggest that as the brain ages, the specific chemical profile of an essential oil matters far less than the novelty of encountering an enriched sensory environment at the onset of learning.

Rather than treating aromatherapy as a passive background cure-all, the findings indicate that olfactory cues work best when deployed strategically to introduce novelty during latest learning experiences.

Recent findings suggest that “If we want to support memory in older adults, we need to think beyond simply whether a stimulus helps or hurts memory and consider when and how it is experienced,” Leal noted. “A massive component of learning in aging is novelty. Engaging in learning in an enriched context may make it easier to learn latest things.”.

By linking baseline smell sensitivity, subjective pleasantness, and timed sensory novelty to hippocampal memory precision, the research offers practical insights for designing enriched cognitive interventions aimed at supporting healthy brain aging.

Does diffusing lavender essential oil automatically improve memory?

In a recent development, no. Researchers at UCLA and Rice University found that overall, both younger and older adults performed no better on memory tests in a lavender-scented room compared to an unscented room.

Why did encountering the scent first help older adults remember better?

According to recent reports, older adults who smelled lavender during the very first learning block recalled objects more accurately than those exposed during the second block. This suggests that the novelty of entering an enriched sensory environment at the start of a task helps the aging brain anchor new memories.

How does sense of smell connect to Alzheimer’s disease and aging?

Age-related loss of smell is closely linked to early neurodegenerative changes in Alzheimer’s disease. In this study, older adults with healthier baseline olfactory function, and those who found the scent pleasant, demonstrated better detail memory, highlighting the close tie between olfactory processing and hippocampal memory circuits.

Funding: The researchers involved in this project were funded by the National Science Foundation, the BrightFocus Foundation, the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation, and the Alzheimer’s Association.

Olfactory context and memory across the adult lifespan: effects on mnemonic discrimination and olfactory function.

Odor is a powerful contextual cue that can influence memory and is closely linked to brain regions involved in episodic memory, including the hippocampus.

Age-related olfactory dysfunction is among the earliest behavioral changes associated with cognitive decline and may contribute to memory impairments in older adults. Hippocampal pattern separation, or the process of reducing interference among similar experiences, provides a sensitive measure of age-related memory decline, yet little is known about how olfactory context influences mnemonic discrimination.

Recent findings suggest that in the present study, we examined whether odor context during encoding affects subsequent mnemonic discrimination in young and older adults. Participants completed a mnemonic similarity task in which object stimuli were encoded in both odor (lavender) and no-odor contexts prior to a memory test.

Sources indicate that across participants, odor context did not significantly influence target recognition or mnemonic discrimination. Consistent with prior work, older adults exhibited poorer mnemonic discrimination and reduced olfactory function relative to young adults.

However, odor presentation order influenced mnemonic discrimination in older adults, such that performance was better when the odor context was encountered during the first encoding block compared to the second. Additionally, poorer olfactory function was associated with reduced mnemonic discrimination, and this relationship was largely explained by age-related differences in olfactory ability.

These findings suggest that the influence of olfactory context on memory depends on both age and the timing of odor exposure, highlighting the importance of individual differences in olfactory function when evaluating odor-based approaches to support memory in aging.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A chronobiology study in mice reveals that while the brain’s 24-hour circadian rhythms persist into old age, shorter multi-hour “ultradian” rhythms in physical activity and core body temperature significantly weaken. Simultaneously, aging decouples movement from internal temperature regulation and triggers neuroinflammatory gene shifts, glial remodeling, and neuronal loss inside the brain’s master circadian clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).

Recent findings suggest that throughout every 24-hour day, mammalian physiology follows an intricate temporal choreography. Governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a tiny cluster of neurons in the hypothalamus that acts as the brain’s master biological clock, core body temperature, hormone release, and physical activity rise and fall in predictable ~24-hour circadian rhythms.

Layered atop this overarching 24-hour cycle are faster, multi-hour biological oscillations known as ultradian rhythms, which pulse every few hours to coordinate bursts of activity, metabolic demand, and thermoregulation.

While age-related sleep fragmentation and impaired temperature regulation are well-documented clinical hallmarks of aging, precisely how ultradian rhythms evolve across the lifespan, and how they relate to cellular changes inside the SCN, has remained poorly understood.

Now, a comprehensive chronobiology investigation examining mice across the adult lifespan (from 3 to 21 months of age) reveals that while the 24-hour circadian framework remains detectable in old age, the faster 2- to 6-hour ultradian rhythms deteriorate, accompanied by a breakdown in coordination between physical activity and internal body temperature.

To separate externally driven daily routines from internally generated biological timing, the researchers continuously recorded locomotor activity and core body temperature in mice across multiple age brackets under both standard 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycles and constant darkness, an experimental condition that removes environmental light cues to expose the brain’s intrinsic pacemaker.

The physiological telemetry revealed a striking divergence between macro- and micro-rhythms:.

To explore the neural underpinnings of these physiological shifts, the investigators analyzed cellular architecture and gene expression profiles directly inside the SCN of young and aged mice.

Even though core circadian clock genes continued cycling, the cellular microenvironment of the aging SCN indicated pronounced signs of biological wear:.

By demonstrating that shorter ultradian rhythms and temperature-activity coupling falter even when overall 24-hour circadian rhythmicity persists, the findings offer a fresh lens through which to view age-related sleep disturbances and vulnerability to heat or cold stress.

Further experimental work will determine whether targeting neuroinflammation or supporting glial-neuronal communication inside the SCN can restore ultradian stability, potentially paving the way for interventions that alleviate sleep fragmentation and thermoregulatory decline in older adults.

What is the difference between circadian rhythms and ultradian rhythms?

According to recent reports, circadian rhythms are biological cycles that repeat roughly every 24 hours, such as the daily sleep-wake cycle. Ultradian rhythms are shorter biological cycles that repeat multiple times within a single day, typically every 2 to 6 hours, regulating smaller bursts of physical activity, alertness, and core body temperature fluctuations.

How does aging affect these biological rhythms?

According to recent reports, researchers found that while older mice kept their basic 24-hour rhythms and core clock gene cycles, their shorter 2- to 6-hour ultradian rhythms weakened significantly. Furthermore, physical movement and internal body temperature became disconnected, no longer rising and falling together as closely as in younger animals.

What changes happen inside the brain’s master clock during aging?

Inside the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the brain’s master clock, aging was linked to increased activity of immune-related genes, changes in supportive glial cells, and a reduction in neuron density, which may impair how the brain coordinates fine-tuned daily bodily rhythms.

Aging remodels the suprachiasmatic nucleus and weakens ultradian rhythms and activity–temperature coupling.

Aging alters daily physiology, but how these changes relate to remodeling of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) remains incompletely understood.

Here, we examined time-resolved SCN transcriptomic profiles alongside longitudinal recordings of core body temperature and locomotor activity, using separate cohorts for the molecular and physiological analyses.

Aging was associated with extensive SCN transcriptomic remodeling, including enrichment of innate immune, interferon-related, complement-associated, and glial programs, while selected canonical clock genes retained detectable rhythmic expression.

Recent findings suggest that the composition and temporal profiles of broader rhythmic transcriptional programs also differed between young and aged SCN samples. Aged mice retained detectable circadian rhythms but showed reduced 2–6 h ultradian wavelet power in locomotor activity and body temperature, lower activity–temperature correlations, and altered optimal integration windows and time-of-day-dependent relationships. Histological analyses revealed glial remodeling and reduced neuronal marker-positive cell density in the aged SCN.

These findings identify parallel age-associated changes in SCN molecular and cellular organization and in physiological rhythmic power and activity–temperature associations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, researchers discovered that taste buds actively process and filter mixed flavors before sending signals to the brain. The study shows that sour stimuli trigger serotonin release inside taste buds, dampening neural responses to sweet, bitter, and salty flavors while downstream neurons sort tastes into two broad categories: pleasant or unpleasant.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

According to recent reports, biting into a tart lemon bar or sipping a sweet-and-sour beverage delivers a complex blend of chemical stimuli to the tongue simultaneously. For decades, neuroscientists have worked to determine whether the brain mixes these individual flavor signals centrally, or whether taste buds themselves edit and shape flavor combinations before a single electrical impulse ever leaves the tongue.

It has been revealed that in a study published in Journal of Neuroscience, neuroscientists led by Dr. Stephen Roper at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine recorded gustatory nerve signaling in mice exposed to mixed taste solutions.

The findings reveal that sourness exerts a dominant, suppressive effect over other primary tastes right inside the taste bud, driven by local serotonin signaling.

To trace how mixed tastes travel from peripheral receptors to the central nervous system, Roper and colleagues measured neural responses along the gustatory pathway while exposing mice to single tastes and multi-taste mixtures.

Comparing neural firing across taste conditions revealed two striking principles of gustatory coding:.

To uncover how sourness mutes competing tastes so early in the sensory pipeline, the investigators zeroed in on serotonin, a neurotransmitter released inside each taste bud by specialized sour-responsive receptor cells (Type III taste cells).

Manipulating local serotonin levels directly controlled the strength of flavor suppression:.

These results demonstrate that taste buds function as miniature computational hubs, using paracrine serotonin signaling to inhibit neighboring receptor cells before gustatory information is handed off to cranial nerves.

Sources indicate that “Taste buds not only respond to and transduce taste compounds, they also integrate and manipulate gustatory signals before transmitting them to the brain,” explained Roper. “The neurons that collect signals produced in taste buds are themselves organized into two large groups or clusters, neurons that convey gustatory signals associated with pleasure and neurons that convey unpleasant taste signals.”.

By establishing how peripheral serotonin signaling shapes flavor dominance and how downstream neurons sort palatability, the study lays groundwork for identifying the genetic signatures of pleasure- versus aversion-coding taste neurons, and exploring whether targeted molecular interventions could one day modulate taste perception in clinical nutrition or sensory disorders.

Why do sour flavors overpower sweet, salty, and bitter tastes?

Researchers at the University of Miami found that sour-responsive cells inside taste buds release the neurotransmitter serotonin. This local serotonin dampens the signals of neighboring sweet, bitter, and salty receptor cells before the taste information even reaches the nerves leading to the brain.

Do taste buds simply send raw flavor data to the brain?

Sources indicate that no. The study shows that taste buds act like miniature processing centers that actively mix, filter, and modify taste signals locally before transmitting them to sensory neurons.

How do taste nerves organize flavors on their way to the brain?

According to the researchers, the sensory neurons collecting signals from taste buds are broadly organized into two major functional groups: neurons that carry pleasant taste signals and neurons that carry unpleasant taste signals.

Sour Suppresses Sweet, Salty, and Bitter: Implications for Signal Processing in Taste Buds.

Taste is typically encountered as complex blends, yet how peripheral taste organs process heterogeneous mixtures remains poorly understood. Here we asked how sour stimuli influence the encoding of sweet, salty, and bitter tastes in primary gustatory sensory neurons.

Sources indicate that using in vivo calcium imaging in mice of either sex to record neurons in geniculate ganglia during oral delivery of tastants, we compared responses to naturally occurring taste stimuli presented alone versus in binary mixtures that activate acid (sour)-sensing (Type III) taste bud cells. Adding citric acid or HCl robustly suppressed sucrose-evoked responses in geniculate ganglion neurons, even though acid itself did not activate those neurons.

According to recent reports, acid-induced suppression generalized to bitter and salty tastes, which, like sucrose, are believed to activate Type II taste cells. Additional stimuli that activate acid-sensing taste cells (NH4Cl, KCl) also reduced sucrose responses, supporting a common mechanism linked to Type III cells. Manipulating levels of serotonin (a paracrine transmitter released by Type III cells) in taste buds altered taste suppression: increasing serotonin with 5-hydroxytryptophan enhanced acid-induced suppression whereas depleting serotonin with para-chlorophenylalanine weakened it.

Finally, population analyses, including UMAP dimensionality reduction, indicate that taste suppression is not limited to a particular subset of gustatory sensory neurons. The findings are consistent with serotonin-dependent paracrine inhibition within taste buds as a contributor to sour-driven suppression in taste mixtures and reveal a compression of gustatory information into hedonic categories as early as at the level of primary sensory neurons.

#302. Anorexia and the Gut-Brain Connection

Anorexia and the Gut-Brain Connection

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • Sources indicate that for generations, scientists and doctors believed the brain was the unquestioned command center of the body.
  • Sources indicate that your digestive tract is home to an intricate network of more than 100 million nerve cells—so many, in fact, that scientists often refer to it as the body's second brain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

Sources indicate that for generations, scientists and doctors believed the brain was the unquestioned command center of the body. It sent instructions and the rest of the body obeyed. Today, we know the relationship is far more complicated.

Sources indicate that your digestive tract is home to an intricate network of more than 100 million nerve cells—so many, in fact, that scientists often refer to it as the body's second brain. Known as the enteric nervous system, this remarkable network coordinates digestion, communicates with the immune system, influences hormone production, and remains in constant contact with the brain inside your skull.

These two "brains" are linked by an elaborate communication system known as the gut-brain axis. Messages travel in both directions, carried by nerves, hormones, immune cells, and chemical messengers produced by the trillions of bacteria that live within the intestines. It's a constant conversation—one that helps regulate not only digestion, but also mood, stress, appetite, memory, and behavior.

This discovery has transformed the way we think about both physical and mental health.

It has been revealed that for decades, psychiatrists understandably focused almost exclusively on the brain. Depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, ADHD, and anorexia nervosa were viewed as disorders of brain chemistry. But over the past 20 years, an explosion of research has revealed that the gut is an active participant in all of these conditions. Rather than functioning as separate organs, the gut and the brain operate as partners. When one suffers, the other often does, too.

That insight is especially key in anorexia nervosa.

For people with anorexia nervosa, this two-way conversation has profound implications. Recovery isn’t only about restoring body weight or correcting abnormalities in the brain. It’s also about rebuilding a healthy digestive system capable of supporting the brain’s healing processes.

One of the cruelest aspects of anorexia nervosa is that the illness often convinces people that food and eating are problems.

As recovery begins and eating increases, many patients experience bloating, constipation, abdominal pain, nausea, and a feeling of fullness after only a few bites. These symptoms can be frightening. They seem to confirm the eating disorder's central lie: See? Eating makes you feel worse.

But that's not what's happening. In most cases, these digestive symptoms are not caused by eating. They are caused by starvation.

When the body is deprived of adequate nourishment for weeks, months, or years, it begins conserving energy wherever it can. Digestion slows dramatically. The muscles that normally move food through the stomach and intestines become less active. The stomach empties more slowly, intestinal motility decreases, and constipation becomes common. Food remains in the digestive tract longer than it should, producing bloating, abdominal discomfort, and an uncomfortable sense of fullness after meals.

Ironically, the very symptoms that make eating difficult are often the result of not eating enough in the first place.

Understanding this dynamic can be enormously reassuring as it highlights that the digestive system has not been permanently damaged. The symptoms are signs of a body adapting to prolonged starvation and so, as nutritional rehabilitation progresses and the gut begins receiving the nourishment it needs, digestive function usually improves—although it often takes weeks or months for the gastrointestinal tract to recover fully.

In a recent development, in anorexia, another notable change occurs deep within the intestines, where trillions of bacteria collectively known as the gut microbiome reside. These microorganisms help digest food, produce vitamins, regulate immune function, maintain the integrity of the intestinal lining, and manufacture compounds that influence the brain. Like every other living organism in the body, they depend on a steady supply of nutrients to thrive.

When food intake becomes severely restricted, then, the microbiome changes as well.

Recent findings suggest that over the past decade, researchers have consistently found that people with anorexia nervosa have a gut microbiome that differs significantly from those of healthy individuals. Some beneficial bacterial species decline, while others become more abundant. Overall microbial diversity—the hallmark of a healthy ecosystem—often decreases. These changes are now believed to contribute not only to digestive symptoms, but also to inflammation, anxiety, and difficulties with weight restoration.

The good news is that the gut is remarkably resilient. Unlike many organs, the digestive tract is constantly renewing itself. Cells lining the intestines are replaced every few days. The microbiome is continually adapting to changes in diet, medications, stress, and environment. Even after prolonged starvation, the digestive system has an extraordinary capacity for recovery—provided it receives the nourishment and support it needs.

Industry observers note that eating enough food. No supplement can substitute for dietary rehabilitation. Restoring adequate calories, protein, healthy fats, and food-delivered vitamins and minerals remains the cornerstone of recovery from anorexia nervosa.

Digestive enzymes. Digestive discomfort can make every meal feel like a battle. Bloating, cramping, constipation, and abdominal pain often reinforce the fear that eating is making things worse. Breaking that cycle sometimes requires giving the digestive system additional support while it heals. One of the simplest ways to do that is through digestive enzyme supplementation.

Digestive enzymes help break food into smaller molecules that can be more easily absorbed by the body. Although digestive enzyme supplements have not yet been studied in anorexia, decades of clinical experience suggest they can can substantially reduce gastrointestinal discomfort during nutritional rehabilitation.

It has been revealed that probiotics. Another important tool is the use of probiotics—live, beneficial microorganisms that help restore a healthier balance within the gut microbiome. For centuries, traditional cultures have consumed probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, kimchi, miso, and sauerkraut. Today, probiotic supplements provide carefully selected bacteria strains that can help replenish beneficial microbes disrupted by illness, antibiotics, stress, and prolonged food restrictions. Their companion nutrients, known as prebiotics, serve as food for these beneficial bacteria, helping them grow and flourish.

Learn more in my new book, Finally Nourished: A Science-Based Proposal to Correct Malnutrition in Anorexia Nervosa—and Achieve True and Lasting Recovery.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

Maybe you did marry the love of your life, but that still doesn't guarantee you'll win over the people who raised them. Some in-laws are loving and accept you with ease, while others seem to spend decades waiting for their son to finally come to his senses.

As a couples therapist, I've listened to stories of complicated in-law dynamics, ranging from mildly irritating to downright abusive, on a daily basis.

Industry observers note that maybe your career ambitions don't align with your in-laws' traditional expectations of what a wife and mother should be. You’re selfish for working or having a self-care routine, but if you stay home, you're accused of being lazy and mooching off their son.

Perhaps your mother-in-law was perfectly lovely for years, until your children reached adolescence, got their own phones, and your services in orchestrating family get-togethers were no longer needed. Suddenly, the woman who used to call you every week barely acknowledges your existence.

Maybe your sister-in-law crashed your family vacation, or your mother-in-law feels entitled to drop by your home whenever she pleases, and everyone expects you to go with the flow. Or your father-in-law has barely acknowledged you for a decade but couldn't contain his relief when your newborn baby looked exactly like his son and nothing like you.

You are bombarded with unsolicited advice about your finances, your diet, and your children's education.

In a recent development, family relationships are complicated, and nobody should expect their in-laws to agree with or approve of every decision they make. However, repeatedly being made to feel unwelcome is not the same as a disagreement.

Secure-functioning relationships are built on the couple bubble, a protective partnership in which emotional safety and connection for the couple are prioritized. This includes managing thirds, which can be anything the couple navigates, including relationships, careers, hobbies, obligations, and even addictions that can interfere with the stability of the partnership (Tatkin, 2024).

Managing extended-family dynamics doesn't mean cutting ties, although in some circumstances, distance may be necessary. Nor does it mean demanding that everyone accommodate you at all costs. But it does mean recognizing that as you build your life together with another person, you become one another’s primary attachment figure. Protecting the stability and safety of that relationship is a shared responsibility.

Both partners should be able to trust that they won't be abandoned when things get uncomfortable, especially when the discomfort comes from each other's family of origin.

Sources indicate that consider a husband whose mother repeatedly criticizes his wife, dismisses her parenting decisions, or excludes her from notable family conversations. The husband may feel that because his mother treats him warmly, the problem is between the two women. He may even insist that his wife is being too sensitive and expect her to let it go in order to keep the peace. This is exactly how the couple bubble begins to break down.

One of the more challenging dynamics in extended families is the relationship that seems perfectly pleasant until someone sets a boundary.

Your in-laws may be affectionate, attentive, and generous when you are agreeable, show up every Sunday for dinner, accept their unsolicited advice, and remain available whenever they need something. But the moment you decide to spend the holidays elsewhere or decline a financial request, the warmth disappears.

Industry observers note that in healthy families, people are not loving only when they are being accommodated and unpleasant the minute someone exercises their autonomy. Boundaries around your home, time, money, and decisions that affect your immediate family are part of being an independent adult and building a life with your partner. Your in-laws might not agree with or love these boundaries, but they do have to respect them.

Children depend on their parents and caregivers to provide them with a safe container where they can play and grow. Their early attachment figures help them determine whether people are safe and predictable, whether conflict can be managed, and whether the people they depend on have the capacity to protect them.

Imagine a child at a family gathering where one parent is repeatedly interrupted, criticized, or excluded from the conversation. Perhaps their parenting decisions are openly questioned, or they are surrounded by relatives who make jokes at their expense while everyone else laughs. The child may not understand the content of the disagreement, but they can sense the tension.

When a parent is undermined, ignored, or humiliated in front of them and other family members, children may feel unsafe and receive damaging messages about loyalty and commitment.

In a recent development, this doesn't mean children need to see their parents as invulnerable or that witnessing an occasional disagreement will be irreparable. In fact, seeing adults navigate conflict respectfully and repair ruptures is an important part of development. However, repeatedly watching a parent be treated as though their feelings, authority, or presence don't matter disrupts the child’s sense of safety and trust.

In a recent development, protecting children doesn't require pretending that everyone gets along. It does, however, require showing them that the adults responsible for their well-being can stand up for themselves and one another.

In couples therapy, one of the recurring challenges I see is the tension between loyalty to one's family of origin and loyalty to the partnership.

For some people, setting boundaries with parents can evoke a tremendous amount of shame and guilt. They may have grown up believing that keeping their parents happy was how they would be lovable, that disagreements were unacceptable, and that love meant accommodating everyone else's needs. As adults, they may continue to prioritize avoiding parental disappointment, even when doing so comes at the expense of their own family they're trying to build.

The partner who grew up in a family that is the source of conflict may have learned to tolerate behaviors that feel unacceptable, intrusive, or outright hostile to the other partner.

Damage to the couplehood is more preventable when the partner whose family is involved assumes responsibility for communicating boundaries.

According to recent reports, the goal isn't to force everyone to like each other or to turn every insensitive comment into a family dispute. Healthy relationships don’t require everyone to be best friends, but they do require mutual respect.

Your in-laws don't have to think you're the greatest thing that ever happened to their family, but they do have to recognize that disrespecting you means disrespecting the family he's chosen to build.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

According to recent reports, the tradition of Thanksgiving is an inspiring example of community and sharing that has strengthened North America for centuries. In February and March 2026, Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation asked 6,732 American citizens what motivates them to give to their communities. They wanted to know whether opportunity, another powerful American driving force, is still going strong. They asked whether people believe they can shape their own futures to build better lives and stronger communities, and how those views influence their willingness to give back.

They found that regardless of location or demographics, 72% of U.S. adults surveyed say the area where they live is worth investing in, even though nearly half do not agree that people in their community look out for one another or work together to solve common problems. Only 1 in 3 believe that if they had an idea to improve their community, someone would listen, and 60% do not trust their local leaders to act in the community's best interest. However, if they believe they will be heard, 2 out of 3 respondents are motivated to give back.

According to recent reports, beyond being listened to, citizens cited other factors that shape their love for and support of their communities. More than 8 in 10 say access to nature improves their quality of life. Americans living in places with closer interpersonal ties are more likely to feel like they can shape the direction of their lives. More than three-quarters believe housing is unaffordable, and nearly half say their communities do not offer enough stable jobs.

Industry observers note that the researchers believe these responses reflect the psychological concept of agency, defined in the Cambridge Dictionary as the ability to take action or choose what action to take. They find that self-determination, or agency, is the most vital predictor of adults’ assessment of their life satisfaction. Their data show that in communities that build strong foundations and connections among their residents, well-being and optimism flourish.

The foundation’s statistics are affirmed by the 2026 findings of Payne & Schimmack, professors at the University of Toronto's Psychological & Brain Sciences department. They also study the impact of opportunity, or agency, on individuals. They surveyed 1,200 adults from Canada and the United Kingdom to measure their positive and negative feelings, life satisfaction, and three psychological traits: autonomy—the feeling of being free to make choices; competence—feeling effective and capable; and relatedness—feeling close and connected to others.

Sources indicate that their findings unwrap the statistics and responses reported by Gallup and Walton. They find that whether happy or sad, autonomy—the sense of freedom to make choices—is the strongest indicator of life satisfaction. "Those who felt more autonomous were more satisfied with their lives," noted Payne, who said the findings have practical implications for public policy. "Programs and interventions designed to improve well-being may succeed in improving feelings, but if they restrict people's choices, then they could ultimately backfire and lead people to judge their lives as worse overall.”.

The Walton Family Foundation sums it up: “Communities grow stronger when people have a voice and a way to contribute.” They find that those closest to challenges are also closest to local solutions for local problems if they are supported to speak up and contribute. “When we listen to the people who know their communities best, we can turn their ideas into lasting change.”.

#299. "Born to Be Wild": How Zoos Fail to Protect Their Residents

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1114 w)

"Born to Be Wild": How Zoos Fail to Protect Their Residents

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • It has been revealed that the existence of zoos of all sorts in which a wide variety of animals are held captive raises countless ethical questions.
  • I found the book to be a valuable, balanced view of what really is happening on the ground at most zoos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

It has been revealed that the existence of zoos of all sorts in which a wide variety of animals are held captive raises countless ethical questions. Despite the best of intentions, most zoos do not overcome what are called "captivity effects" and existing laws do not protect their residents. For these and other reasons, I was pleased to learn of a fresh, well-researched book titled Born to Be Wild: Reckoning with the Zoo in the Age of Extinction, in which readers are taken behind the scenes of the most iconic zoos by award-winning writer Andrew Westoll, who indicates that zoos often fail to protect the animals they work to save.

I found the book to be a valuable, balanced view of what really is happening on the ground at most zoos. It is not an anti-zoo rant but does ask a lot from them in the years to come.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Born to Be Wild?

Andrew Westoll: The central idea at the heart of the book is that no matter what you think about the zoo, we can all agree that absent a convincing argument to the contrary, every animal should be able to live the life it evolved to live.

One of my goals is to model how to explore a topic that challenges or confuses us with an open mind. Another is to help open a renewed dialogue about the position and power of a place that, aside from houses of worship, are the most influential public institutions in our society. Around the world, about 700 million people visit a zoo or aquarium every year. That’s about a tenth of humanity. Shouldn’t we all know a little more about how these places work?

And finally, my other main goal is to take the reader to the heart of the modern zoo by taking them behind the scenes at some of the most interesting zoos on the planet. Readers get to go on every adventure I did, from the urban wilds of Central Park to the remote jungles of Central Africa.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

It has been revealed that recent reporting suggests that giant panda breeding programs in China have very little to do with actual conservation efforts, and everything to do with exporting Chinese “soft power” (sorry for the pun) around the world. I visited the giant pandas of Vienna, at the Schönbrunn Zoo, to understand why the Austrians have had such success in breeding the bears naturally (i.e., without artificial insemination). It’s a remarkable story of persistence and expertise. But I also explored the fact that most countries to receive cute and cuddly diplomats from Beijing have first signed major trading deals with the Chinese state.

Panda diplomacy is a troubling, exploitative practice in which the bears’ welfare is rarely the main priority. The next time we see a head of state posing with pandas at their local zoos, we should remember this fact.

Breeding programs at zoo are enormously controversial, because no matter what a zoo tells us, animals born into zoos are destined to live their entire lives in a zoo. These breeding programs are supposed to be about building “assurance populations,” genetically robust populations that could one day be released back into the wild.

However, when you look deeply at the breeding data, you discover that the majority of vertebrate populations being bred in zoos are not genetically viable (i.e., not genetically diverse enough to counteract the impacts of inbreeding). In other words, zoos around the world are failing at their most fundamental task: to build healthy, sustainable populations into the future.

MB: How does your work differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

Industry observers note that AW: Most books about the zoo are either scholarly or theoretical in nature, focused on specific histories or through the lens of animal rights. But most of them don’t do a great job of meeting regular people where they live. I want to engage everyday people in these ethical and moral questions, to help them think through their impressions of the modern zoo without feeling they’ve missed an entire semester of college!

MB: What has it been like to levy criticisms at the modern zoo as a whole, when so many people who work in them are well-intentioned and clearly care a great deal for their animals?

AW: This is probably the hardest part of my job as a journalist, to separate the people I’ve met and spoken with from the larger topics I’m dealing with. And this was especially hard in this case. Just about every zoo employee I interviewed or met while researching this book was a passionate animal person, wholly dedicated to the well-being of their charges, whether they were curators, keepers, or marketing folks.

But after reading so much of the zoo literature, where so many progressive people in the industry are begging their institutions to modernize and change for the better, and after learning just how deeply the zoo is failing to meet its own targets, it became clear to me that many zoo professionals have a permanent blind spot when it comes to considering the role of the modern zoo and the ethics of captivity in the 21st century.

Sources indicate that it seems to me that if the zoo wants to maintain its social license to operate, it is going to have to radically update its thinking and its operational mandate. Zoo insiders have been calling for this to happen for more than 30 years now. Unfortunately, we’re still a long way off from the zoo renaissance we’ve been promised.

In conversation with former zoologist, presently a professor of Creative Writing and English at the University of Toronto Scarborough, and award-winning bestselling journalist Andrew Westoll.

#298. Breaking: The Harmful Consequences of a Frictionless Life

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (699 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Breaking: The Harmful Consequences of a Frictionless Life

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • I recently wrote a post titled, “The Impact of AI on Who We Are and Who We Become”.
  • Sources indicate that the counterpart to friction is perhaps perfection, a theme I discussed in a more recent post.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

I recently wrote a post titled, “The Impact of AI on Who We Are and Who We Become”. In it, I stated that development of the “self” relies heavily on friction, trial-and-error and navigating the unknown. I asserted that by replacing these struggles with optimised, predictable convenience, AI threatens active self-discovery and perhaps even challenges the very concept of “self”. The concept of a frictionless life is one I’ve continued to contemplate. We need friction. It invites us to examine our biases and assumptions. It helps us to develop and grow.

Sources indicate that the counterpart to friction is perhaps perfection, a theme I discussed in a more recent post. The promise of perfect communication is one of the allures of AI companionship. People turn to chatbots in an effort to avoid the messy, imperfect realties of human relationships. But guess what? A frictionless life is a fantasy, and so, when friction does inevitably show up in human relationships, people then can’t handle it. They panic. They employ psychological defences. They attack. I see this play out on social media, where the algorithm traps us in silos where everyone agrees with us. I don’t think we learn much in silos. There’s no friction. There’s no space to explore biases and assumptions. There’s no room to grow. I’ve also seen what happens when an adversary slides in from left field: Fear. Ragebait. Cancellation.

Sources indicate that I often hear the phrase, “I don’t like conflict,” and who does? But what that phrase often means is, “I don’t know how to manage it; I haven’t got the skills.” In psychoanalytic literature there’s a concept called “rupture and repair”,1 which describes what happens when there is a split or lack of attunement (the rupture) followed by a renewed closeness and connection (the repair). This comes from psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott’s observations of what he termed “good-enough” mothering, where ruptures are inevitable, though hopefully occasional. During infancy, the baby uses opportunities of misattunement to learn to tolerate frustration, regulate their emotions and develop a sense of self. They learn to manage friction. A rupture in any relationship, including therapeutic ones, presents an opportunity. It is often the struggle moments, if we can survive them, that facilitate connectedness and change.

But what if we cannot survive them? What if we never learned or have forgotten how? Whereas a lack of “good-enough” early experiences deny infants the opportunity to develop the skills necessary for reparation, AI chatbots generate a kind of unlearning which leads to unrealistic expectations about the complexities of human relationships. This can lead to social atrophy and a lack of conflict resolution skills. It can lead to emotional detachment and withdrawal. It can fuel fear and rage.

Human connections are messy, imperfect, unpredictable and clumsy. We “um” and we “er”. We say the wrong thing. We misunderstand and are misunderstood. We make mistakes. We are vulnerable. We might cause offence or be offended. We might cause or be hurt. These are the struggle moments that AI chatbots eradicate. Artificial companions never misunderstand. They are always validating and affirming, infinitely agreeable and sycophantic. They never get frustrated or impatient. They don’t misunderstand us or tell us we’ve made a mistake. They are not vulnerable and they can’t get hurt or offended. Our interactions with chatbots are always frictionless and they carry zero risk. They teach us nothing, however, about what it’s like to be in relationship with an imperfect human.

Recent findings suggest that the development of emotional intelligence requires us to be vulnerable, take risks, hurt, be hurt and survive. The development of social intelligence requires friction – experiences of getting things wrong and being wronged and surviving. Struggle moments present valuable opportunities to deepen relationships. A frictionless life is a fantasy. Opting out of messy human relationships and choosing to live in that fantasy helps no one.

Winnicott, D.W. (1965). The maturational process and the facilitating environment: Studies in the theory of emotional development. International Universities Press.

#297. Why Leaving an Abusive Partner May Not End the Pain

Why Leaving an Abusive Partner May Not End the Pain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (627 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Recent findings suggest that many people have left an abusive relationship feeling heartbroken and relieved at the same time.
  • In a recent development, shahida Arabi (2023) investigated the impact of partner narcissism and psychopathy on posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptomology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Recent findings suggest that many people have left an abusive relationship feeling heartbroken and relieved at the same time. Whether the abuse was emotional, physical, or both, many victims experience a temporary sense of relief, realizing their mental health is no longer linked to a partner’s toxic behavior. Or is it? Because recognizing symptoms helps identify appropriate treatment, it is helpful to understand the potential fallout from a maladaptive relationship, even after the fact.

In a recent development, shahida Arabi (2023) investigated the impact of partner narcissism and psychopathy on posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptomology. She explains that both dark triad traits share numerous common traits that may cause aggression within intimate partnerships, including grandiosity, manipulation, lack of empathy, and exploitation. Such personalities also engage in manipulative behavior, designed to keep partners insecure and emotionally unsteady. They shower romantic prospects with excessive attention and flattery commonly referred to as “love bombing,” shut down conversations or "stonewall," and “gaslight” partners by questioning their memory, reality, or perception.

Recent findings suggest that describing the characteristics of two narcissism subtypes, Arabi explains that grandiose narcissism is linked with higher amounts of self-esteem and self-confidence, while vulnerable narcissism is associated with fearfulness and hypersensitivity. Regarding the potential for victimization through aggression, Arabi recognizes the strong association between narcissistic and antisocial personality traits and perpetrating intimate partner violence, and the impact of intimate partner violence on the victim, including mental health problems and PTSD.

Recent findings suggest that of the dark personality traits, one type of narcissism may be uniquely damaging over time. Studying 1,294 subjects romantically involved with individuals expressing a high degree of narcissistic or psychopathic traits, Arabi found that grandiose and vulnerable narcissism were significant predictors of PTSD symptomology for ex-partners who had exited the relationship, even after factoring in the impact of previous abuse and manipulation.

Arabi found that grandiose narcissism expressed by a partner was the strongest predictor of PTSD, more so than frequency of abuse, childhood abuse, or physical abuse. It was also a stronger predictor than vulnerable narcissism or psychopathy, which Arabi opines may be due to the fact that grandiose narcissism is linked with a higher degree of self-aggrandizement, which could produce elevated self-blame and intrusive thoughts in victims who are abused by a more confident and ruthless person who has such traits.

Considering the frequency with which we learn about and discuss the potential impact of dark personalities on romantic relationships, the goal is to ferret out such characteristics sooner rather than later. And although we gain more information as we spend time with someone over time, many people detect cues as early as a first date.

Industry observers note that detecting grandiose narcissism involves more than recognizing elevated self-esteem and self-confidence, which are not inherently negative characteristics on their own. Instead, look past the confident veneer to the cunning, venomous behaviors emerging over time as dark personalities begin to reveal their true colors.

In a recent development, be attentive to subtle tactics of emotional manipulation, consider whether flattery is authentic and appropriate, and recognize that healthy romantic attention makes you feel desirable, but also valuable, cared for, and comfortable. Getting to know a potential paramour at a pace that is slow and steady affords time to decide if your upcoming love interest genuinely possesses the traits of a good partner and will be a good fit for you.

Sources indicate that arabi, Shahida. “Narcissistic and Psychopathic Traits in Romantic Partners Predict Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Symptomology: Evidence for Unique Impact in a Large Sample.” Personality and Individual Differences 201 (February 2023): 1–6.

#296. MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1260 w)
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily

MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful.
  • It has been revealed that researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain.
  • It has been revealed that the finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an crucial opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function.

It has been revealed that researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF.

It has been revealed that the finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta.

Industry observers note that "We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," notes Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

It has been revealed that lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine, with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory.

How Sleep Helps the Brain Remove Waste.

Cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy.

In 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep.

Building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves.

According to recent reports, "You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis says. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?".

How Pink Noise Amplifies Brain Waves.

According to recent reports, to test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance.

It has been revealed that timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI.

It has been revealed that combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and rapidly enough to synchronize the sound.

In a recent development, the team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment.

Stronger Brain Cleaning Waves During Sleep.

Sources indicate that the researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants.

In a recent development, the brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens.

In a recent development, by enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality.

Could Pink Noise Improve Sleep and Help Fight Alzheimer's?

The researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances.

According to recent reports, this possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a new way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions.

"Brain waste clearance is really crucial for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt says.

The technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has introduced a company that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow.

Industry observers note that for now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an crucial question for future studies.

The research received funding from a McKnight Scholar Award, a Sloan Fellowship, a Pew Biomedical Scholars Award, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, the MIT EECS Transformative Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Corundum Convergence Institute, and the Panasonic Well Fellowship for AI and Wellness.

#295. Growing Older on the Spectrum: The Unique Needs of Autistic Adults

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (886 w)

Growing Older on the Spectrum: The Unique Needs of Autistic Adults

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.
  • According to recent reports, our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years.
  • Sources indicate that but even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.

According to recent reports, our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years. Today, many autistic adults who were overlooked or misdiagnosed in childhood are finally pursuing a proper evaluation and diagnosis.

Sources indicate that but even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most. Why? Because less than 1 percent of all indexed autism research has focused on midlife and older age.

Industry observers note that that means we still don’t understand the cognitive, health, and social experiences of autistic adults as they age. And this lack of research influences clinical practice: Historically, clinicians haven’t been trained and equipped with an understanding of autism in older age.

An analysis of health records from the United Kingdom indicates that around 90 percent of autistic people in midlife (ages 40 to 59), and 96 percent of older adults (ages 60 and beyond), are undiagnosed.1 Until autism research and diagnosis rates improve, we won’t understand the full autistic experience, but here are the truths coming into focus.

[Read: “How Can I Get Evaluated for Autism as an Adult?”].

Autism in older age is associated with complex health needs. Compared with the general population, middle-aged and older autistic adults have higher rates of several physical and mental health conditions, making frequent and proactive screenings important for this group.

Despite the higher rates of dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and cognitive difficulties found among autistic adults, we should not assume that autism is linked to accelerated cognitive aging. Autistic people are no more likely to experience rapid cognitive aging than are members of the general population, according to research.

Recent findings suggest that however, one study found that about 20 percent of autistic people had highly variable cognitive profiles; this subgroup developed an old-age profile earlier than expected compared to non-autistic adults. For these individuals, red flags for cognitive decline and dementia may present at a younger age than we’d expect in the general population. Autistic adults who fit this profile may require additional help and support as they age to remain safe and independent.

Sleep typically deteriorates with age, however, adults with high autistic traits are more likely than others to report moderate or severe sleep problems as they grow older, including problems with falling and staying asleep, sleep efficiency, and daytime tiredness.

Sleep is a lynchpin for general and mental health. Sleep problems, for example, tend to worsen anxiety, a condition that is highly prevalent among autistic adults. Improving sleep quality by blocking out light with curtains, using earplugs or a white noise machine, choosing pajamas and bedsheets made from soothing fabrics, and/or using a weighted blanket can significantly benefit the mental health of autistic people as they age.

[Read: This is Why You’re Always Tired].

Sources indicate that sensory processing differences are part of the autistic experience. Over a lifetime, exposure to difficult and unpleasant sensory experiences, like crowded, noisy environments, is linked to mental health problems in older autistic adults. At the same time, even small changes, such as noise-canceling headphones or wearing a face mask in public, can help. Adjustments and accommodations such as these should not be overlooked when thinking of health and quality of life.

Industry observers note that compared with non-autistic people, autistic adults experience higher rates of loneliness — the subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connection. While middle-aged and older autistic people tend to have small social networks, about one in five autistic adults has no contact with family or friends in a given month, compared with one in 20 neurotypical adults. Certain neurodivergent traits — rigidity, flat affect or an aloof personality, and communication challenges — may help explain social difficulties.

Industry observers note that interestingly, in the general population, we found that women tend to be lonelier than men. In the autistic population, the feeling of loneliness was more common in men.

Connections with family and friends seem to provide a protective mental health benefit and lead to a better quality of life. Supporting autistic people in forming meaningful relationships on their own terms and in relation to their passions and interests could be a key target for interventions.
