#294. Beyond Us Versus Them

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1071 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Beyond Us Versus Them

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • Industry observers note that on election day this month, Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, stripping Republicans of a supermajority.
  • Whether or not you’re a fan of Talarico, he might be on to something.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

Industry observers note that on election day this month, Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, stripping Republicans of a supermajority. Headlines surrounding the midterms focused on the rising tension between Democrats and Republicans amid the Trump administration, which has created a lot of rifts between neighbors, friends, and even family members across the country. After winning his race, Democratic U.S. Senator-Elect James Talarico of Texas pleaded with Americans to reframe the narrative, not as a "left versus right" ideological struggle, but as a "top versus bottom" economic divide between wealthy elites and working-class people.

Whether or not you’re a fan of Talarico, he might be on to something. The idea of “us versus them” is as old as the human race, and likely comes from our propensity to form categories. The ability to categorize is a natural and automatic part of the human brain; it allows us to store an incredible amount of information in our memories and make inferences about things we’ve never seen before. Imagine for a second that we didn’t have the ability to form categories; it would mean that every time we encountered a brand-upcoming object, we’d have to learn about it from scratch. The fact that we have categories means that whenever we encounter an apple, for example, we can apply what we know about other apples and safely assume that this new apple is a piece of fruit that tastes sweet and is nutritious. Likewise, whenever we encounter a new dog, we’d know something about the way it likely behaves, what it eats, and whether it’s safe to approach.

Our propensity to categorize starts very early in our lives. By 2 months of age, infants can distinguish broad categories of animate versus inanimate objects. By 3 to 4 months, infants can make basic-level categories for things like cats, dogs, and birds, and by 6 to 7 months they can even form subordinate categories distinguishing among different types of dogs (e.g., Beagles versus St. Bernards). By 14 to 18 months, they can use an object’s function to form categories (even in the absence of physical similarity), and they begin to use labels to organize categories. Needless to say, categorization develops quite early in our lives and over time becomes automatic.

In a recent development, but despite its benefits, our natural propensity to categorize has some downsides when we extend the ability beyond the categorization of objects to the categorization of people. When we form categories for groups of people, we can easily make false assumptions about someone latest purely based on their category membership. This behavior is the very definition of “prejudice,” which is the tendency to make assumptions about someone purely based on their membership in a particular group. On top of that, when people tend to place themselves in a group, or what we might call an “ingroup,” there will inevitably be others who are left out of that group—people we call “outgroup” members. Infants begin to do this based on perceptual features like gender and race by 6 months, and slightly older children expect that people in the same group—usually marked in research by sharing some arbitrary feature, like a shirt color—should like the same things and behave in similar ways (e.g., Liberman, Woodward, & Kinzler, 2017).

In a recent development, why is this notable? Not surprisingly, we treat people better when we think they’re part of our ingroup, even if that ingroup is completely arbitrary. For example, in a recent set of studies, researchers put adults in groups based on an arbitrary similarity (e.g., people who like green versus blue, or people who prefer squares versus triangles), along with more meaningful ones (e.g., political orientation, religious affiliation, ethnicity), and then had them play a game that required cooperation. The researchers found that the more group memberships people shared—regardless of whether they were meaningful groups or were completely arbitrary—the more people cooperated with each other (Uğurlar et al., 2024). And the fact that we cooperate more with group members who share commonalities with us that are completely trivial suggests that membership isn't necessarily fixed.

Sources indicate that and in fact, the boundaries between “us” and “them” can shift depending on which aspects of our identities we emphasize. I've experienced this firsthand. I was only a 21-year-old college student on September 11, 2001, when the planes hit the World Trade Center in Newly introduced York. Despite it being the scariest day of my life, I remember hundreds of students gathering on the quad, arms around each other’s shoulders, swaying and singing America the Beautiful. I never felt togetherness like that before, and I’m not sure if I’ve ever felt it since. During that tragedy, we weren’t Democrats and Republicans; we were all Americans. We were forced to reframe the ingroup that day—instead of being in separate smaller circles, we made the circle wider.

In a recent development, in real-life research testing this observation, researchers conducted a series of studies where they made participants’ American identity more salient (e.g., by writing a paragraph on why they are proud to identify as American). At the end of the exercise, both Democrat and Republican participants evaluated members of the opposing party more positively (Levendusky, 2018).

So perhaps one way to move past the “us versus them” mentality in politics, or in life more broadly, is to stop thinking about people as Republicans versus Democrats and instead, to find something you have in common—maybe you are fellow parents, fellow community members, fellow music lovers, or just fellow humans. As Talarico alluded to, by reframing our ideas of group membership—by defining our groups more broadly instead of narrowly—people who might otherwise seem different can now become members of a shared community.

According to recent reports, liberman, Z., Woodward, A. L., & Kinzler, K. D. (2017). The origins of social categorization. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 21(7), 556–568.

Sources indicate that levendusky, M. S. (2018). Americans, not partisans: Can priming American national identity reduce affective polarization? The Journal of Politics, 80(1), 59–70.

Industry observers note that uğurlar, P., Dorrough, A. R., Isler, O., Yilmaz, O., et al. (2024). Shared group memberships mitigate intergroup bias in cooperation. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 16(2).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A upcoming wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most important stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery. Developed by researchers led by the University of Texas at Austin, the device uses gentle ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, helping people enter REM sleep sooner and spend more time in this restorative stage.

It has been revealed that known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time. This allows researchers to influence brain regions involved in sleep while simultaneously tracking how the brain responds.

REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs. It also plays an important role in processing emotions, consolidating memories, and adapting to stress. Disturbances in this stage of sleep have been associated with several mental health conditions, making it an important target for fresh treatments.

It has been revealed that "This is the first time we've been able to noninvasively target deep brain regions involved in REM sleep, while simultaneously monitoring brain activity," stated Kai Wing "Kevin" Tang, a recent UT biomedical engineering Ph.D. graduate who led the research effort.

Sources indicate that "Our skin-attached NEUSLeeP patch opens up new possibilities for understanding sleep and treating sleep disorders in home settings," added Huiliang "Evan" Wang, assistant professor in the Cockrell School of Engineering's Department of Biomedical Engineering. Wang supervised Tang's research and served as the principal investigator (PI) overseeing the project.

Sleep Patch Helps People Reach REM Sleep 43 Minutes Faster.

The early results suggest that the technology can make a measurable difference in how people experience REM sleep.

In a study involving 28 participants, published in Nature Communications, people using the patch entered REM sleep an average of 43 minutes sooner and spent approximately 16 additional minutes in that stage.

Recent findings suggest that these improvements were observed in both healthy sleepers and participants experiencing certain sleep difficulties. The volunteers also reported that the patch was comfortable to wear, with minimal adverse effects.

Unlike medications that affect the body more broadly, NEUSLeeP is designed to deliver stimulation to specific brain regions involved in sleep regulation. It uses ultrasound, a form of sound energy with frequencies beyond human hearing, to reach areas beneath the surface of the brain without requiring an invasive procedure.

The findings are encouraging, although the relatively small study means that larger trials will be needed to determine how consistently the technology works and whether its benefits persist over time.

Potential Benefits for Stress and Emotional Health.

The researchers also found evidence that the patch's effects may extend beyond increasing REM sleep.

Recent findings suggest that among healthy participants, ultrasound stimulation improved heart rate variability, a measure of the natural differences in time between consecutive heartbeats. This measurement provides insight into how the body's nervous system responds to stress and adjusts to changing conditions.

Brain imaging revealed changes in neural circuits involved in emotional processing. Together, these findings suggest that improving REM sleep through targeted stimulation could potentially support emotional regulation and the ability to cope with stress.

Sources indicate that "REM sleep is not just about dreaming -- it's about emotional reset and stress adaptation," explained Gregory Fonzo, assistant professor in the Dell Medical School's Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and one of the project's co-PIs. "By enhancing REM, we may help people better cope with stress and improve their overall well-being.".

These possibilities are especially interesting because REM sleep disturbances have been linked to depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Sources indicate that current approaches to sleep problems often involve medication or behavioral therapy. Although these treatments can be effective, medications may produce unwanted side effects, and existing approaches do not always directly address the biological processes responsible for disrupted REM sleep.

Industry observers note that A device capable of influencing those processes without drugs or surgery could therefore offer an additional treatment option. However, the researchers have not yet established whether NEUSLeeP can improve symptoms of mental health disorders.

A New Direction for Treating Insomnia and PTSD.

Building on the initial findings, the research team aims to conduct larger clinical trials to confirm the patch's effects and investigate its potential use in people with PTSD, depression, and chronic insomnia.

In a recent development, beyond treating sleep disorders, the technology could eventually support sleep monitoring at home and provide scientists with a newly introduced way to study how deep brain regions influence sleep. Researchers also envision personalized therapies that could be adjusted to individual sleep patterns and needs.

It has been revealed that "Our vision is a future where patients with mental health disorders can optimize their sleep with a noninvasive and safe treatment," mentioned Vincent Mysliwiec, M.D., a professor at UT Health San Antonio, a leading expert in sleep disorders, and another co-PI on the project. "This technology could help millions of people get the restorative sleep they need.".

The team is already taking steps toward making NEUSLeeP available beyond the research setting. Working with the university's commercialization unit, Discovery to Impact, the researchers are exploring how to bring the device to market and have filed a patent application covering the technology.

If future studies confirm the early results, this wearable ultrasound patch could become a valuable latest tool for improving REM sleep and potentially addressing conditions associated with poor sleep.

#292. What Does It Mean to Believe in God?

What Does It Mean to Believe in God?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • In his Ethics, Aristotle indicates that we should seek to understand each thing according to the kind of account it permits.
  • If we are adding or subtracting single-digit numbers, we can reasonably expect a reliable answer from a third grader.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

In his Ethics, Aristotle indicates that we should seek to understand each thing according to the kind of account it permits. In solving an arithmetic problem, for example, we should expect an answer that is both accurate and precise. In the moral life, by contrast, we should seek an account that accords with what a practically wise person would have to say.

If we are adding or subtracting single-digit numbers, we can reasonably expect a reliable answer from a third grader. If, however, we are talking about friendship, marriage, or the relationship between a parent and offspring, we should turn elsewhere for insight, perhaps to the works of George Eliot or Leo Tolstoy.

Recent findings suggest that A similar shift in expectation is appropriate when we think about belief in God. If God were a phenomenon susceptible to the sort of reasoning that we find in an arithmetic problem or a proof in symbolic logic, then it should be relatively easy to construct a knock-down argument for the existence and nature of God.

If, however, God is not quantifiable, then arithmetical approaches are not likely to serve us well, and if God is not like the major or minor premises of a syllogism (such as: All things we can conceive of exist; we can conceive of God; therefore, God exists), then we should not expect to “solve” God like a proof.

It has been revealed that likewise, if God is not made of matter, we should not expect to be able to reproduce the divine presence through scientific means, whether physical or chemical. The mere fact that God does not have mass, dimension, shape, location, or color does not establish that God is nothing more than a figment of human imagination.

Sources indicate that after all, we believe in numbers, although they lack all the physical properties just mentioned, and we also believe in love, justice, beauty, and truth, although they too cannot be counted, logically proved, or reproduced in a laboratory flask. There are things we believe to be real that we cannot see with our eyes or touch with our hands.

If sacred texts are any guide, the best means we have of accounting for God are not the methods of mathematics, logic, or science, but those more closely aligned with literature or narrative. The Bible, for example, is full of stories, and while a few of these stories include God directly, many more address the effects of God’s presence in the unfolding of the human story.

In one well-known metaphor, God is not something we directly apprehend, but we can sense God at work in the world much as we see and hear the breeze rustling the leaves on a tree. When Moses first senses God’s presence, it is in the form of a bush that is burning but not consumed by the flames, something only he has the curiosity and patience to see.

At this point, a skeptic might ask, If God is real, is it too much to ask that the divine should simply appear before us, work a few miracles, and thereby remove all doubt? But what if the problem is not God’s but ours? What if God cannot be put into any humanly constructed box because the divine is far beyond our meager intellectual and imaginative capacities?

It has been revealed that what if we are talking about a reality that undergirds all of reality, not only as we know it but also far beyond our capacity to comprehend? What if we are seeking not just a clockmaker who set things in motion billions of years ago but a creator who sustains the universe from moment to moment as it continues to unfold even now in space and time?

Even the physical universe is far beyond our capacity to keep tabs on. A mature human organism consists of about 40 trillion cells, each one of which performs about 1 billion chemical reactions per second, which in turn requires the presence of about 100 trillion atoms of hydrogen. Of course, these are just round numbers – only God knows for sure.

Sources indicate that it is quite possible, perhaps likely, and based on past experience, all but certain that there is a great deal that we do not yet know about even the physical universe. It was only in 1895 that we first learned of the existence of x-rays and only in 1962 that we verified extra-terrestrial x-ray sources. What else still awaits our discovery?

It has been revealed that yet even to say that we still have a great deal more to discover hardly captures the full extent of the problem. For one thing, there may be more out there and in here, even if it is susceptible to our awareness or understanding, than we will ever uncover. And it is also possible that the greater part of it does not conform to our ways of knowing.

Sources indicate that perhaps being itself, as well as its source and end, is not an entirely anthropomorphic thing, in the sense that it is not built for our minds. It may have many other purposes far beyond us. And yet, here we are, blessed with the ability to perceive and understand some truly remarkable things, even if we can’t begin to get our hands around the whole thing.

Perhaps when it comes to God, poetry, music, art, and narrative are the best we can hope for – intimations, always allusive and never definitive. And yet, even here, we find truth and beauty for which we have every reason to be deeply thankful, for perhaps it is above all when we sense God’s presence, maybe with the aid of Eliot and Tolstoy, that we come most fully to life.

How “Touch Starvation” Hurts Mental Health—and Sex

  • Personal computers became appliances in 1977.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

Personal computers became appliances in 1977. The internet became a public utility in 1995. The iPhone debuted in 2007. These events meant that life increasingly revolved around screen time, today more than ever.

Tech has replaced a good deal of face-to-face human interaction, causing what some psychologists call “an epidemic of loneliness.” The issue became a public health problem in 2020 when the COVID pandemic enforced extended social isolation to a degree never experienced by those spared solitary confinement. Many studies agree that chronic loneliness aggravates stress, contributes to depression, weakens immunity, dramatically increases risk of heart disease and stroke, and in the elderly, accelerates cognitive decline. But loneliness is only one dimension of the harm inflicted by social isolation. Another is the loss of gentle, affectionate, massage-like touch.

Recent findings suggest that of course, gentle, loving touch is fundamental to partner sex. Some sexologists call sex “whole-body massage that eventually extends to the genitals.”.

Gentle touch activates special nerves in the skin, C-tactile fibers, aka CT afferents. When stimulated, these nerves trigger release of three compounds key to erotic pleasure:.

It has been revealed that with touch deprivation, these compounds don’t get released, and people can’t experience their benefits. When infants don’t receive regular loving touch, when they aren’t cuddled, their little bodies may shut down from what pediatricians call “failure to thrive,” a condition that may prove fatal. Beyond infancy, touch starvation isn’t fatal, but it drives some people quietly crazy.

A great deal of research shows the benefits of gentle touch, and by extension, the harm suffered from touch starvation. The largest and most ambitious study was conducted by German and Dutch researchers who reviewed several decades of touch/massage research involving some 13,000 men, women, and children (Packheiser, 2024). Most of the studies compared subjects who received gentle, massage-style touch for around 20 minutes with those who did not. Some compared people who touched things like kittens or stuffed animals with those who did not. Both touch recipients—and providers—experienced what the researchers called “massive” benefits: “The evidence is clear that touch is beneficial across a large number of physical and mental health conditions, for all ages, and for both healthy individuals and those with diagnosed conditions.”.

In a recent development, for all age groups but one, it didn’t matter who administered the massages. The exception was newborns born prematurely. Compared with massages administered by medical personnel, for reasons that remain unclear, those infants benefited more from being touched by their parents.

According to recent reports, massage produced significant benefits for everyone, but the greatest life enhancement accrued to those with diagnosed physical or mental health conditions. The researchers encouraged physicians and mental health professionals to incorporate massage routinely into clinical care.

Recent findings suggest that vision, hearing, smell, and taste all deteriorate with age. Touch does not. The elderly enjoy as much pleasure from gentle touch as young people.

In a recent development, while gentle touch helps everyone, compared with men, women experience greater benefit. So, it should come as no surprise that women crave the gentle touch and massage of erotic foreplay, often a great deal more of it than many men provide.

The word “foreplay" is problematic. It implies things that happen before the main event, intercourse. Actually, gentle, leisurely, playful mutual massage fits neatly into lovemaking not only before intercourse, but also during and after. Many sexologists prefer the term “loveplay.”.

If you’re a heterosexual man, you’re likely to enjoy better sex and get better reviews as a lover if you spend at least 20 minutes kissing, hugging, and gently massaging your partner from head to toe first.

Industry observers note that many sex therapists suggest that couples trade foot massages before getting into bed. Foot massage feels marvelous. But in the review of touch, foot massage did not produce the greatest benefits. That distinction went to massage of the face and scalp. Try five to 10 minutes of massage above the shoulders before you touch much below them. If men do this, by the time the action moves south, their bodies are more likely to function as they wish, and their partners are more likely to display the sexual responsiveness men want.

Letting the Film Breathe: A Conversation with Filmmaker Julie Bayer Salzman

  • According to recent reports, just Breathe grew into Mindful Shorts, an ongoing series of experiential documentaries that follow mindfulness across the life span.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in 2013, Julie Bayer Salzman’s five-year-old son came home from kindergarten talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala. She was so struck that she signed up for the same mindfulness course his school used to train its teachers. During one of her meditations, she pictured a short film. That film became Just Breathe, in which elementary school kids describe how mindfulness helps them work with anger. It was featured on Oprah’s Super Soul Sunday and has since been translated into six languages and shown in classrooms around the world.

According to recent reports, just Breathe grew into Mindful Shorts, an ongoing series of experiential documentaries that follow mindfulness across the life span. The five films so far cover anger in childhood, anxiety in middle school, depression in high school, addiction in midlife, and grief in the elder years. Made with her husband and creative partner, cinematographer Josh Salzman, through their company Wavecrest Films, the series is funded by donations and offered free to anyone who needs it.

In a recent development, former Mindful editor Ava Whitney-Coulter first spoke with Salzman in 2024. After the recent release of Bayer’s latest film, Broken & Beautiful, Mindful Chief Editor Siri Myhrom caught up with her at her home in LA. They spoke about what it’s like to work on creative projects with her partner, what advertising taught her, how her practice shows up on set, and what she’s learned from the people at the heart of her newest films.

Siri Myhrom: You spent more than a decade producing commercial campaigns before directing your own work. What did advertising teach you about storytelling, and what did you have to unlearn?

Julie Bayer Salzman: Advertising taught me the importance of strong visuals in nonfiction filmmaking. Sometimes documentary filmmakers don’t place as much value on the visual style as they do on simply capturing the action unfolding in order to tell the best story, and of course that makes a lot of sense in some respect, because story is everything; however, film is a visual medium, and a documentary needs to be more than journalistic. It’s worth taking time to capture reality as beautifully as you can. That said, sometimes when documentaries look too slick, it can be a distraction. To me it’s key to find the balance.

We ask ourselves a simple question: What kind of value does it add to our shared human experience on this planet?

Industry observers note that commercials also taught me how to distill a story to its essence in a short amount of time. And yet, taken too far, that can be a detriment to any story. I had to unlearn to some extent the tendency to truncate a scene out of learned impatience, or playing into the audience’s short attention span. I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but there is not a lot of breathing space in a commercial!

This may seem corny or cliché, but when I started practicing mindfulness, I actually started to lean more into the idea of allowing a film to breathe. As I was learning to breathe more consciously myself, my filmmaking style started to evolve differently, more experientially—slowing the pace, and allowing more pauses between the thoughts or statements.

Recent findings suggest that SM: Wavecrest’s mission is to make content with a positive social impact, and you’ve said you choose projects carefully so you don’t add to the noise. How do you decide whether a project is worth making?

In a recent development, JBS: We ask ourselves a simple question: What kind of value does it add to our shared human experience on this planet? Meaning: Does the project help us evolve collectively? Change the way we see the world? Inspire us to be better humans? Cultivate connection with nature or other humans? Laugh? If none of those things, then we’ll pass, thanks.

SM: You and Josh are married as well as creative partners. How do you divide the work, and how do you handle creative disagreements?

It has been revealed that JBS: We’re incredibly lucky to have very complementary skill sets, while often sharing feelings as well as values. I’m major-picture; he’s details. I’ve got a million ideas and my antennae up at all times, taking in everything around me. I “see” the film conceptually, and have my producer skill set from years in commercials, therefore I tend to take the lead as director and producer; but he’s the cinematographer, and I trust him implicitly to capture my vision in the best possible way.

I can’t say we have creative disagreements, because honestly, we don’t. We respect each other’s strengths in a really beautiful way. It’s a unique creative synergy that I do not take for granted.

In a recent development, when it’s time to edit, I lay out the story, then pass it to him to sculpt the fine details that I usually have no patience for, like on which exact frame to place a cut. He enjoys tedium in a way I don’t.

Sources indicate that I can’t say we have creative disagreements, because honestly, we don’t. We respect each other’s strengths in a really beautiful way. It’s a unique creative synergy that I do not take for granted.

SM: When did mindfulness become part of your personal life, and when did you realize it could be the subject of your films?

JBS: Mindfulness became part of my life when my son started kindergarten in 2013. He came home at the age of five, talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala, thanks to the social-emotional learning curriculum at his school, and I immediately enrolled in the course that the school’s principal used to train the teachers. While meditating one day, I envisioned the first film in the Mindful Shorts series, Just Breathe, and promptly made that film. Once I saw the success it was having, I realized that people were hungry for this type of learning, and the rest of the series evolved from there.

SM: You describe the Mindful Shorts as “experiential” films. What does that mean to you, and how do you design a film that viewers experience rather than just watch?

JBS: It means artfully crafting a film that results more in an embodied experience for the audience, rather than a passive viewing. We don’t conform to traditional standards in order to tell a story; we shape it in such a way that we hope the viewers walk away from the film feeling different energetically than they did at the start. That there is an actual impact on the nervous system—a sense of calm, of understanding—a certain kind of peace within.

In a recent development, when I’m interviewing people, I rarely consult my list of predetermined interview questions. Instead, I like to have a more intimate conversation, where the responses lead to more questions, rather than just asking questions in search of answers.

SM: Does your own mindfulness practice change how you behave on set, such as how you listen, when you stay quiet, or how you handle the unexpected?

JBS: Absolutely. The quality of presence, of attention, are much greater now. I’m far less in my head than I used to be, and it allows for more spontaneity and creative problem solving. I think my practice allows me to be much more fluid and present than I used to be.

Industry observers note that when I’m interviewing people, I rarely consult my list of predetermined interview questions. Instead, I like to have a more intimate conversation, where the responses lead to more questions, rather than just asking questions in search of answers. The goal is not to cross items off a list; it’s to have an experience with the process itself.

SM: Mindfulness is an inner experience, and film is a visual medium. How do you show something that happens inside a person?

It has been revealed that JBS: When you’re talking about something in one’s interior world, the exterior world must match it. Yes, film itself is a visual medium, but filmmaking as an art form is multisensory. In addition to having a distinct visual style, we place an enormous value on sound—ambient noise, music, everything—as well as on editorial pacing. It all must reflect the emotional tone behind what is being remarked, the changes and transformation that a character is going through when they are learning how to mindfully show up in the world.

We are not intimidating folks; I think we are warm and open by nature.

Sources indicate that SM: Your films are unscripted and often feature people talking about very personal struggles. How do you create the kind of safety and trust that lets people be that open on camera?

According to recent reports, JBS: I’m not sure I can answer this question, because it’s not something I consciously do. I think it’s mostly inherent to who both Josh and I are as human beings. We are not intimidating folks; I think we are warm and open by nature. I like to think that people just instinctively trust that we are safe to be vulnerable with, that we emanate an air of security.

Sources indicate that SM: The series follows mindfulness from childhood through old age, moving from anger, to anxiety, depression, addiction, and grief. Was that structure planned from the beginning, or did it develop as you went?

Sources indicate that JBS: Both. After the success of Just Breathe (on anger and elementary school kids), I recognized there was more work to be done. I awoke at 3 a.m., seeing the rest of the series in my head, so I grabbed my journal, sat on the couch, and wrote the progression of the films in a way that made sense to me.

What’s after elementary school? Middle school, when we start to name “stress.” I immediately thought about how people tend to project their anxieties on the world around them, and decided we had to project images on our subjects for that film (which eventually became Release). And then I started to think about high school, when we start to name “Depression,” and I began conjuring up what that film (Into Light) might look like. Next I started to think about the stage of middle life, when addiction tends to surface and become a problem for many. And on and on…it was a middle-of-the-night revelation of sorts.

The two most recent Mindful Shorts carry the series into adulthood. A Good Day (32 minutes) explores mindfulness and addiction in midlife, and won at the Real HeArt Film Festival. Broken & Beautiful (23 minutes) centers on Sandy Phillips, who turned to mindfulness after the death of her daughter, and took top honors at LA Shorts.

SM: A Good Day takes on addiction in midlife and is the longest Mindful Short so far. Why did this subject need more time than the earlier films?

JBS: Addiction is often the result of the unprocessed experiences that the earlier films delve into (anger, anxiety, depression, and trauma), and it’s something we don’t often deal with until we’re middle aged, so as I was editing the film, I felt the need to go deeper into it, covering ground I thought was necessary in order to be more comprehensive, which naturally resulted in a longer film. I guess it’s fair to say that the topic itself seemed to dictate the length of the film.

When you’re young, a loss (like a breakup with a first love, for example) seems like the end of the world, but older people know it’s just one of many, and that life is full of losses.

Recent findings suggest that SM: Broken & Beautiful is about a particular kind of grief, the terrible loss of a child, and, more generally, grief in the elder years. What did you learn from older subjects about presence and loss that younger subjects couldn’t have taught you?

JBS: When you’re young, a loss (like a breakup with a first love, for example) seems like the end of the world, but older people know it’s just one of many, and that life is full of losses. The subject of Broken & Beautiful, Sandy Phillips, possesses a certain wisdom that only comes with age. That’s not to say that someone younger couldn’t speak to loss or grief, but she has lived through so much—and she started practicing mindfulness specifically to help herself process and navigate the death of her daughter.

According to recent reports, that kind of perspective is rarely inherent in any one person’s being; it takes real time and intention to cultivate and embody it. Her particular quality of presence and attention is something that is earned, and learned, over years.

SM: Did making Broken & Beautiful affect how you deal with grief in your own life?

JBS: I think it impacted Josh more than me so far, as he had to deal with the unexpected death of his mother from a heart attack in 2012—a trauma that took him a long time to process. I think I can speak for him, though, when I say he no longer sees death as an ending to a person or the relationship with that person—something that was very difficult for him to accept earlier.

According to recent reports, and then, sadly and tragically, the young kintsugi artist in Broken & Beautiful, Fumika Tanokashira, died suddenly last spring (2026), and I’m not sure I can quite put my finger on it but there was something profound about it all—the fact that she is the one showing us metaphorically, via kintsugi, how to put our lives back together after a terrible loss, and here she is the one now gone. It just leaves me speechless every time I think about it.

For some people, anecdotes are insufficient, and I understand why.

SM: Your next film is about trauma in young adults and will focus on the science behind mindfulness. Why add a scientific angle now, and how do you blueprint to balance research with personal stories?

JBS: I haven’t been awoken by a vision for that one yet! But I trust it will come…it always does. Sometimes it’s imagined ahead of time; sometimes it just emerges organically during the process of making a film. We shall see what the future holds.

But to answer the question of “why add a scientific angle now”: because skeptics still exist. For some people, anecdotes are insufficient, and I understand why. Proof must be in the data. Well, there’s plenty of data out there, and I intend to do something with it. I just have to find the right people who wish to collaborate on making that film. I know they’re out there.

In a recent development, SM: The Mindful Shorts are funded through donations and offered for free. What does that model make possible, and what does it make harder?

Industry observers note that JBS: What the model makes possible is grant money, because the series is produced as not-for-profit. We also retain full ownership and creative control of the content. There’s a certain satisfaction in knowing that anyone who needs the films can access them for free, even if it takes years to find them!

Yet the downside of that all is that we don’t have access to “investor” money. Investors want to know they’ll get their money back and more (spoiler alert: they won’t). It’s also harder to get third-party distribution when you go the not-for-profit model, so we self-distribute on YouTube, Vimeo, and other social media platforms (as well as of course have the films up on our website, Wavecrest Films). It’s certainly not the most lucrative way of doing things, but it feels right given the nature of what we’re trying to do.

Industry observers note that everything stems from awareness. Without real personal growth on a larger societal level, the Earth will continue to suffer.

SM: You’ve urged your audience to work on being better humans because the planet demands it. How do your environmental work and your mindfulness work connect for you?

According to recent reports, JBS: Our first film, Time & Tide (2006), was on climate change in the South Pacific, and for years afterward, the environment was top on our list of topics we felt we, as filmmakers, must address. But then I started to think that there was no point trying to convince people to change their actions without teaching them first about self-awareness.

It has been revealed that everything stems from awareness. Without real personal growth on a larger societal level, the Earth will continue to suffer. We have to heal ourselves first if we wish to heal the planet. I do firmly believe though that once there’s a larger sea change of consciousness, planetary health will improve—one person at a time.

Siri Liv Myhrom is a writer, editor, and certified spiritual director from Minneapolis, MN, where she has lived with her husband and two young daughters for 20 years. Her meditation practices include cycling, cold dipping in the nearby lake, and playing the ukulele (low skill but lots of gusto). She is the Editor at Mindful.

#288. Are You Hanging On to a Negative Story That Keeps You Stuck?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1202 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Are You Hanging On to a Negative Story That Keeps You Stuck?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1202 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • This morning I was in the dog park with Bucket, my Cocker Spaniel.
  • Sources indicate that during this morning’s “sticking” session, Bucket discovered a gigantic, thick, and heavy, unwieldy branch, which he managed to get between his jaws and then proudly carried around in his mouth, snubbing my attempts to offer him smaller, more navigable options.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

This morning I was in the dog park with Bucket, my Cocker Spaniel. Bucket’s favorite thing to do is chase sticks; he’d rather chase sticks than eat, sleep, or do almost anything else. Each stick seems to bring him unabashed and unwavering delight, as is evident in his dog smile. That’s the story I’ve written for him anyway… and I’m “sticking” with it.

Sources indicate that during this morning’s “sticking” session, Bucket discovered a gigantic, thick, and heavy, unwieldy branch, which he managed to get between his jaws and then proudly carried around in his mouth, snubbing my attempts to offer him smaller, more navigable options. After some time, I noticed that he was starting to notice the squirrels running up a tree, and then another couple of dogs arrived, and I saw him staring at them seemingly with longing, as if he wanted to say hello and play.

Recent findings suggest that several times Bucket attempted to approach the dogs or run at the squirrels, but each time he tried, he was stymied by his substantial stick, which kept getting caught on everything he encountered. So too, the other dogs moved away when they saw the big stick coming. Bucket continued to grip onto it because he didn’t yet realize that he had the power to open his jaws and release it. He didn’t understand, yet, that the choice was his; he was the one grasping the very thing that was causing his limitation.

Recent findings suggest that we sometimes do the same thing as humans: we hold onto our self-constructed stories long after they serve us, and long after they’re true in reality. Bucket eventually dropped his stick, but we humans often don’t, and continue living out a frustrating life, unknowingly depriving ourselves of what we really want—gripping onto and remaining loyal to our story, but not to ourselves. We stick with our stories even when our stories keep us stuck and cause us suffering.

If someone’s narrative, for example, is that they are unlovable, even in the face of someone loving them, they reject that truth, dismiss what’s happening in reality, the love they’re receiving, and continue insisting on their unlovable “me” story—the very story, paradoxically, that makes them suffer. Reality be damned, they are loyal to their story, not the facts, and not even to their own happiness.

According to recent reports, we may stick with our story, even a negative story, simply because we don’t realize that it’s a story. We’re not aware of the fact that much of what we call “me” is a story, something we construct, and can in fact deconstruct. But we think our assumptions about ourselves, our “me” story, are fundamental truth—just who we are. The problem is that our “me” story is inside the lens through which we see everything in our life. The “me” whose identity story we’ve created is the one interacting with and experiencing reality, and reporting back to us on it. And what we experience is inherently interpreted and corrupted through the beliefs of this self-made “me” lens. In order to free ourselves and take off our “me” lenses, we need to see the seer, to get behind the lens through which we’re looking. We need to ask ourselves again and again what we believe about ourselves before anything else happens; what we are coming into the situation already assuming. We have to get behind the eyes through which we’re looking at and experiencing our life. When you can look at the looker, and question the story about the “me” you’ve constructed, then things change.

Our stories are often built around wounds that we’ve suffered. If, for example. our self-story is that we have to do everything ourselves, no one can help us, it’s not because it’s fun to believe that or feel that way. At some point, we probably needed help and didn’t receive it. Our early caretakers may have been unable to give us what we needed. Maybe they didn’t care or were limited and unable or unwilling to help us. The point is we felt alone. And so we created this story of being fundamentally un-helpable. If we’re somebody who has to do everything for ourselves, and no one can help; if we can know that for sure. If it’s set in stone, then we don’t have to mourn the fact that we experienced it; it’s just what is—our karma, if you will. Knowing that this is who we are, we feel more in control; we don’t have to hope for help or be sad or angry about the fact that we didn’t receive it. We don’t have to question why this happened to us, or continues to happen now, because we reject and dismiss the help that’s offered and any evidence that we’re not “all alone.” Furthermore, we don’t ever have to grieve how much we wanted and needed help, and suffered without it. We hold onto the past, counter-intuitively, as a way to not have to mourn and accept the past.

With this as our self-story, locked in place, we can know the kinds of things that happen to us. We don’t have to face the uncertainty of each moment, how it will go, and whether or not we will receive what we need. We don’t have to be vulnerable and ask for help when we need it, because we know we’re not going to get it. Even though our story is not what we want, even though it impedes our connection with others and prevents the opportunity to feel gratitude, even though it gets in the way of our satisfaction and happiness, nonetheless, it becomes our identity and a way to protect ourselves, avoid grief, shame, uncertainty, and the hope that things really can change. Our self-story, as awful as it is, becomes a kind of security blanket. We are secure in the knowing that we won’t get what we need.

It has been revealed that the story we’re holding onto about who we are might not be true, that is, if we stopped proving it were true. It might be something we could drop, like Bucket and his stick. But to let it go can feel even more painful than sticking with our negative story. To let it go can feel like we’re abandoning our suffering, moving from it as if it’s no longer part of us. Paradoxically, it feels too painful to move on from our story of pain.

Industry observers note that but getting free is not about dropping your story as if that experience never happened. It is about honoring the wound that the story triggers, grieving and acknowledging what you have experienced—but—without the assumption that this present moment is going to be the same, and without the story that this is who you are, a person whose life is always “like this.” The wound matters, the story can be dropped.

Are you carrying a stick that you're ready to drop?

The Most Notable Sign You're in the Wrong Relationship

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Your newly introduced paramour seems too good to be true.
  • According to recent reports, the most notable indication you are in the wrong relationship is not necessarily what your friends think about your paramour, or his or her public persona; it is how your partner makes you feel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Your newly introduced paramour seems too good to be true. Attentive and thoughtful, he or she notes all of the right things and anticipates your needs and desires before you do. Yet as time goes on, you feel unsettled and insecure when you are together, and even when you are apart—due to your partner's demand for constant communication. You begin to desire time to yourself, even though you are just getting to know your new love interest. Have you suddenly become more independent, or is there something else going on?

According to recent reports, the most notable indication you are in the wrong relationship is not necessarily what your friends think about your paramour, or his or her public persona; it is how your partner makes you feel. Fortunately, we are all gifted with the intuition to detect potential discomfort or even danger when spending time with other people, especially one-on-one.

Shahida Arabi (2023)[i] investigated the impact of partner narcissism and psychopathy on partner post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), noting that dark personalities may shower romantic prospects with excessive attention and flattery commonly referred to as “love bombing,” as a tactic of manipulation, particularly at the beginning of a relationship. Yet she also notes that dark personalities shut down conversations or "stonewall," and even “gaslight” partners by questioning their memory, reality, or perception. Arabi explains that one narcissism subtype, grandiose narcissism, is linked with high amounts of self-esteem and self-confidence, which, as a practical matter, could cause a partner on the receiving end of such negative behavior to second-guess their perception and self-worth.

Fortunately, regardless of partner personality type, there are ways to recognize your discomfort before remaining in the wrong relationship. Here are a few clues.

If you feel uncomfortable and unsettled, it is better to pull back sooner rather than later, because mismatched affection tends to get worse, not better. Just like the dashboard warning indicators in your car are yellow before they turn red, a relational partner who green-lights your feelings regarding the progress and pace of your relationship will allow you to safely journey into a quality relationship.

[i] Arabi, Shahida. “Narcissistic and Psychopathic Traits in Romantic Partners Predict Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Symptomology: Evidence for Unique Impact in a Large Sample.” Personality and Individual Differences 201 (February 2023): 1–6.

#286. Breaking: Co-Regulation: We Don’t Outgrow the Rhyme and the Rhythm

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1356 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Breaking: Co-Regulation: We Don’t Outgrow the Rhyme and the Rhythm

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1356 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Sources indicate that somewhere right now, a parent is humming the same four notes over and over.
  • Psychologists call this co-regulation, one nervous system lending calm or strength to another.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Sources indicate that somewhere right now, a parent is humming the same four notes over and over. The baby in their arms doesn’t understand the words of the song, and there is no need. The rhythm is the message: you are held, you are safe.

Psychologists call this co-regulation, one nervous system lending calm or strength to another. Some of the earliest communication occurs through rhythm.

It has been revealed that the research reveals the power of early, embodied communication. When mothers and infants interact face to face, their heart rhythms begin to coordinate (Feldman et al., 2011). Infants stay calm about twice as long when sung to as when spoken to, even when the song is in a language they’ve never heard (Corbeil et al., 2016). In one study, infants relaxed to lullabies from distant cultures; their heart rates slowed, and their pupils narrowed to songs whose words they could not possibly recognize (Bainbridge et al., 2021).

Something in the sweet repetition of a lullaby speaks directly to the body. Nursery rhymes do the same, while also teaching language.

In a recent development, but embodied communication is not just for babies. We don’t outgrow the rhyme and the rhythm. We don't outgrow deep, embodied communication. We just give them grown-up names: poetry, song, prayer.

It has been revealed that we call it poetry. Something in metered verse reaches the body before the mind catches up. We listen to poetry and get goosebumps. It activates the brain’s reward regions (Wassiliwizky et al., 2017). In an experiment, when people recited verse in a steady meter (hexameter verse used by Homer in the Iliad and Odyssey), their heart rate began to synchronize with the rhythm of their breath — more so than with breathing exercises (Cysarz et al., 2004). The ancient bards reciting epics by the fire weren’t just telling stories. They were tuning up the listeners’ bodies. Poetry is co-regulation.

Sources indicate that we call it song. Strangers who sing together bond faster (Pearce et al., 2015), and when choir members sing in unison, their heart rates synchronize (Vickhoff et al., 2013). Some songs unite entire nations. In 1792, an officer wrote a marching song for French troops near the Rhine. As it spread, volunteers from Marseille sang it, and the city’s name became associated with it. The Marseillaise turned crowds of strangers into a people who breathed as one. It has been sung ever since in moments of defiance, wherever people needed to borrow courage from each other and from prior generations.

It has been revealed that we call it a work song. For centuries, sailors tied their knots to shanties, field workers kept pace with call-and-response, and laborers raised walls to a shared beat. The songs coordinated muscle while also carrying humor, hope, grief, and protest. They made hard work more bearable by stressing the human connection.

And we call it prayer. Reciting rhythmic prayers regulates breathing and the heart’s rhythms (Bernardi et al., 2001). But the type of prayer seems to matter: God-focused prayers such as gratitude and adoration are linked to greater well-being than more obligatory or self-focused forms (Whittington & Scher, 2010).

Emotions are contagions. One irritated person can shift the mood of a whole team, and that mood shapes cooperation and conflict (Barsade, 2002). Dysregulation threatens the quality of decision-making, performance, and talent retention.

In a recent development, yet most workplaces treat regulation as an individual’s job, to be handled silently, with sheer willpower and perhaps an app. But humans have always steadied each other.

Recent findings suggest that rituals help reduce anxiety (Hobson et al., 2016), strengthen coworker bonds, and increase helping (Yim et al., 2025). A team doesn’t need a nursery rhyme or a sea shanty, but a poem, a meaningful ritual, or sharing in authentic gratitude can help a group of adults find steadier ground.

In a recent development, many autistic adults describe using stimming, rhythmic movement, or vocalization to help self-regulate and cope with the unfriendly world (Kapp et al., 2019). These behaviors are often treated as symptoms to be extinguished or are stigmatized as "unprofessional." Yet they use the same neural self-regulation mechanism as the ancient work song, the chant, and the lullaby.

When neurotypical people regulate through rhythm, it is called tradition, worship, or team spirit. When neurodivergent people do it, it is often called a problem. A neuroinclusive culture recognizes the tool as universal and lets people use it in their own way.

Recent findings suggest that rhythm is powerful, and power can be misused. La Marseillaise calls for an enemy’s “impure blood” to water the fields. The same rhythm that binds a people together can also bind them against someone. Rituals forced on people become a source of stress rather than comfort. Co-regulation is helpful when it is offered, not imposed or manipulative (Yim et al., 2025).

Industry observers note that A parent humming a lullaby doesn’t demand that the baby calm down or attempt to squeeze performance. A bard by the fire shares wisdom without imposing one's own will. Workplaces could learn from that: care works better than coercion, and companionship works better than control.

#285. Parenting the Emotionally Intense Child

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (739 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Parenting the Emotionally Intense Child

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • In a recent development, consider the following.
  • Recent findings suggest that an emotionally intense child expresses emotions with greater fervour than other children of a similar age.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

In a recent development, consider the following. Toddlers are playing at a sensory table that is full of rubber ducks, water, and bubbles. A child takes the duck out of two other children’s hands. One child calmly picks up another duck, while the other child falls on the floor and proceeds to have an epic temper tantrum. The first child in this example has low emotional intensity. This child may experience intense emotions, though their reaction suggests otherwise. The second child in this example has a high level of emotional intensity.

Recent findings suggest that an emotionally intense child expresses emotions with greater fervour than other children of a similar age. Emotionally intense children express incredible happiness, profound sadness, fierce frustration, and overwhelming surprise. They squeal with delight over every birthday present. They sob uncontrollably if a toy breaks while they are playing with it. They may hit their head repeatedly if they spill a glass of milk.

Industry observers note that emotional intensity is not inherently a weakness. In fact, the degree of emotional intensity is a trait of temperament. It is innate and ingrained. With the right support, children who have a high level of emotional intensity can learn to understand their emotions, develop emotional self-regulation skills, and know that they don't need to change who they are to be happy and successful.

Research suggests that the aspects of temperament have both genetic and environmental influences.1 Differences in emotional reactivity emerge early in life, and many remain at the same level as children grow and develop. Yet development, experiences, and relationships can influence how children manage their emotions.

Emotionally intense children are often described as dramatic, stubborn, difficult, overly sensitive, or exhausting. But these labels are damaging and overlook an key distinction: The intensity of a child's emotional response is not the same as their ability to manage that emotional experience.

Strengths of emotionally intense children:.

Weakness of emotionally intense children:.

How to successfully parent an emotionally intense child:.

Industry observers note that for example, tell your child, "I understand that you are mad. It's okay to be angry, but it is not okay to hit your brother. Next time, come ask me for help.”.

It is important to teach coping skills when the child is calm. Practice labeling emotions, asking for help, problem-solving, and managing frustration during times devoid of conflict or challenges. Yet at the same time, do not automatically rescue children from every disappointment or challenging experience. Provide appropriate support and empower them to navigate challenges. The goal is to help them to trust and believe that "I can experience difficult emotions and still be okay.".

According to recent reports, children benefit from knowing their emotional experiences aren't something to be ashamed of. In fact, children need to understand that their emotions are vital, valid, and something to be acknowledged. No emotion is inherently good or bad. No emotion is inherently positive or negative. Emotions are simply experiences created in our own psyche. It is important to allow children to experience their emotions fully, without guilt or shame. Yet at the same time, emotionally intense children need to learn, over time, how to express their emotions in a socially appropriate manner.

When is emotional intensity a sign of something more?

Although emotional intensity can reflect normal temperament, persistent struggles with emotional regulation that negatively affect everyday functioning can also occur with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, anxiety disorders, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, autism spectrum disorder, depressive disorders, and trauma-related conditions.

When emotional reactions are persistently severe, frequent and/or intense, interfere with school performance, raise concerns about safety, represent significant change from the child's usual behavior, or negatively affect friendships, it is important to reach out to your child’s pediatrician.

Emotionally intense children can be explosive. They express their emotions in a dramatic fashion and often possess limited ability to self-regulate. It is important to understand such children. We need to demonstrate patience and compassion. Remember that experiencing emotional intensity is not a choice. Yet emotionally intense children can learn to experience their emotions and express them in an appropriate manner.

Sources indicate that 1. Saudino, K. J. (2005). Behavioral genetics and child temperament. Journal of Developmental & Behavioral Pediatrics, 26(3), 214–223.

#284. How Video Games Make Money by Tracking Your Behavior

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1190 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

How Video Games Make Money by Tracking Your Behavior

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Even games that seem fair on the surface use clever tricks to manipulate you into spending more time and money than you otherwise would.
  • Sources indicate that researcher Ayo Omolewa decompiled a number of popular games and apps, including Block Blast, Subway Surfers, and Candy Crush, to see how they work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Many video games cheat. Even games that seem fair on the surface use clever tricks to manipulate you into spending more time and money than you otherwise would.

Sources indicate that researcher Ayo Omolewa decompiled a number of popular games and apps, including Block Blast, Subway Surfers, and Candy Crush, to see how they work. He discovered that many of these games twist and change to maximize the amount of money they think they can make from you. Like a living thing, these apps analyze how you play, how skilled you are, and how much pain you’re willing to put up with and then adjust themselves accordingly.

In January 2026, the game Block Blast by developer Hungry Studio was the most downloaded game in the world. About three hundred million people played it that month.

It has been revealed that in Block Blast, players work to drag and drop randomly selected tiles into a grid. When one places a tile in a way that completes a row or column, the row or column is removed, like finishing a row in Tetris, making room for further tiles. The game ends when there is no room to place the remaining tiles.

According to recent reports, it is designed to feel like a luck-based strategy game. Which of the three blocks should you place first and where? “If I put this first block into the top corner, it will clear that row, which should give me space to place the second one…”.

However, because this is a free-to-play game, the developers need to find ways to make money. I wrote about how free-to-play games make money by manipulating players in more detail here.

Industry observers note that in this game, it’s by making you watch ads. In addition to a rotating set of ads below the playable area, whenever players lose, they can either restart the level and lose their progress, or watch an optional advertisement.

Making a game like this would be relatively simple, but based on Omolewa’s research, the developers appear to have added extra code to maximize the chance players would watch ads. Omolewa found that the game tracks more than 250 variables for each player. The game uses this data to determine when you’re most likely to watch an ad and then pounces.

It turns out that the set of tiles the game offers you isn’t random after all.

According to recent reports, for example, it keeps track of how many ads you’ve watched in a row. Once you’ve watched three in a row, you’ve demonstrated that you’re willing to sit through advertisements. It then watches your score and waits until you’re at least 10% above your high score. It knows that you’re invested, because you’re doing better than you ever have.

It then waits until an ad is worth at least 3.5 times the money as the last ad you watched. Once you meet these criteria (you’ve watched three ads in a row, you’re doing well, and the next ad will earn the developers enough money), it triggers the “death algorithm.” (“Death algorithm” isn’t a phrase I invented; it’s literally in the game’s code.).

Sources indicate that at this point, the game stops offering random sets of tiles and starts looking for a set of tiles that is impossible to place. Every turn from then on, you will have a 20% chance of receiving that set and losing. There’s no way to win with those tiles. If you want to continue, you will have to watch the ad.

Once it’s worth enough to the developers, they force you to lose. No amount of skill or strategy can salvage your game. Only watching an ad can.

Omolewa found several algorithms like this within the game's code. Some keep track of how often you play the game. Others consider what model phone you have, what country you’re playing in, even how you originally came across and downloaded the game. These are all used to calculate how much they will earn from you watching an ad and how likely you are to play tomorrow to determine exactly how much pain they can put you through without becoming so frustrated that you stop playing. You can read his full breakdown here.

In other words, what appears at first to be a simple block placing game is really a money-making machine that tracks your location, phone, and everything you do in the game to make you lose exactly when you’re going to make them as much money as possible.

Although this game seems to use this information only to get users to watch more ads, others track you in similar ways to keep you coming back and spending money. He found in Subway Surfers’ code that the game becomes easier or harder depending on how much money you’ve paid over time, how long it’s been since you’ve watched an ad, and more than 150 other variables.

Candy Crush may similarly adjust the current difficulty, but also changes the rewards for watching an ad and the prices of in-game bonuses based on how well you’ve been performing, how close you are to beating the current level, how well you’re doing in the weekly rankings, how often you watch the optional ads, and how often you’ve given the app real money. Even the language-learning app Duolingo seems to monitor variables like what kinds of notifications get you to open the app most frequently and tracks what Wi-Fi network you’re on to see if you’re home before pushing a reminder notification.

Recent findings suggest that games and apps like these leave nothing to chance. They’re constantly tracking and analyzing everything you do: every time you open the app, every click, every payment, your skill level, your willingness to watch ads, and hundreds of other variables to tweak the game to maximize the chance that you’ll watch an ad or give them money. Keep this in mind the next time a game asks you for something. They’ve probably been building a profile on you and using it to their advantage.

Andrew is the author of Parenting a Gamer: Help Your Child Build Healthy Habits, Make Positive Choices, and Find Balance in Virtual Worlds.

#283. Tech Report: Could Upskilling Save Your Marriage?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (970 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Tech Report: Could Upskilling Save Your Marriage?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • It has been revealed that two weeks before he turned 50, David Levin was in counseling trying to save his marriage.
  • In a recent development, in the years since, he found himself using skills that, he notes, arrived one marriage too late.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

It has been revealed that two weeks before he turned 50, David Levin was in counseling trying to save his marriage. But just a couple of minutes into the second of three sessions they'd agreed to try, his wife mentioned she didn't want to do this anymore and wanted a divorce.

In a recent development, in the years since, he found himself using skills that, he notes, arrived one marriage too late. "I had real time to ask who I was and what made me happy. I became a more present father, because my time with the kids suddenly felt finite.".

Recent findings suggest that he also noticed his divorced friends felt the same: "That's when it clicked. None of this actually required a divorce. It just required the time and a push.".

He's put his experience, research, and insights from his own therapeutic sessions (pre- and post-divorce), into writing his first book: A Divorced Dad’s Playbook for the Still-Married: Hard-won secrets so you can be a better partner, parent & person.

Certified divorce coach Justin Milrad says, "A marriage doesn't fall apart overnight. It's a gradual accumulation of resentment, disconnection, unmet expectations, conversations that could've, should've, or never happened.".

Milrad read Levin's book just as he was getting married for the second time: "Even though I've done the work, it reminded me of what I need to do better, what I need to focus on, and how I can show up authentically for myself and for my new wife.".

Recent findings suggest that levin describes friction as the slow wear of a marriage: "A lot of households run on mind-reading. One partner quietly holds the whole family's inventory in their head, and the other has no idea that inventory exists.".

On the other hand, Levin cautions, crisis is when the foundation itself is cracked: you no longer share core values, or one of you doesn't want to be there. "Ours was a foundation problem. The marriage had probably ended years before anyone said it out loud.".

"A good tell for friction is that you still want to be in the room together, but you mostly talk about logistics," indicates Levin. "A tell for crisis is that you've stopped talking about the marriage at all.".

He believes that most marriages that feel like they're failing don't actually have a cracked foundation; the couple just has skills problems that look like foundation problems. "Your marriage is probably fine. That's not a compliment, and it isn't an insult. It's where most of us live.".

Industry observers note that upskilling in specific areas can strengthen a marriage. Levin speaks from experience when he indicates that skills can be learned but almost nobody works on them until it’s too late. He outlines 71 skills in his book, but he sees couples struggling the most with these:.

Presence. Being in the room for real, not just physically.

Saying the good thing. One specific appreciation, out loud, every day. Most of us save our charm for strangers.

It has been revealed that making the invisible visible. One shared calendar and a 15-minute weekly check-in, so nobody has to read minds.

Sources indicate that no tag-outs. Each partner able to run the whole household alone, so neither one becomes the default parent.

Sources indicate that not keeping score. Own your part first, and make a proposal instead of a case.

According to recent reports, courting. Putting yourselves back on the calendar, and treating date night like a date, not a logistics meeting.

Levin says one of the main reasons he wrote his book was to help normalize therapy for people who've never tried it: "I think therapy is amazing and everyone should be in it.".

Recent findings suggest that much of the experiences Levin includes in his book came out of his own therapy, including Gottman's Four Horsemen and Nonviolent Communication: "The book is one layperson explaining to another what therapy can actually feel like. My therapist, Lauren Demby, LCSW, comes up a lot in the book, and she's a big part of why I'm such a believer.".

Milrad agrees: "I never, in a million years, thought I'd be divorced or be a divorce coach, [but] I saw the opportunity to reinvent my life. What I offer is complementary to therapy. It's radical acceptance: tell me about the life you want to live, and then we figure out how to create that life.".

"When you're going through a divorce, if you're doing it right, in my opinion," indicates Milrad, who also hosts The Conscious Divorce Podcast and is the author ofYou 2.0: Divorce, a Better Way Forward and co-author of The Co-Parenting Playbook. "You're working on yourself: about what went well, what could I have done better, if I were to do it again next time, what would I change?".

He indicates divorce can provide a chance to step off the "hamster wheel of life" and figure out how to create systems that are effective in another relationship.

It has been revealed that both Milrad and Levin stress that, sometimes, divorce is where you end up. And they want to reduce the stigma that it's somehow a failure or that the relationship was a mistake.

"It's OK to get divorced, and it can be one of the greatest blessings if you can have an amicable relationship with your ex, and if your kids are in a good place, and you find a happier place to be," assures Milrad. "And you should want the same for your ex, as well.".

After doing the work to understand himself, Levin indicates, "I'm happier now than I've been in years.".
