#282. What If Talking About Your Anxiety Isn't Helping?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (832 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

What If Talking About Your Anxiety Isn't Helping?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • “What’s on your mind today?” “What’s been going on lately?” “What is activated for you today?” “How have you been feeling?".
  • Over the years, I have cycled through various go-to opening questions in my anxiety therapy sessions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

“What’s on your mind today?” “What’s been going on lately?” “What is activated for you today?” “How have you been feeling?".

Over the years, I have cycled through various go-to opening questions in my anxiety therapy sessions. Sometimes I don’t have to say a word: A client pulls open their Notes app or a journal the moment they sit down on the couch.

Yet, even if I ask the perfect question, or my client has already prepared a list of subjects for the session, the truth is: talking about anxiety doesn’t always lead to healing.

Industry observers note that anxiety runs in a loop. By the time the anxious client has entered my office, they have probably gone over these worries many times. Anxiety likes to replay the same line of thinking until it blurs the border between truth and fiction.

Industry observers note that anxiety venting encourages speaking in extremes, which sometimes distorts our thinking. The other person in the conversation may feel the need to validate our emotions and be supportive, but our brains can interpret this social nicety as an agreement with the content of our worries.

When we engage in a monologue about our anxiety, we are effectively overthinking out loud.

Our brain is trying to self-soothe by overthinking. The hope is that thinking will lead to a solution, clarity, or insight, and then we will feel much better. But as we all know, overthinking our worries can be counterproductive at best and dysregulating at worst.

According to recent reports, thinking about and talking about worries can deepen anxiety. When we spiral down into our thoughts, we go deeper into our heads. We can get lost in the effort to figure out our thoughts.

As an anxiety therapist, my job is to break the cycle of overthinking and help my client spiral up into action. Sometimes, this means that we cannot spend our session talking about anxiety. We cannot analyze and replay the anxious line of thinking.

We have to disrupt the pattern.

According to recent reports, the remedy for overthinking is an action that takes you out of your head and back into your life. We change our behavior to change our mindset.

For certain people, such action takes the form of ERP (exposure response prevention). In this type of therapy, a person intentionally faces fears and resists compulsions (including overthinking).

Exposure therapy is quite different from traditional talk therapy. In this approach, a person creates and executes a brave to-do list (formally known as an exposure hierarchy). For example, a person worried about speaking up to their boss practices role-playing the conversation and then sends an email to get a meeting on the books. Someone anxious about driving at night practices driving two blocks in their neighborhood at dusk. The aim is to create a pathway toward facing fears rather than thinking and talking about them.

Exposure therapy means committing to action rather than staying stuck in the analysis of anxiety.

This is not to say that talking about one’s anxiety is never helpful. In some cases, the other person in an anxiety conversation is a valuable source of insight.

Recent findings suggest that when anxiety has caused someone to depart significantly from reality, sharing one’s worries can be grounding. The second person might be able to show where the worrier has created anxious distortions—self-blaming, catastrophizing, or personalizing.

Industry observers note that talking about one’s anxiety also helps when someone feels very alone in their worries. Having a person to share with can help the worrier feel supported, even if the other cannot change their mindset.

Conversations about anxiety will happen, inside and outside of the therapy room. Following these guidelines can help make sure the talk is productive.

Recent findings suggest that anxious looping is all about repeating the same well-worn thoughts without making progress. Notice and stop yourself if you are doing this out loud. You are perpetuating a cycle.

Too often, we seek insight from another person, but then ignore their view. If you are deep in your anxious worry, someone else’s thoughts are likely a helpful anchor to reality. Do not immediately dismiss what you are hearing from your trusted confidante.

Discussing your anxiety can be productive to a point, but notice if it is interfering with taking real action. Anxiety can be paralyzing. Remember that spiraling up often involves taking one brave step toward a fear.

Be aware of how discussing your anxiety is taking you out of your present moment. Are you less connected to today because you are talking about fears for the future or worries about the past? Conversations can help people cope, but sometimes they pull people deeper into thought.

It has been revealed that if you are stuck, take a break from talking about worries. Instead, today, do one small thing for yourself that brings joy.

#281. Why a Short Week Can Feel So Long

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1051 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Why a Short Week Can Feel So Long

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • Recent findings suggest that in interviews for my research on leaders, I asked executives to describe a difficult week.
  • Sources indicate that she could handle the questions, meetings, and requests.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

Recent findings suggest that in interviews for my research on leaders, I asked executives to describe a difficult week. One leader talked me through an annual report, tax paperwork, fundraising, board work, and decisions about products and events. When I asked what was hard, she didn't single out any one task, but said, “It's not that those things are too much; it's just the changing of direction every day.”.

Sources indicate that she could handle the questions, meetings, and requests. What wore her down was having to stop all the normal stuff to deal with the annual report or tax filing, then switch to something else, and then figure out where she'd left off.

According to recent reports, I drive my ninth-grade son to school, and yesterday he said it “felt like a long school week.” Interestingly, he had Tuesday off, an early dismissal Wednesday, and a late start Thursday… he actually spent less time at school. So, how could it feel longer!?

It has been revealed that it reminded me of the leader story. He and I talked about routines and how little attention we pay to things when we know what comes next. Bottom line… it felt exhausting to have his normal schedule interrupted.

Let's go take a look at what research says about having to change directions so often.

Recent findings suggest that what did our interrupted leader do? She tried to put some order around the week, setting aside one morning for product development and another stretch of time for board work. Then an event would need attention, or another responsibility would intrude. One day, a staff member left with little notice, and the website, online store, and event preparation were back on her desk. She could proposal the week, but keeping it that way was basically impossible.

According to recent reports, in 2001, researchers Joshua Rubinstein and his colleagues asked people to switch back and forth between simple tasks, like sorting shapes or doing math. Even small changes took extra time. Harder tasks made it worse, while a clue about what was coming next helped. This wasn't the same as someone interrupting you at work, but it highlights that changing gears isn't free. My son knew that his strange school schedule would be back to normal the following week, but the executive had no idea what would interrupt her next.

Recent findings suggest that but the lost time isn't the only problem. I get to interview spouses in my work. The leader mentioned above? Her husband saw what those days did to her. He told me she came home worn out with a long to-do list still on her mind. When she couldn't finish it, he stated it “really puts a burden... a strain, on her.” Researcher Sophie Leroy studied something similar in 2009. In two experiments, she found that people had trouble letting go of a task they hadn't finished. Even after moving on to something else, part of their attention was still on the earlier job. She called that “attention residue.”.

Think about sitting down to talk with an employee while you're still worrying about the budget you left unfinished.

Here's the most surprising finding to me around this subject: in 2008, Gloria Mark and her colleagues had people do typical office email tasks. Some were interrupted by calls or instant messages. The interrupted people actually finished their work FASTER… and their work wasn't noticeably worse (although their email replies were shorter). So why not be interrupted all day if you’re more productive? Those interrupted workers felt more stressed, frustrated, and rushed, and noted the work took more effort.

Sources indicate that the executive's week wasn't hard because of any one task. It was having to stop, switch, and figure out where she'd left off, over and over again. My son's week wasn't harder because of the assignments. It was having to think about what comes next and what comes after and hold that in the front of his mind.

Remember Sophie Leroy's finding about “attention residue”? In 2018, she and Theresa Glomb tested a way to reduce it. In their studies, people took a moment before switching tasks to think about where they'd stopped and how they'd pick up again. They called it a “ready-to-resume” strategy. It helped people focus on the new task instead of worrying so much about the unfinished one.

Sources indicate that so, here's how to fix a heavy, mixed-up week. You're halfway through a report when the phone rings. Before taking the call, jot down where you stopped and what you'll do next when you return. That's it. Now you can give the caller your attention without trying to remember every detail of the unfinished report.

It has been revealed that my son's schedule will be back to normal next week. The executive can't count on that. But when she has to change direction, she can take a moment to write down where she left off. That won't stop the interruptions, but it will keep her from spending so much time trying to get back to work.

To lead sustainably, when you have to stop what you're doing, take a moment to blueprint how you'll start again.

Recent findings suggest that leroy, S. (2009). Why is it so hard to do my work? The challenge of attention residue when switching between work tasks. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 109(2), 168–181. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2009.04.002.

It has been revealed that leroy, S., & Glomb, T. M. (2018). #280. Love Beyond Words

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (828 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Love Beyond Words

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • It has been revealed that many popular magazines and websites offer advice on how to improve "communication,” which they claim will improve marriages.
  • When couples describe the early part of their relationships, they report that they communicated very well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

It has been revealed that many popular magazines and websites offer advice on how to improve "communication,” which they claim will improve marriages. Some of those same venues regularly publish diets and weight-loss tips. You probably know the research findings about the latter—they range from unhelpful to harmful. The better weight-loss tips are as informative as the better communication recommendations. Eat less, move more; speak respectfully, listen attentively.

When couples describe the early part of their relationships, they report that they communicated very well. (Not many newlyweds mouth the great marriage lament: "We just can't communicate!") The prevalence of communication tips in the media implies that for many people, something about marriage degrades the neurons responsible for communication skills.

Industry observers note that of course, problems in love relationships do not occur because people are too stupid to figure out common-sense methods of communication or too dispirited by relationship experience to remember how they used to communicate. It’s misleading to say that people in distressed relationships have communication problems at all, though it can feel that way in their frustration and sadness. It’s more helpful to recognize that they have connection problems.

Recent findings suggest that communication in love relationships is a function of emotional connection. When people feel connected, they communicate fine, and when they feel disconnected, they communicate poorly, regardless of their choice of words and communication techniques.

When people are emotionally disconnected, the use of communication techniques makes them feel manipulated, and not just because the most popular ones are unnatural, more suited for a therapist's office than a living room. There is usually a hidden agenda in the use of communication techniques—to manipulate partners into giving the response we think is right.

Almost all my newly referred couples feature one partner accusing the other of misusing the communication techniques they learned from previous therapists.

"You're purposely not doing it right.”.

"Anyone with common sense could get this.”.

"I'm validating you more than you're validating me!".

According to recent reports, I've often heard people who've been through communication therapy take great care to use "I-statements" when addressing a partner: "I feel blamed right now," which is, of course, blaming the partner for blaming. These are not communication problems. The partners communicate in subtext exactly what they mean: "You’re failing me.”.

People do not fight and stonewall for lack of communication techniques. They fight and shut down because they feel like their partners don't care or aren't interested in how they feel. They fight and shut down to numb the pain of disconnection.

Feelings of connection are rooted in attunement of emotional states. Though it doesn't have to be positive (you can be attuned to your spouse at the funeral of a loved one), attunement cannot exist in a state of emotional reactivity, when a negative feeling in one causes chaos or shutdown in the other. It is extremely difficult to regulate emotional reactivity with words, even when there is no hidden motivation to convey that the other is failing or defective.

Negative reactivity can be regulated into positive attunement only through interest and caring; they have to be interested in and show sympathy for each other. Interest and caring, like all emotional states, are conveyed primarily by facial expressions, body language, and tone of voice, not by words or communication techniques.

Sources indicate that don't think of how to get your partner to do what you want—or, if you prefer the euphemism, how to communicate. Rather, ask yourself these questions:.

Do you want to feel emotionally connected with your partner?How curious are you to learn your partner’s perspective?Do you care how your partner feels right now?What do you love and value about your partner?

Recent findings suggest that having answered those questions, decide whether your connection is more important than the topic of your communication. You must convey that you will love and value your partner despite disagreement. Anything short of this devalues the connection—it's less important than what you want to talk about—thereby guaranteeing negative reactivity.

Recent findings suggest that think of times when you felt emotionally connected to your partner. Communication was not a chore that required techniques, strategies, precise timing, or careful choice of words. You were interested. You put things awkwardly sometimes, but it didn't matter, because you cared.

Emotional connection is a mental state and a choice. Early in your relationship, you chose to feel connected—just as, if you're thinking about communication techniques now, you may be choosing to feel disconnected.

Industry observers note that forget about communication techniques and choose to feel connected right now. If you do, you'll have a reasonable chance of your partner reciprocating. You can then communicate better. More importantly, you will move closer to re-creating a love beyond words.

#279. 10 Subconscious Reasons You Buy Things You Don't Need

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (773 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

10 Subconscious Reasons You Buy Things You Don't Need

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • Justin Owens offers a brilliant sociological diagnosis that categorizes the propensities of people from different social classes: “Rich people buy time, poor people buy things, and middle class people buy the appearance of being rich, which is why they stay middle class… Performing wealth costs you the real thing while producing only the appearance of it.”.
  • Would you ever admit to performing being wealthier than your bank account affords?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

Justin Owens offers a brilliant sociological diagnosis that categorizes the propensities of people from different social classes: “Rich people buy time, poor people buy things, and middle class people buy the appearance of being rich, which is why they stay middle class… Performing wealth costs you the real thing while producing only the appearance of it.”.

Would you ever admit to performing being wealthier than your bank account affords?

It has been revealed that for those of us without infinite income, every purchase costs hours of our precious finite lives. When we shop for something other than essential items, often we’re actually also shopping for belonging, escapism, repairing the past, justifying the present, trying to control the future, rebelling, and for many other reasons not listed on the packaging. The dopamine spike of each purchase is real enough; however, it simply doesn’t address the root causes of our consumption or recognize that each shopping victory has an expiration date that’s probably much sooner than we imagine.

Here are 10 reasons we may buy things we don’t need.

Status coding is the everyday practice of sending signals to our fellow tribe members; its anxious version is status climbing, which is when we project a class above the one we were born into in the hope that the higher-status tribe we admire will recognize us as one of their own.

We reward ourselves for a long and arduous workweek with something that temporarily promises to make the time-sacrifice worthwhile. Then on Monday morning, we’re back on the same hamster-wheel adding value to billionaires’ stock portfolios when Friday night’s Dubai chocolate is long gone.

We want others to think we’re virtuous sustainability warriors and not just self-indulgent hedonists, so we buy the “right” brand or the carbon offset or donate to charity to signal to our friends that we are really decent humans.

Babies are easily distracted by shiny objects, and adults can be just like babies with larger wallets.

We grew up “limited” and couldn’t have everything we wanted when we wanted it, so now we feel it symbolizes success to not have to ration and budget like we did when the only money we had was what we earned from our newspaper routes.

We see a upcoming object and believe it has the magical ability to make us look or feel younger. My body doesn’t naturally produce enough quercetin, NAD, NAC, curcumin, fish oils, or any of the other 10 million supplements that promise to make me look and feel like a teenager again. But do they really work and how much is the placebo effect?

We were thrown into an economic system that we didn’t choose, yet we can’t imagine any other, which is why Burning Man or “all-inclusive” holidays where you don’t need or can’t use money are so psychologically interesting. Go seven days without buying anything if you want some insights into who you really are when you’re not a wallet with legs.

In a recent development, purchasing things we don’t need provides the illusion of autonomy and control. We want to feel like the masters of our destinies and clicking on Amazon buttons makes us feel like Captain Kirk commanding the Starship Enterprise.

In the 1980s, there was a bumper sticker that read, “Whoever dies with the most toys wins.” Some people are playing capitalism as if it were a me-against-them game.

Every day, we grow closer to dying, and yet we don’t want to believe it. Filling our lives up with possessions that require our attention lessens the dreadful time we can spend pondering the nature of our brief existences, how we are interacting with others, and how we are impacting the earth.

According to recent reports, owens’ piercing insights about consumers should help raise consciousness around what we’re really trying to accomplish when we shop and especially when we impulse-buy. Have we been duped into believing magical characteristics of consuming that don’t really exist? Do we believe that each next purchase represents opening a new and potentially happier chapter of our lives?

Keeping up with the Joneses is both futile and exhausting.

A deep breath while watching a magnificent sunset doesn’t require a financial transaction.

We might want to spend less time trying to fill our lacks with consumption and more time filling them with what our souls really crave: loving relationships.

Fussell, P. (1983). Class: A painfully accurate guide through the American status system. Summit Books.

#278. When the Bully Is an Adult

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (613 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

When the Bully Is an Adult

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • Teachers are often underappreciated and underpaid.
  • Industry observers note that teachers, and other adults in the lives of children, can treat children in ways that are hurtful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

Teachers are often underappreciated and underpaid. In high school, I (EB) had the celebrated teacher and author of Angela’s Ashes (1996), Frank McCourt. And he was as good as they say, if not better. He was inspirational, built my confidence, and taught me to read and write in ways I am forever grateful for. I had less famous, but also fantastic, teachers, who inspired me to learn and grow. At the same time, I have had teachers who filled me with dread. I still remember my kindergarten teacher who, among other things, made me stand, as a 4-year-old, so that the other kids could see the “baby” because I briefly put my thumb in my mouth. Many of us harbor fondness for some of our teachers and anger towards the ones who lacked empathy, even if their behavior did not rise to the level of “abuse,” but rather was adult-sized bullying.

Industry observers note that teachers, and other adults in the lives of children, can treat children in ways that are hurtful. Adult observers are often reluctant to see and act on the warning signs, despite the direct and indirect impact on kids. Some of the warning signs include: insulting comments, even when couched in humor, humiliating remarks or directives, making children cry, publicly calling attention to children’s foibles, and being physically aggressive and controlling, even if it isn’t assaultive. If a behavior would be inappropriate when directed to another adult, it is probably inappropriate when directed toward a child, unless specifically related to normative school-oriented activities. In other words, if an interaction would feel upsetting or humiliating to an adult, it likely would to a child as well. Children may also indicate a problem with a particular adult by telling concerning stories, changing their behavior around the adult, or avoidance of the adult or the activity the adult is involved in.

Industry observers note that adults have more power than children, through their size, their role in the community, and almost every other relevant metric. Because of this power differential, some adults can behave in hurtful ways without realizing the potential impact on children with whom they interact. Why is it that we fail to identify these behaviors as bullying? Some of the reasons include: the privacy inherent in some of these interactions, the wish to avoid confrontation, desire to think the best in other adults, discomfort with the whistleblower role, and self-protection.

Sources indicate that witnesses have to assess whether it is serious enough to have a conversation. When I was a young psychologist, I made extra income by doing psychological testing in a public school. There was a very inappropriate teacher, who anyone, even visiting the school only briefly, could hear yelling and making derogatory comments toward her students. The principal approached me and asked whether I thought there were problems with this teacher. I responded, “Don’t you know?” He nodded. It is hard to take action in such situations, even when it is obvious.

Sources indicate that as a psychologist, I continue to hear stories about adult bullying that trouble me. Teachers and other adults in children’s lives are special as they play such a significant role in the lives of the children with whom they interact, most often creating positive experiences. They are afforded status with children which makes the few who are bullies, or otherwise inappropriate, have ample opportunity to use their power to do harm.

According to recent reports, mcCourt, F. (1996). Angela’s Ashes. Flamingo.

#277. Is Water Better Than Diet Soft Drinks For Weight Loss? A Two-Year Trial Put Them To The Test

Is Water Better Than Diet Soft Drinks For Weight Loss? A Two-Year Trial Put Them To The Test

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (453 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
  • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
  • People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.

Among those who completed the trial, average weight loss was 4.8 kg in the diet drink group and 3.7 kg in the water group (which was not a statistically significant difference).

Both groups took part in a weight management programme and remained lighter a year after regular support ended.

They also reported similar changes in hunger, despite the difference in how sweet their drinks tasted.

Almost 500 adults with overweight or obesity began the trial after being randomly assigned to drink water or commercially available diet drinks each day.

The study included regular diet drink consumers alongside those who rarely or never chose them.

Everyone began with 12 weeks of active weight loss, followed by 40 weeks of support to help them maintain their progress.

Sugar intake fell by similar amounts in both groups.

One theory is that people learn to expect energy when they taste something sweet.

If the expected calories fail to arrive, the theory goes, that mismatch might affect hunger and lead people to make up the difference by eating more later.

Comparing water with a diet soft drink allows researchers to ask whether sweet taste matters during weight management, since both drinks provide little or no energy.

By the end of the trial, hunger ratings had risen slightly in both groups, and the change was similar whether participants drank water or diet drinks.

Professor Joanne Harrold, the study’s first author, stated:.

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial.”.

When water or a diet drink replaces a sugary soft drink, the swap also cuts the calories in that serving.

A review of 17 randomised trials found small reductions in body weight when people replaced sugary drinks with low- or no-calorie sweetened alternatives, with results broadly similar to those for water (McGlynn et al., 2022).

The two-year trial adds a longer view of what happens when people keep the sweet taste in their drinks while working to maintain weight loss.

The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition (Harrold et al., 2026).

#276. Are Psychological Evaluations Needed for AI Developers?

Are Psychological Evaluations Needed for AI Developers?

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • On March 24, 2015, a Germanwings pilot with severe mental issues purposefully crashed a passenger plane with 150 people on board in the French Alps, resulting in the tragic deaths of all passengers.
  • To ensure this, psychological evaluations are occupationally mandated in some jobs (American Psychological Association, 2017).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

On March 24, 2015, a Germanwings pilot with severe mental issues purposefully crashed a passenger plane with 150 people on board in the French Alps, resulting in the tragic deaths of all passengers. This horrible incident highlighted how crucial it is that people who work in high-risk fields and have a responsibility for the survival of others are mentally stable.

To ensure this, psychological evaluations are occupationally mandated in some jobs (American Psychological Association, 2017). Jobs in which psychological evaluations are common before starting a job in many states of the U.S. include:.

According to recent reports, moreover, in some jobs, psychological evaluations may be conducted with people who are already employed if they show signs of impaired mental health or thinking abilities. This includes, for example, physicians and other healthcare workers.

Should people in certain high-risk AI development roles undergo psychological evaluations?

Industry observers note that one group of people that does not routinely undergo mental health screenings is programmers involved in the creation of AI. Over the course of the last few weeks, there has been a lot of discussion in the media about the extent to which rogue AI agents may potentially cause harm to humans in the future or even kill all of humanity. While experts debate about whether AI agents turning on humanity is a real risk or not, one potentially more likely risk of AI often gets ignored.

Recent findings suggest that just like a pilot could cause a plane to crash on purpose, an AI developer could purposefully build AI models that lack the necessary checks and balances to prevent them from hurting humans, or even an AI that exists with the purpose to harm humans, e.g., by performing hacking attacks on critical infrastructure. Thus, AI does not need to turn rogue by itself to harm humans; one developer doing so on purpose could lead to massive economic and personal harm. Since a scenario like this seems more likely to occur in the near future than AI turning rogue by itself, measures to prevent such an incident are needed. Because there are mental health conditions like antisocial personality disorder, which has been linked to violating the rights of other people without feelings of guilt, or dark personality traits such as psychopathy, such a scenario is not entirely unlikely.

I believe occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers should be considered.

In a recent development, given that the massive AI companies themselves warn about the potential risks of AI, more psychological research is needed into whether severe, untreated mental health conditions in AI developers could lead to the risk of real harm for other human beings. While no one knows how likely catastrophic events akin to the Germanwings airplane catastrophe would be in the field of AI development and what impact they would have, occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers could help ensure that only mentally stable people are involved in the development of frontier models with the potential to cause real harm to humans. Thus, professional organizations for psychologists, companies that make hiring and employment decisions in relation to the development of AI tools, and government agencies involved in the regulation of tech companies should consider occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers.

#275. Empowering a Competitive Advantage to Optimize Team Play

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1112 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Empowering a Competitive Advantage to Optimize Team Play

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Industry observers note that this post is part two of a series.
  • Welcome back for a dive into the Miami Mindset, a methodology for shaping a mental approach to competition trained by Travis Steele, the head basketball coach of the Miami RedHawks, a basketball team that has compiled a 36-0 regular-season record, extending back to the 2024-25 season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Industry observers note that this post is part two of a series. Read part one here.

Welcome back for a dive into the Miami Mindset, a methodology for shaping a mental approach to competition trained by Travis Steele, the head basketball coach of the Miami RedHawks, a basketball team that has compiled a 36-0 regular-season record, extending back to the 2024-25 season.

These are the four core values of the Miami Mindset:.

An explanation of each value follows, shared by Coach Steele in an interview for these two posts.

Industry observers note that “I need guys that live for competition,” explained Steele. “Competition brings out the best in each other. It’s how we practice. It’s how we lift. It’s how we do academics. Every day’s an audition.”.

It has been revealed that “We always talk about being the hunter, and not the hunted in everything we do, and it starts with having that competitive mindset,” Steele continued. “We recruit guys that have that gene, but we make sure that comes to life with how we do practice. We create a very, very competitive practice structure that makes that come to life.”.

“I use those words because I want it to be a family environment and I want these guys to be great teammates both on and off the court,” detailed Steele. “Elite teammates have a common characteristic, amongst them, that they can make (optimize) others around them. ‘One plus one equals three.’ I can make you better than you are by yourself.".

Recent findings suggest that “We get to three if we’re truly invested in each other,” Steele shared. “Pushing each other, holding each other accountable. Accountability is a really notable piece, being very direct with teammates.”.

In a recent development, “We want guys that are giving energy to others,” Steele noted. “How do we make this come to life? If a teammate falls down on the floor, everybody on the floor sprints over and picks him up. We acknowledge the passer. The guy that scores the basket is the one that gets all the credit, so we point to the passer, which I think is important to show connectivity. Another way (for brotherhood) is tight huddles during timeouts and stoppage of play.”.

“You’ve got to embrace the process,” Steele explained. “Everybody’s going to go through tough times. Even if you’re a great shooter, you’re going to miss three or four in a row, and the next time you’re open, you’ve got to be able to shoot.”.

According to recent reports, “We talk a lot about mental toughness,” he mentioned. “We train our guys about how to respond (to adversity) in different ways. ‘What is your response to adversity?’ because we’re all going to face it. It’s a lot easier to talk about it, but you have to apply it. So, we do a lot of adversity training.”.

“We coach the response piece to adversity harder than we do our schematic stuff because, ultimately, our team is going to go through tough times in the middle of the game,” shared Steele. “How can we reset our minds back to neutral and be able to continue to do our jobs at a very high level?”.

“I put them in adverse situations every day,” he explained. “I want practice to be harder than the game. You have to work on your response to adversity every single day, and that’s been critically notable to our success.”.

“Embodying undeniable confidence is done by embracing the process and being mentally tough and understand that your response (to adversity) has to be bigger than the event that just happened,” Steele summarized.

It has been revealed that “We talked about adversity,” said Steele as he introduced this final core value. “Handling prosperity is just as crucial. Sometimes guys take their foot off the gas pedal when they’ve won 10 games in a row, or maybe the guy’s playing really well for three or four games in a row, and he takes his foot off the pedal. That’s a pattern for a lot of people, and we have to fight that urge.”.

He fights that urge with a picture of a guy driving a car from an inside-the-car view. "Fellas," he explains, "the rearview mirror, there’s a reason why they’re so small. All the games that have happened are in the past ... There’s a reason why the front windshield’s so gosh darned big, because we’ve got to keep our eyes forward. We got to learn from the past, but we’ve got to keep our eyes ahead to see what’s in front of us.".

One of the players added, “If we’re listening to everybody telling us how good we are, it distracts us from keeping in front of us.”.

“That’s what happens if everybody starts listening to all the people around,” Steele elaborated. “They’re telling them how good they are and then you take the foot off the pedal. You gotta keep your eyes forward. Keep your eye on the ball, or you’re going to strike out. Our guys really understood that.".

“My job as one of the leaders of the team, along with our captains, is to make sure that if we sense just an ounce of complacency," Steel explained. "We have different things we can do within practice to ratchet it up quick.".

“I try to always gauge the temperature of the room,” he continued. “Where’s their mindset at? Before practice I go up to the players, talk to them, look them in the eyes. I may have to make adjustments. I’ve got a few drills that will raise the competitive spirit in the practice.".

“I think the 'Strive for Magis' got really tested last year, more than any year,” Steele reflected, "just because of the run we were on, and I give our guys a lot of credit. We had great player leadership, and we did a great job staying focused on the task at hand and through the whole run that we had.”.

As NBA legend Michael Jordan shared with golfer Tiger Woods: “No matter how good they say you are, always keep working on your game.”.

Those four core values closely parallel an Acceptance and Commitment Training (ACT) concept called psychological flexibility, defined as:.

The ability to stay present with difficult circumstances, thoughts, and feelings, without letting them dictate your behavior, so you can respond effectively.

Coach Steele and his Miami RedHawks basketball team have embraced and empowered all that!

#274. Modernizing Nursery Rhymes for the 21st Century

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1050 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Modernizing Nursery Rhymes for the 21st Century

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • Recent findings suggest that back in the 1960s when I was growing up, nursery rhymes were an initial gateway to music for children.
  • Sources indicate that revitalizing these classic verses—by preserving their developmental benefits while modernizing their themes—has become the life's passion of early childhood music educator Pam Gittleman.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

Recent findings suggest that back in the 1960s when I was growing up, nursery rhymes were an initial gateway to music for children. Their simple melodies, repeated lyrics, and predictable rhyming schemes gently introduced infants and toddlers to the fundamentals of music. What the words actually meant was of little, if any, concern to us young listeners. But times change and these traditional rhymes fell out of favor.

Sources indicate that revitalizing these classic verses—by preserving their developmental benefits while modernizing their themes—has become the life's passion of early childhood music educator Pam Gittleman. Raised in a musical family, Gittleman was a talented flutist through her college years. However, she did not plan on a career in music. After earning an MBA in marketing, she spent a decade in the corporate sector at a prominent advertising agency before leaving to raise her family.

Industry observers note that drawing on a desire to work with children, she leveraged her musical background to reinvent herself as a preschool music teacher. Over seven years at a summer day camp, she experimented with various teaching methods for children aged three to five, ultimately designing a curriculum centered on singing, movement, and call-and-response activities. As her own children grew up, she pivoted to teaching at nursery schools during the academic year.

According to recent reports, over the years, Gittleman noticed a striking trend: the young children in her classrooms were unfamiliar with the traditional nursery rhymes that prior generations knew by heart. Curious, she questioned parents and fellow educators and discovered that the internet had changed how families vetted content. Today’s parents were consulting childhood development experts and sharing their findings online. Many of them found traditional nursery rhymes to be outdated, dark, and inappropriate for young minds, so they avoided the genre entirely.

It has been revealed that while recognizing the validity of these concerns, Gittleman’s professional training and instincts told her that the time-honored nursery rhymes still held value for teaching language skills as well as social and emotional intelligence. To bridge this gap, she began rewriting the lyrics.

According to recent reports, her venture received a major boost in 2020 when she enrolled in the year-long Advanced Leadership Initiative (ALI) at Harvard University. Despite pandemic-related disruptions, she had access to advanced graduate courses in education, thus establishing a firm theoretical foundation for how music and storytelling contribute to social and emotional learning (SEL) in early childhood.

In a recent development, gittleman emphasizes that the linguistic structure of nursery rhymes is vital for early language acquisition. For instance, in the verses of “This old man, he played one, he played knick-knack on my thumb," children begin to learn the concept of rhyming. Educators can then challenge them to find other words that rhyme with "one," effectively expanding their vocabulary. Furthermore, because "one" and "thumb" don’t rhyme strictly speaking, children also learn that the concept of rhyming has flexibility.

Industry observers note that since many nursery rhymes are songs—set in a rhythmic structure and vocalized to musical notes—they stimulate notable neurological pathways. Rhythm, for example, is processed simultaneously in the auditory and motor regions of the brain. Nursery rhymes capitalize on this connection, helping children regulate their motor functions through alternating periods of movement and rest. Gittleman notes that mastering this physical self-regulation translates to better behavioral and social functioning with others.1.

Nursery rhymes can introduce basic math skills, too. Returning to the example of “This Old Man,” the song helps children learn to count, reaching ever higher numbers as they grow older. The rhymes are also repetitive—as children catch on to patterns, they learn to predict and reproduce them on their own. The excitement and anticipation of what comes next feeds the motivation and reward centers of the brain, allowing young children to experience joy while making music and learning language.

Yet another contribution of nursery rhymes is found in call-and-response verses. The call-and-response structure mirrors conversational patterns, teaching young children the social importance of taking turns.2.

Equipped with decades of classroom experience along with academic knowledge obtained through her program at Harvard, Gittleman has systematically updated classic lyrics to be of service to social and emotional learning.3 Prioritizing kindness, empathy, and gratitude, she transformed "Three Blind Mice" to "Three Kind Mice" and, under her pen, the story of “Humpty Dumpty” has been reimagined so that when he falls off the wall his friends come to his aid, rather than leaving him in pieces on the ground.

Gittleman has since published several volumes of her work under the title Nursery Rhymes for Kinder Times®.4,5 These books feature engaging illustrations for young children and structured text to help growing children develop literacy skills. Pairing each rhyme with emojis and guiding questions, she provides adults with tools to enhance their children’s engagement with the stories while nurturing rich conversations that support emotional intelligence. When she introduced the curriculum to a local preschool, an informal survey of parents and teachers confirmed a positive impact on the children's social and emotional learning.6.

According to recent reports, seeking to expand her reach, Gittleman utilized her advertising background to pitch her updated rhymes to the music industry. Her efforts won major support in 2022 when legendary children's performer Raffi—along with his protege, Lindsay Munroe—recorded 15 of her modernized rhymes. Since then, prominent children's recording artist Laurie Berkner has also recorded some of her material.

#272. Tech Report: The Four Buddhist Mantras for Turning Fear into Love

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1538 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Themarginalian

Tech Report: The Four Buddhist Mantras for Turning Fear into Love

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, “Fearlessness is what love seeks,” Hannah Arendt wrote in her magnificent early work on love and how to live with fear.
  • Sources indicate that this notion of presence as the antidote to fear and the crucible of love is as old as the human heart, as old as the consciousness that first felt the blade of anticipatory loss pressed against the exposed underbelly of the longing for connection.
  • In the general Buddhist style of befriending complexity through simplicity and with his particular gift for simple words strung into a rosary of immense wisdom radiating immense kindness, Thich Nhat Hanh writes:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “Fearlessness is what love seeks,” Hannah Arendt wrote in her magnificent early work on love and how to live with fear. “Such fearlessness exists only in the complete calm that can no longer be shaken by events expected of the future… Hence the only valid tense is the present, the Now.”.

Sources indicate that this notion of presence as the antidote to fear and the crucible of love is as old as the human heart, as old as the consciousness that first felt the blade of anticipatory loss pressed against the exposed underbelly of the longing for connection. It is at the center of millennia-old Buddhist philosophy and comes alive afresh, in a splendidly practical way, in Fear: Essential Wisdom for Getting Through the Storm (public library) by the great Vietnamese Buddhist teacher and peace activist Thich Nhat Hanh, who continued to enrich, ennoble, and empower with his teachings well into his nineties.

In the general Buddhist style of befriending complexity through simplicity and with his particular gift for simple words strung into a rosary of immense wisdom radiating immense kindness, Thich Nhat Hanh writes:.

Sources indicate that we have a great, habitual fear inside ourselves. We’re afraid of many things — of our own death, of losing our loved ones, of change, of being alone. The practice of mindfulness helps us to touch nonfear. It’s only here and now that we can experience total relief, total happiness… In the practice of Buddhism, we see that all mental formations — including compassion, love, fear, sorrow, and despair — are organic in nature. We don’t need to be afraid of any of them, because transformation is always possible.

Such transformation is possible only through deliberate practice — none more challenging, or more rewarding, than the practice of transforming fear into love. In consonance with his teaching that “to love without knowing how to love wounds the person we love,” he anchors this transmutation practice in four mantras “effective for watering the seeds of happiness in yourself and your beloved and for transforming fear, suffering, and loneliness.”.

Sources indicate that unlike a prayer — which channels a hope at some imagined entity capable of interceding in favor of that hope and has only as a side benefit (though arguably its only real and robust benefit) the psychological self-clarification that comes from honing our hopes in language — a mantra is not addressed at anything or anyone external and is entirely devoted to distilling the object of hope to its clearest essence. This, in and of itself, transforms the hope into an intent, making it more actionable — but also saving it from the particular complacency against which Descartes admonished as he considered the vital relationship between fear and hope. A mantra is therefore not a form of magical thinking, for while there is a sense of magic to how such distillation seems to shift the situation by its very utterance, it is an entirely practical sort of magic, for a mantra simply clarifies, concentrates, and consecrates intent, and all meaningful transformation springs from purposeful, devoted intent.

A mantra is a kind of magic formula that, once uttered, can entirely change a situation. It can change us, and it can change others. But this magic formula must be spoken in concentration, with body and mind focused as one. What you say in this state of being becomes a mantra.

Within this conceptual framework, he offers four mantras for transforming fear into love, beginning with “Mantra for Offering Your Presence.” A generation after Simone Weil insisted that “attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity,” he writes:.

The most precious gift you can give to the one you love is your true presence. So the first mantra is very simple: “Dear one, I am here for you.”.

Simple though this mantra might seem, he reminds us that actually cultivating the capacity for it — the capacity for presence, which is where our capacity for love resides — is intensely difficult against the tidal wave of demand and distraction that sweeps everyday life and sweeps us along with it, leaving us always on the brink of drowning, bereft of what Emerson celebrated as “the power to swell the moment from the resources of our own heart until it supersedes sun & moon & solar system in its expanding immensity.”.

A century after Tolstoy insisted that “love is a present activity only,” Thich Nhat Hanh gently reminds us that the greatest resource of our own heart — our greatest source of power, our mightiest antidote to fear — is the quality of love we give through the quality of our presence:.

When you love someone, the best thing you can offer that person is your presence. How can you love if you are not there? Come back to yourself, look into [their] eyes, and say, “Darling, you know something? I’m here for you.” You’re offering [them] your presence. You’re not preoccupied with the past or the future; you are there for your beloved. You must say this with your body and with your mind at the same time, and then you will see the transformation.

Such crystalline presence is the prerequisite for the next mantra — “Mantra for Recognizing Your Beloved”:.

The second mantra is, “Darling, I know you are there, and I am so happy.”.

Recent findings suggest that to be there is the first step, and recognizing the presence of the other person is the second step. Because you are fully there, you recognize that the presence of your beloved is something very precious. You embrace your beloved with mindfulness, and he or she will bloom like a flower. To be loved means first of all to be recognized as existing.

In a sentiment of especial relevance and consolation in these disembodied times, he reminds us that these mantras can be performed across distance, across wires and cables and screens, not requiring the physical presence of the beloved — however they are articulated, they are at bottom meditations containing all four elements of true love as described by the Buddha: love, compassion, joy, and freedom.

While the third mantra, “Mantra for Relieving Suffering,” could be magnified and deepened by the atomic rewards of Thich Nhat Hanh’s “hugging meditation,” it too can be extended across the digital distance:.

Even before you do anything to help, your wholehearted presence already brings some relief, because when we suffer, we have great need for presence of the person we love. If we are suffering and the person we love ignores us, we suffer more. So what you can do — right away — is to manifest your true presence to your beloved and say the mantra with all your mindfulness: “Dear one, I know you are suffering. That is why I am here for you.” And already your loved one will feel better.

Recent findings suggest that your presence is a miracle, your understanding of his or her pain is a miracle, and you are able to offer this aspect of your love immediately. Really try to be there, for yourself, for life, for the people you love. Recognize the presence of those who live in the same place as you, and try to be there when one of them is suffering, because your presence is so precious for this person.

The fourth and final mantra, “Mantra for Reaching Out to Ask for Help,” seems on the surface to be self-concerned, but is in fact the crucible of self-care from which all unselfish love and presence spring. It is also, Thich Nhat Hanh observes, the most difficult of the four, for it dwells in the place of our greatest vulnerability and at the same time pushes us to lean on our most crippling crutch:.

This mantra is for when you are suffering and you believe that your beloved has caused you suffering. If someone else had done the same wrong to you, you would have suffered less. But this is the person you love the most, so you suffer deeply, and the last thing you feel like doing is to ask that person for help… So now it is your pride that is the obstacle to reconciliation and healing. According to the teaching of the Buddha, in true love there is no place for pride.

When you are suffering like this, you must go to the person you love and ask for his or her help. That is true love. Do not let pride keep you apart. You must overcome your pride. You must always go to him or her. That is what this mantra is for. Practice for yourself first, to bring about oneness of your body and mind before going to the other person to say the fourth mantra: “Dear one, I am suffering; please help.” This is very simple but very hard to do.

Complement this particular fragment of the wholly soul-salving Fear: Essential Wisdom for Getting Through the Storm with Seneca on overcoming fear and Audre Lorde on turning fear into fire, then revisit the great Buddhist teacher Pema Chödrön on transformation through difficult times.

Tech Report: How to Have Enough: Wendell Berry on Creativity and Love

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (816 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that “Enough is so vast a sweetness, I suppose it never occurs, only pathetic counterfeits,” Emily Dickinson sighed in one of her love letters to Susan an epoch before Kurt Vonnegut, in a short and lovely poem, distilled happiness to the knowledge that you have enough.
  • Against this backdrop, to take a sabbath is a radical act, an act of countercultural courage and resistance, none more radical than a sabbath taken in nature — that eternal pasture of enoughness, which knew from the outset to create just enough more matter than antimatter for the first small seed of something to bloom into everything; which knows daily to make everything, from the electron to the elephant, take up just as much space and energy as it needs to be exactly what it is; which made every life finite and set a limit even to the speed of light.
  • To be in nature, without doing, is to be reminded that we are nature, too; that we cannot force the creative force that made us; that we need not keep breaking our own hearts on expectation’s cold hard edge of not-enough.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that “Enough is so vast a sweetness, I suppose it never occurs, only pathetic counterfeits,” Emily Dickinson sighed in one of her love letters to Susan an epoch before Kurt Vonnegut, in a short and lovely poem, distilled happiness to the knowledge that you have enough. It is not an easy knowledge to live with amid the commodified counterfeits of happiness that light up these sunset days of Western civilization, with its mesmerism of maximums and its cult of more, materially and spiritually — capitalism goads us to do more in order to own more while the secular church of self-improvement goads us to be more in order to do more.

Against this backdrop, to take a sabbath is a radical act, an act of countercultural courage and resistance, none more radical than a sabbath taken in nature — that eternal pasture of enoughness, which knew from the outset to create just enough more matter than antimatter for the first small seed of something to bloom into everything; which knows daily to make everything, from the electron to the elephant, take up just as much space and energy as it needs to be exactly what it is; which made every life finite and set a limit even to the speed of light.

To be in nature, without doing, is to be reminded that we are nature, too; that we cannot force the creative force that made us; that we need not keep breaking our own hearts on expectation’s cold hard edge of not-enough.

The poet, farmer, and wise elder Wendell Berry, who once defined wisdom as “the art of minimums,” takes up these immense and intimate questions throughout his wonderful collection This Day (public library) — his series of sabbath poems composed between 1979 and 2013, celebrating the sabbath as a “rich and demanding” idea that “gains in meaning as it is brought out-of-doors and into a place where nature’s principles of self-sustaining wholeness and health are still evident,” a place where “the natural and the supernatural, the heavenly and the earthly, the soul and the body, the wondrous and the ordinary, all appear to occur together in the one fabric of creation.”.

In the preface, Berry considers how nature calibrates expectation — even in the creative act itself, where inspiration is not a reach for more but a letting be of what is, a surrender to reality, which is miracle enough:.

Industry observers note that on Sunday mornings I often attend a church in which I sometimes sat with my grandfather, in which I sometimes sit with my grandchildren, and in which my wife plays the piano. But I am a bad-weather churchgoer. When the weather is good, sometimes when it is only tolerable, I am drawn to the woods on the local hillsides or along the streams… In such places, on the best of these sabbath days, I experience a lovely freedom from expectations — other people’s and also my own. I go free from the tasks and intentions of my workdays, and so my mind becomes hospitable to unintended thoughts: to what I am very willing to call inspiration. The poems come incidentally or they do not come at all. If the Muse leaves me alone, I leave her alone. To be quiet, even wordless, in a good place is a better gift than poetry.

Sources indicate that in how it thrives on the freedom from expectation, in how it demands a total surrender and breaks the moment it is demanded of, creativity has a lot in common with love. It may be that nature invented love to teach us the art of enoughness — to learn how to open the heart to another without condition or expectation, to be fully welcomed in another heart in order to learn the hardest axiom of being: that we are, and always were, enough.

Love’s salutary alchemy of enoughness comes alive in the second part of Berry’s eight-part sabbath poem of 1994:.

Finally will it not be enough, after much living, after much love, after much dying of those you have loved, to sit on the porch near sundown with your eyes simply open, watching the wind shape the clouds into the shapes of clouds?

Even then you will remember the history of love, shaped in the shapes of flesh, ever-changing as the clouds that pass, the blessed yearning of the body for body, unending light. You will remember, watching the clouds, the future of love.

According to recent reports, couple with John J. Plenty and Fiddler Dan — a lovely vintage illustrated fable about the meaning and measure of enough — then revisit this soulful animated adaptation of Berry’s poem “The Peace of Wild Things” and his prose meditation on the nature of the universe lensed through a sunflower.

#270. Are Your Dating Standards Too High?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1008 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Are Your Dating Standards Too High?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • Here's something that you never see on social media: men accusing women of having dating standards that are too high.
  • Recent findings suggest that umm, not exactly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

Here's something that you never see on social media: men accusing women of having dating standards that are too high. Yep, that's never happened. Neither has women accusing men of the same. In fact, no one of any gender has ever accused anyone else of such things, right?

Recent findings suggest that umm, not exactly. Anytime someone posts something about having certain dating requirements—unless it's something irrefutable like "I would like someone human"—it's not too surprising to see responses like "you are being unrealistic," "you are too high-maintenance," "no wonder you are single," or "look at yourself." Then the person may fire back with something like "Well, sorry for having standards," and then back and forth it goes.

In a recent development, the question then is where you fall on the whole "got to have some kind of standards" to "being unrealistic" spectrum. That ranges from people who clearly should lower their standards—because a supermodel may not want to date a guy who spends all his days in pajamas posting about red pills on Reddit—to those who actually should raise their standards. Well, here are some signs that your standards may be too high:.

If your standards focus on superficial things like looks, then it could be impeding your looking for a partner. For example, a 2020 survey by Pew Research Center found that 15% of respondents “Definitely/probably would not” date someone of a different race/ethnicity—which could end up ruling out lots of people who could be great fits from personality and values standpoints. The same might happen when you base your standards around hair (beyond asking that it be washed occasionally), clothes (with the possible exception of ruling out those who wear a hazmat suit all the time), and other stuff that in the long run won't matter that much for a relationship.

In a recent development, many superficial things like looks, hobbies, and fame can change with time—as could your perception and feelings about them. So, be careful about anchoring your preferences on something that may be fleeting versus enduring—especially since the enduring stuff is what often becomes most endearing.

Beware of sticking rigidly to any rules such as the so-called "6-6-6 rule" that I detailed before for "A Funny Bone to Pick." If you are completely unwilling to consider anyone who's a bit under any of the sixes—height, salary, or abs—ask yourself why. Otherwise, you could end up like the guy I knew who specified that his wife needed to look a certain way, speak at least five languages, and have certain types of degrees, but kind of neglected putting "kind" and "loyal" on that list. Guess what ended up happening?

Sources indicate that the "6-6-6 rule" is just one example of a standard that you may have heard from elsewhere and then adopted it without really thinking why. Using standards set by others may make others—like fake friends, advertisers, politicians, and Hollywood execs—happy. But what about you?

Recent findings suggest that of course, don't summarily reject all suggestions from others—especially when those who are close to and care about you tell you repeatedly that your standards are too high. That includes your therapist, whom you are presumably paying to care about you.

Sources indicate that another potential sign is when dates for you have been about as rare as Halley's Comet sightings. Sure, there may be legit reasons for your dry spell—such as a lack of singles or diversity around you. But what exactly is keeping you from dating the single Halley, who's already expressed interest in you?

A flip-side of this sign is treating dating like casting calls for the next James Bond or Wonder Woman—where you go through a ton of first looks but very, very few second looks. You may believe that dating is a numbers game in some ways. But too exacting standards may be wasting a number of people's time.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of numbers, how about those social media posts that use census data to calculate the actual chances of meeting someone based on your dating standards? Or calculators like the one from Keeper? These may be rough calculations, but they can show how rough things may be for you—especially when your probabilities of success dip below 1%.

It has been revealed that it's a bad sign if you've never, ever seen anywhere on Earth anything that comes close to what your standards indicate. And someone from Middle Earth, a persona portrayed by some celebrity, or any other fantasy character doesn't count. Reality is a lot messier. So, use the successful pairings around you, instead, to help benchmark what's possible.

According to recent reports, remember, too, that your standards should be based in part on what you presently offer in return. If you yourself aren't loyal and haven't yet gone through an emotional healing journey, then, maybe, just maybe, you can't expect the same out of others. And remember each demand of yours demands more trade-offs from you. If, for example, you want someone driven to achieve boatloads of money and high social status, expect to play second fiddle to that person—or maybe even third or fourth fiddle.

Finally, check how well your standards match what truly would be a match for you. Will your criteria help or hurt your chances of finding someone with a personality and core values that fit well with yours? If, for example, a primary interest of yours is finding someone who will be very loyal, then maybe being super rich and having a hot, hot, hot body shouldn't be such absolute criteria. You could remove at least one of the "hots" from there.

Ultimately, it is important to have standards. But they do have to stand—stand the test of time and really stand for who you are. If not, you might end up with someone you simply cannot stand.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know that the price of life is death, that the price of love is loss, and still you watch the golden afternoon light fall on a face you love, knowing that the light will soon fade, knowing that the loving face too will one day fade to indifference or bone, and you love anyway — because life is transient but possible, because love alone bridges the impossible and the eternal.

I think about this and a passage from Louise Erdrich’s 2005 novel The Painted Drum (public library) flits across the sky of my mind:.

Life will break you. Nobody can protect you from that, and living alone won’t either, for solitude will also break you with its yearning. You have to love. You have to feel. It is the reason you are here on earth. You are here to risk your heart. You are here to be swallowed up. And when it happens that you are broken, or betrayed, or left, or hurt, or death brushes near, let yourself sit by an apple tree and listen to the apples falling all around you in heaps, wasting their sweetness. Tell yourself that you tasted as many as you could.

It has been revealed that this, of course, is what life evolved to be — an aria of affirmation rising like luminous steam from the cold dark silence of an indifferent cosmos that will one day swallow all of it. Every living thing is its singer and its steward — something the poetic paleontologist Loren Eiseley captures with uncommon poignancy in his 1957 essay “The Judgment of the Birds,” found in his altogether magnificent posthumous collection The Star Thrower (public library).

According to recent reports, eiseley recounts resting beneath a tree after a day of trekking through fern and pine needles collecting fossils, dozing off in the warm sunlight, then being suddenly awakened by a great commotion to see “an enormous raven with a red and squirming nestling in his beak” perching on a crooked branch above. He writes:.

Into the glade fluttered small birds of half a dozen varieties drawn by the anguished outcries of the tiny parents. No one dared to attack the raven. But they cried there in some instinctive common misery, the bereaved and the unbereaved. The glade filled with their soft rustling and their cries. They fluttered as though to point their wings at the murderer. There was a dim intangible ethic he had violated, that they knew. He was a bird of death. And he, the murderer, the black bird at the heart of life, sat on there, glistening in the common light, formidable, unmoving, unperturbed, untouchable. The sighing died. It was then I saw the judgment. It was the judgment of life against death. I will never see it again so forcefully presented. I will never hear it again in notes so tragically prolonged. For in the midst of protest, they forgot the violence. There, in that clearing, the crystal note of a song sparrow lifted hesitantly in the hush. And finally, after painful fluttering, another took the song, and then another, the song passing from one bird to another, doubtfully at first, as though some evil thing were being slowly forgotten. Till suddenly they took heart and sang from many throats joyously together as birds are known to sing. They sang because life is sweet and sunlight beautiful. They sang under the brooding shadow of the raven. In simple truth they had forgotten the raven, for they were the singers of life, and not of death.

Couple with Hannah Arendt on love and how to live with the fundamental fear of loss, then revisit Loren Eiseley on the warblers and the wonder of being.

#268. Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
